An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was found to be 1.440 picoseconds by employing two methods with varying degrees of uncertainty, specifically 0.096 (statistical) ± 0.008 (systematic) ± 0.003 (model-based). This result tightens existing limits on a similar quantity by factors of at least 10 and also sets an minimum lifetime of 1.256 picoseconds with a confidence level of 95%. Furthermore, this research also provides an early estimate of the $B^0_s$ meson's proper lifetime at 1.280 picoseconds with a confidence level of 68%. Both figures are in line with theoretical predictions made before the discovery of $B^0_s$ mesons. Additionally, this research constrains the ratio of $B^0_s$ to $B^0$ decay times to be greater than 1.3 with a confidence level of 95%. 

Note: Almost contemporaneously with ATLAS, a similar study by this collaboration produced a more precise result with a different method, specifically 1.440 ± 0.096 (statistical) ± 0.008 (systematic) ± 0.003 (model-based) picoseconds.

To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. In this study, a high-speed optical transmission system is demonstrated, achieving a data rate of 72Gbit/s using the on-off keying technique, over a distance of 18.8km in a South China Sea submarine cable that lacks dispersion compensation.  Chromatic dispersion in this underwater cable causes four signal nulls in a 36GHz bandwidth, severely hindering BER performance. To address this issue, a decision feedback equalizer was initially applied with satisfactory results, however its effectiveness was impeded due to the occurrence of burst errors resulting from unpredictable marine conditions. To mitigate this issue, a weighted DFE method was developed but proved insufficient as it was unable to fully compensate for the spectral distortions due to the limited scope of its feedback symbols. To address these limitations, the introduction of maximum likelihood sequence estimation after WDFE proved capable of both rectifying the spectral distortions and providing optimal detection, ultimately yielding a maximum 2.9dB enhancement in signal quality and eliminating BER floors, thereby providing a viable solution for mitigating the detrimental effects of burst-error propagation in fiber-optic communications systems. This technique was successfully field-tested over the extended 18.8km underwater cable link. To further validate its effectiveness, the system was subjected to various burst-error scenarios resulting from artificial distortion, alongside two other scenarios involving actual marine conditions, all of which showed significant improvements in signal quality, confirming the practical viability of this technique in tackling the complex challenge of burst-error propagation in fiber-optic communications over ocean cables. To better understand the potential for application, the technical advantages of this method are highlighted in comparison to other advanced equalization techniques such as maximum likelihood sequence estimation and blind equalization methods.  To facilitate easier implementation, a step-by-step protocol is provided detailing how this method can be effectively employed to restore distorted signal quality in real-world fiber-optic communications over ocean cables.  To facilitate the adoption of this technique in practical applications, a theoretical analysis of its performance is conducted, along with the derivation of an accurate metric for evaluating the spatial distortion profile, alongside two concrete examples that demonstrate the optimal selection of key system parameters, providing a clear roadmap for the successful deployment of this technology in a variety of fiber-optic communications scenarios.  To address any potential limitations with the method, research into the application of machine learning techniques such as deep learning has been initiated, with first indications suggesting it may hold the key to further breakthroughs, not least in tackling the persistent challenge of three-dimensional cross-space distortion, a complex issue that remains to be fully addressed.

Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy. Our method has far-reaching implications for various time-series modeling techniques that incorporate TCNs and their extensions. We've introduced an open-source implementation of our technique called Pruning In Time (PIT) that can be applied to a broader class of temporal graph convolution networks. We've demonstrated the efficacy of PIT by achieving state-of-the-art performance in several time-series classification and forecasting tasks. The source code of our experiments and the Pruning In Time model is now available at https://github.com/amirzanjani/pruning-in-time. Dilation-aware weight-pruning has also been recognized as a superior alternative to the conventional technique of using recurrent models for sequence processing. Our method has inspired a new line of research that was recently introduced at ICLR 2021 under the name Dilated Learning via Pruning (DLIP. We've further explored an extension of our initial idea that involves applying a reverse process to recover the original dilation factors from the pruned version. This reverse procedure involves treating each channel of the pruned TCN as a single input to a causal convolutional layer with a time-dilated filter. We've successfully applied this technique to the classification of long-time series data. However, this reverse procedure is computationally expensive and results in a model that is only half as efficient as our initial technique. Nonetheless, our method still achieves a significant compactness efficiency in deep TCNs. We've also investigated an alternative to our weight-pruning approach called input-pruning of TCNs, that involves pruning the input series instead of the network weights. This alternative technique obtains a more compact model but one that is less efficient in practice. Nonetheless, it holds great potential for applications where the input series is relatively short, such as speech processing. We've introduced an enhanced version of our method that employs both weight-pruning and input-pruning simultaneously, resulting in an extremely efficient and compact model with minimal overlap between the weights and input features.

The unified correspondence theory leverages the algebraic and order theoretic underpinnings of Sahlqvist correspondence to offer versatile tools for correspondence and canonicity across diverse semantic frameworks and signatures. These tools, specifically tailored to logics whose semantics rely on normal lattice expansions (DLEs), enable computation of first-order correspondents for inductive formulas using the algorithm ALBA. Conversely, our proposed method effectively employs ALBA's rules and algebraic language to reverse its computations in the DLE setting, thereby allowing the derivation of an inductive formula from its first-order correspondent. This reverse approach is also shown to preserve the algebraic language's properties, thereby ensuring that the obtained inductive formula is equivalent in essence to the original. This resulting correspondence technique is both automated and efficient, relying on parametric techniques similar to those employed in the ALBA algorithm. We explore applications of this inverse correspondence for Sahlqvist theories by demonstrating how it may be used to establish connections between different DLEs and logics, thus providing a unifying framework that may be employed across a broad range of semantic frameworks and signatures. This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the veracity of data tuples, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to Four-valued logic and data merging. Additionally, we provide an original solution to query validation and contrast it with existing data repair approaches. With an emphasis on theoretical aspects, our work has implications for practicing database designers but does not offer concrete guidelines on designing databases with missing values and functional dependencies.

This study presents a novel dynamic econometric model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates, specifically designed to analyze and forecast count-based time series data. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. To evaluate the TV-PARX model's performance and forecasting capabilities in real-world scenarios, we conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations. Additionally, we have applied the time-varying specification of the TV-PARX model to empirical data sets, analyzing new daily COVID-19 cases in Italy and corporate defaults in the US. Our findings show that the time-varying TV-PARX model outperforms constant-parameter competitors in most cases, indicating that forecasting based on external variables can benefit from incorporation of structural changes. The R package tvparx, supporting flexible estimation and forecasting of time-varying models, has also been developed and is available for download. 
  The time-varying nature of time series data poses significant challenges to accurate forecasting, and our research indicates that modeling data sets with external influences and varying dynamics results in substantially improved performance. This advantage can be leveraged across all forecasting metrics and is particularly beneficial in long-term forecasting applications.  With the growing recognition of score-driven approaches as valuable tools and the development of the time-varying TV-PARX model, it is now possible to incorporate features such as external covariates and time-varying parameters to achieve optimal results.  Due to its flexibility and the ease with which it can be implemented using the tvparx R package, the time-varying TV-PARX model is now a go-to alternative for researchers and practitioners working with count-based time series data sets.  As a result of our analysis, we recommend exploring time-varying models as a way to enhance forecasting performance.  Although there are some limitations to the TV-PARX model, including the relatively small sample size required for parameter estimation and the complexity inherent in modeling data sets with external influences and varying dynamics, our research provides a clear path forward for addressing these challenges. category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison
method relying on 2D descriptors. The code is available at https://github.com
__/__mit-atlas/Neural-Desc-Fields. The atlas dataset used in training and
tests is also open-sourced. It comprises categories like mugs, bowls, and boxes,
with over 1500 3D models, and includes video recordings of 75 actors that we
use to generate NDFs through self-supervised learning. The dataset can be found
at https://github.com/__mit-atlas/atlas. The NDF implementation is built upon
the Detect-Truncated-Sphere module from CogMap, introduced by Zhang et al. in
2020. We demonstrate that simpler baselines, like concatenating descriptor features
directly, yield poorer performance. Additionally, we explore applications like
path planning and execution, and find that poses resulting in collision-free paths

We performed the first in-depth analysis of seven red giant members in the globular cluster Tononzintla 2. We used the APOGEE-2 near-infrared spectra to examine the abundance levels of multiple chemical species in these stars. Despite the numerous contributions made so far, the ever-expanding nature of the archive still poses certain challenges: locating specific content has become increasingly difficult, making it essential to prioritize reuse and clarity of comprehension. This thesis proposal outlines my research objectives, which focus on these concerns, as well as initial findings, which reveal that the Isabelle Archive exhibits characteristics typical of scale-free networks, as evidenced by the distribution of node in-degrees in its dependency graph. This observation suggests that a power-law relationship between the importance of a piece of content and the number of other related topics it covers can be exploited. Building upon this insight, I plan to investigate effective strategies for optimizing the organization of the Isabelle Archive, with a goal of refining the understanding of the relationship between relevance and connectivity. Additionally, I aim to explore potential avenues for enhancing the readability of proofs by identifying locations with the greatest impact on comprehension, as well as to examine the possibility of leveraging the Isabelle Archive's structure to inform the development of more effective tools for searching and navigating the archive. A key aspect of this research will involve collaborating with the Isabelle Archive curators to ensure that any findings and resulting improvements reflect the needs and preferences of the community. Specifically for QCD's relevant universality classes in three dimensions, we have determined $|z_c|/R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ to be approximately 1.607, 1.589 for $N=2, 4$ respectively. In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish whether a basic optimization method on a non-convex function can eventually enter a region where the function becomes locally convex. To address this, we developed an inequality that enables us to analyze the properties of the optimization landscape surrounding the solutions produced by an approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm. Specifically, we applied our inequality to demonstrate the local convexity of a particular TAP free energy function, which is relevant to the Z2 synchronization problem and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. Additionally, our inequality led to a confirmation of a previous conjecture regarding the efficiency of a sampling algorithm in the "easy" regime of these models. Furthermore, our inequality established a bound on the distortion incurred by a particular encoding process, which may be of independent interest. The techniques we employed, such as the application of a recent inequality due to Sudakov and Fernique, also resulted in a more efficient proof of the local convexity of the TAP free energy than our previous approach. This report outlines a deep learning approach known as the Electron Correlation
Potential Neural Network (eCPNN), which can learn simplified potential functions
that accurately capture the intricate instantaneous relationships among electrons
within complex atomic systems. Trained in an unsupervised manner with constrained
data derived from Full Configuration Interaction one-electron density functions, the
eCPNN model effectively predicts total atomic energies with remarkable precision. For
a diverse set of 29 atoms across the first three rows of the periodic table, the
eCPNN's predictive accuracy is essentially flawless, with an average energy error of
less than 0.0005 Hartree. Furthermore, the model exhibits impressive insight into
electron spatial organization, accurately mapping key features of density and momentum
space as compared to renowned benchmark references. As a result, the eCPNN offers a
promising pathway to a universal electron correlation framework, potentially enabling
the prediction of molecular properties with similar precision. To facilitate further
research, the eCPNN model, along with its training procedures and correlation
potentials, is made openly available for the benefit of the scientific community. 
In addition, the report includes feedback from two anonymous reviewers. 

Abstract:

We describe a novel unsupervised learning approach to represent the instantaneous
electron correlations within complex atomic systems. This approach is based on a
simple neural network that is trained to capture the underlying structure of one-electron
density functions, derived from highly accurate Full Configuration Interaction data.
As a result, this model is capable of predicting atomic energies with great precision.
Furthermore, it accurately models the spatial organization of electrons, including
their density and momentum space behavior, compared to renowned benchmark references.
Interestingly, this model is able to accurately map the correlations between electrons
without being trained on actual energy values, allowing it to provide fresh insights
into the underlying physics of these systems. To facilitate further research, we
openly share the model, along with its training procedures and correlation potentials.
In addition, we include constructive feedback from two anonymous reviewers that we hope
will be beneficial for the scientific community.

We have serendipitously identified a massive arc-like structure, dubbed a Giant Arc, which lies at a redshift of approximately 0.8. Spanning nearly 1 billion light-years, this feature exhibits remarkable symmetry when viewed from space. It was discovered through a novel approach using intervening magnesium-absorbing systems in the light from background quasars. Our analysis leverages a range of techniques: hierarchical clustering, a statistical test, and power spectrum analysis - each method providing unique insights, which together suggest the presence of a massive structure at around 4.5 to 4.8 sigma confidence levels. We employed multiple statistical tests to mitigate any biases that could influence our findings, which suggest that the arc-like feature is an overdensity with a density ratio of about 1.3, with a 30% margin of error. The Giant Arc represents one of the largest and most intriguing examples of a massive cosmic structure that could challenge the cosmological principle underpinning our current understanding of the universe. It may be an early stage in the formation of a massive structure, such as the Sloan Great Wall, which would have emerged around halfway through the universe's age. It is possible that this feature is collapsing under its own gravity, which could have implications for the distribution of absorbing systems along quasar lines of sight. It is also possible that this structure is related to a vast sheet-like formation, which could be aimed directly at our line of sight to quasars, particularly those observed in the direction of the constellations of Centaurus and the Southern Wing of Scorpius. It is essential that future observations, such as those with the Giant Metrology Mission, which will be capable of analyzing the composition of gas within these absorbing systems, are conducted to further understand this feature's implications. While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions. Additionally, we developed a new statistical approach to handle the detection of narrow light rays and implemented a more sophisticated evaluation of the atmospheric conditions using temperature and humidity data measured simultaneously with the aerosol depth, resulting in further improvement of the precision to 0.0086. Nevertheless, the precision of the aerosol depth determination still lags behind that of direct sun photometry. To overcome this limitation, we are upgrading the telescope system to measure the aerosol depth and incorporating a direct sun photometry system, and the new approach we developed can also be applied to this combination. Furthermore, the time resolution and altitude range of this technique make it ideal for detecting changes in the aerosol depth below 1 km over time scales of minutes. Consequently, the new approach we developed will allow us to tackle a wide range of scientific questions related to aerosols. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. The source code is available online at https://github.com/zwang84/DeepHMap++. Furthermore, our model has been uploaded to Model Zoo. Additionally, the tutorial video can be found at https://yewenwang.github.io/3d-pose-estimation-tutorial/. The framework has been found to perform well on real-world applications and has been integrated into popular 3D detection frameworks including CenterNet 3D and FuseFuse. It has also been applied in various competitions and has achieved top ranks. Literature review reveals that direct methods based on feature extraction from descriptor-based methods fail to achieve satisfactory results due to the low dimensionality of feature descriptors. In contrast, CNN-based direct methods can achieve high accuracy but at the cost of computing expensive global optimization techniques such as gradient descent. Furthermore, these methods cannot be applied to video pose estimation due to the limitations of optimizing pose parameters for each frame. In contrast, two-stage pipelines allow for the application of pose estimation in video frames. Peridynamic theories have seen a significant expansion in recent years, being applied to solve various complex problems that pose difficulties for conventional methods, particularly those involving discontinuities, fractures, and material degradation. This family of models is built on a unique concept, the bond function, which reflects the connection and interaction between neighboring points. The bond-based peridynamic model, characterized by integral-type constitutive equations, has demonstrated its strength in tackling problems involving nonlocality, long-range influence, and memory effects. Despite its success, the bond-based model still faces challenges, such as determining the correct measure independence, overcoming numerical issues with integral-type constitutive equations, and comparing PD models to other nonlocal models and theories. Recent efforts to develop PD-based theories for porous media and fluids have also highlighted the necessity of re-examining the bond-based model's constitutive equations. Furthermore, the introduction of Lagrange multipliers to handle constraints within the PD framework offers both opportunities and challenges. The extension of PD to fluid-dynamics is not merely a theoretical problem, but also has practical applications, such as the modeling of fluids with memory effects and the description of material degradation in fluids. Therefore, the PD approach may be a powerful tool for solving a wide range of problems in fluid-dynamics. However, a comprehensive understanding of the model's potential and limitations in this field is yet to be achieved. This article provides an in-depth review of the state-of-the-art in bond-based peridynamic models, exploring their applications, the issues they raise, and the opportunities for further development, particularly in the context of fluid-dynamics. Additionally, the article proposes potential solutions to some of the challenges faced by the bond-based model and highlights the necessity of further research in this field. Furthermore, the article is a result of the BioMechX 2019 workshop on bond-based peridynamic models, where participating researchers shared their work and engaged in lively discussions, culminating in the creation of this survey on bond-based peridynamic models. The article's content reflects the expertise of the workshop's participating researchers, consisting of distinguished academics and professionals in the field of mechanics and applied mathematics. By utilizing the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, recent studies found that the methods' accuracy could be evaluated in terms of the impact of the step size on configurational averaging. Results showed that for harmonic oscillators, some methods yield precise configurational averages, potentially leading to better performance in biomolecular simulations, especially in cases where bond stretches play a crucial role. Through the analysis of alanine dipeptide simulations, both with and without solvent, higher precision was achieved with no decrease in computational efficiency, allowing for large time steps without compromising conformational exploration. However, these simulations start only shortly before the merger and require predetermined initial conditions to proceed. Therefore, a significant task involves identifying the appropriate configuration for the binary system and its environment at this point in the process. In our research, we've been investigating the behavior of dark matter in the vicinity of black hole binaries of equal mass, discovering a consistent, long-lasting profile that emerges over several orbits. Conversely, systems with greater dark matter mass see overdensities scattered due to the binary's motion. Furthermore, regardless of initial configurations, systems typically converge to the established profile after a certain number of orbits; this convergence often results in the emergence of undesirable, short-lived oscillations. It's also been found that if matter is directly overlaid onto a binary system, without properly considering the potential for matter to influence the binary's motion, this leads to inaccurately calculated orbital paths due to artificial factors, rather than a signature of dark matter at play. As such, further study is needed in order to allow a valid comparison of waveform patterns produced by simulations taking environmental factors into account, against their vacuum-based counterparts. As such, a key comparison remains for future study. Additionally, simulations should also consider how information about the surrounding environment can be extracted from waveform patterns produced by detections of binary black hole events, as this could provide a means by which to indirectly investigate the properties of dark matter in a system's surroundings.

We tackle the persistent issue of exponential stability for a stretched Euler-Bernoulli beam on a star-shaped graph with three equal branches. The outer points where these branches meet are fixed while rotating. The inner point is capable of moving in two ways, with rotational movement influenced by both elasticity and friction. A detailed analysis in a Hilbert space reveals how the spectrum's asymptotic behavior and the spectrum's structure contribute to exponential stability. It's demonstrated that only the second mode in each branch possesses the required property of asymptotic differentiability, which is not directly shared by the first mode. This discrepancy creates an inequality that leads to instability in the closest gap, resulting in modes at that gap becoming unstable as well. To counter this, we apply an transformation that distorts the spectrum, ultimately achieving the desired property of asymptotic differentiability in all modes and thus, exponential stability. The associated boundary damping operator becomes smoother, though, which is where this argument reaches its limitation, as it wouldn't be enough to ensure stability in similar scenarios with rotating outer points.  A numerical computation is also performed to validate the theoretical findings. To train this model, we utilize real-world camera data transformed into raw images through a realistic process, mimicking real-world camera functions. By doing so, we demonstrate the advantages of our single-stage model over traditional approaches combining demosaicking and deblurring modules, according to objective performance metrics. Additionally, our method is capable of removing a camera's intrinsic blurring effect, which effectively enables deblurring of sharper images from actual pictures. To enhance educational value, we provide visualizations of the internal processes of our demosaicking and deblurring stages. To make our approach even more effective, we integrate it with a state-of-the-art image denoiser, which further improves results under higher noise levels. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions. A preliminary analysis is conducted on how increased fluid density affects these middle-speed-range water-entry behaviors. Finally, our research extends our knowledge of these dynamics to spheres moving through not just water, but also other non-viscous fluids. Mobile device owners frequently require running sensitive security applications alongside unverified, potentially malicious software, which necessitates reliance on device hardware and system software to safely isolate threats. 

This often misplaced trust is the foundation on which our objective is built – namely to minimize the reliance on device hardware and software components for users to withstand cyber threats. 

We introduce an innovative multi-domain hardware setup consisting of isolated sections, where programs are partitioned statically to prevent malicious interaction. 

A few key hardware components with proven security functionality are integrated to grant secure temporary access to processing resources and external input/output interfaces simultaneously.

To manage these hardware components, we introduce OctopOS, a unique OS comprising several secure subsystems working together in distrust. 

We showcase a functioning prototype, incorporating our hardware and software, utilizing a combined CPU-FPGA board with an acceptable additional hardware expense in comparison to existing SoCs. 

We observe substantial reduction in trust requirements for security applications using our device, delivering better security performance compared to standard security architectures, with little performance impact for non-security programs, matching legacy system speeds. 

We also present Surveyor, an automated security framework operating on top of our system, capable of detecting and containing cyber breaches caused by malicious software. 

During evaluation of our complete security platform, with Surveyor enabled, against diverse malware, we record zero success rates for malware in evading detection and all contained breaches were minimized in trust. 

Furthermore, our device proves superior to standard security architectures and notable security hardening methods in our benchmark tests. 

Finally, we discuss potential improvements to our innovative hardware and software, along with potential adoption strategies for our device. 

We believe that our research provides valuable insights towards creating more secure, reliable mobile devices with lower trust requirements for securing cyber threats.

The adversary's influence is confined to no more than an $\epsilon$ fraction of all training episodes. Notably, this attack model surpasses previously considered methods. We established a key finding that no reinforcement learning algorithm can discover an optimal policy better than $O(\epsilon)$ under these circumstances. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Notably, our analysis reveals that states produced by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit the same characteristics when analyzing the distribution of photons. We thoroughly investigate the unique quantum properties of SPCCSs, including sub-Poisson statistics, anti-bunching effects, and quadrature squeezing. These findings demonstrate that SPCCSs possess abundant non-classical behavior, thereby conferring a quantum advantage for executing various technological tasks. Furthermore, we outline the applicability of these states in amplifying a weak coherent state, as well as in implementing quantum communication networks utilizing entangled states produced from beam splitters or paramometric amplifiers. The simplicity and scalability of quantum-optical catalysis make it an appealing method for generating complex non-classical states using basic quantum components. This approach can be employed to create various catalyzed states through adjustments to the catalytic device, its reflectivity, or the phase of the amplification process. Nonetheless, the success probabilities associated with producing these states generally remain below 50%, limiting their potential for amplifying weak states or generating entangled states from single photons. Nonetheless, these states exhibit exceptional performance when used as receive states in quantum communication protocols. Moreover, we propose a novel approach involving quantum relaying, which enables the conversion of SPCCSs to coherent states and thus amplifies the success probability associated with detecting these states. This process involves three components: a beam splitter, a photon detector, and a Kerr non-linearity, as well as a coherent state used as an "anti-catalyst." In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise solutions to Einstein's field equations. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. As a result, we derive the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism. Additionally, we provide an original derivation of the complex null tetrad basis expressions for the electric and magnetic components of the electromagnetic field, previously obtained by Newman and Penrose. We demonstrate how the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor are interconnected with the electromagnetic field's components in the Minkowski space basis. Furthermore, we express the square of the Weyl tensor operator as a complex first-order differential operator, facilitating the solution of complex self-dual electromagnetic fields. This, in turn, enables us to solve for the conformal curvature tensor's components, resulting in a direct link between the electromagnetic field and the conformal curvature tensor. We establish that a complex self-dual electromagnetic field induces a vacuum solution in spacetime; this connection provides a basis for future investigations aimed at breaking the restrictions of self-duality and satisfying the reality conditions, thereby expanding our understanding of spacetime's properties. Ultimately, this review showcases the power and versatility of the Newman-Penrose formalism in General Relativity. We hope this comprehensive explanation will serve as a valuable guide for researchers and students alike, providing a clear and concise path to solving complex differential equations associated with the Newman-Penrose methods. This new method incorporates a unique way of depicting polymers using monomers, new descriptors that capture their structure, and employs linear regression in the predictive framework. Computational trials have demonstrated that the proposed approach excels in predicting specific chemical properties in polymers, also successfully modeling compounds composed of up to 50 non-hydrogen atoms within a monomeric structure. Achieving optimal well placement and reducing costs necessitates real-time geosteering. This method determines parameters such as resistivity, density, and boundary locations along with their uncertainties by minimizing discrepancies between the measured well logging data and simulated results. Unlike existing approaches which rely on bilingual corpora for TM and employ source-side similarity searches, our proposed framework leverages monolingual data and retrieves memories in a cross-lingual manner. Notably, our framework offers two significant advantages: firstly, it enables vast amounts of monolingual data to be incorporated into TM; secondly, both the memory retriever and the NMT model can be jointly optimized for translation objectives. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method achieves substantial gains in performance and outperforms TM-augmented NMT baselines even when utilizing bilingual TM. Furthermore, our model's capacity to tap into monolingual data allows it to excel in low-resource and domain adaptation scenarios. This involves embedding both the source and target sentences in a single joint space to compute a cross-lingual similarity measure. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on multiple large datasets, utilizing ABIDE with 1,102 subjects and CATI-derived data with 9,037 participants for both training and assessment purposes. Our investigation concentrated on MRIQC preprocessing steps and assessed the pipeline's efficacy with and without these preprocessing methods. Further analysis examined site-specific and study-specific classification probabilities for models trained on ABIDE and CATI data without preprocessing. Our primary findings showed that using MRIQC features without preprocessing yielded the best results in models trained and evaluated on diverse, multi-center datasets with varying population characteristics. This led to an improvement in ROC-AUC scores on unseen data of 0.10 when using a subset of the CATI dataset. Nonetheless, models trained on diverse, heterogeneous populations showed questionable generalizability, as evident from site-specific and study-specific probability predictions and derived classification thresholds. These findings highlight the MRIQC pipeline's effectiveness on diverse, multi-center datasets but also highlight the limitations of generalizing models across diverse population characteristics. Our research underlines the significance of further optimizing and evaluating MRIQC pipelines using diverse, multi-center datasets with varied demographic characteristics. Additionally, there is a need for more robust and diverse training datasets that represent the broader population characteristics, without compromising data quality, to develop reliable and efficient quality control pipelines. The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. Furthermore, we observed that spatial confinement of T centers within photonic crystal structures leads to enhanced T center densities at the node points, allowing for localized control of their optical interactions. These breakthroughs contribute significantly to the development of reliable and versatile devices that can efficiently interface photons with electronic spins, a crucial step towards the implementation of quantum communication networks. Thanks to our successful demonstration, the field now has a clear path towards optimizing device performance through combinations of ion implantation and heat treatment, ultimately enabling widespread production of high-quality T center containing SOI material. Additionally, we have introduced a novel technique for spatially localized creation of T centers within photonic integrated circuits, which provides remote host materials for the defects and allows for precise control over their optical properties. This innovation, combined with the already demonstrated functionality of the T centers, proves that they have the necessary properties to serve as efficient interfaces between photons and electronic spins. The high activity levels of M dwarfs present a significant challenge for discovering exoplanets, as their stellar activity masks the signals from these celestial bodies. This problem requires an effective method for filtering out the stellar activity from the data sets, especially when searching for habitable Earth-like planets. To achieve this goal, we conducted an analysis on how to optimise the line lists used for least-squares deconvolution to minimize the dispersion in RV data sets and thereby eliminate the stellar activity noise. Our research employs optical observations of the M dwarfs EV Lac, AD Leo and DS Leo to compare two approaches to selecting line lists, one based on line properties and the other using a randomised algorithm. The results show that the latter yields a significant >50% improvement in RV RMS reduction regardless of the activity level of the star. This new approach not only enhances the sensitivity of planet detection, but also allows the construction of line lists tailored to detect the stellar rotation period. Moreover, we were able to successfully recover the signals from synthetic planets despite the presence of moderate and high activity levels. This approach is currently applied to data sets for the detection of exoplanets around M dwarfs. For the case of Earth, the analysis indicates that the signal of Earth will be recovered when the data are processed in a way that takes into account the line list randomness over several consecutive nights. This technique is relevant to the present and near-future observational campaigns with the development of highly efficient instruments such as HIRES-Giant at 1.05$\mu$m that will collect a vast amount of data with low scatter. This is accomplished through the use of optical fibres that allow for the collection of a vast number of lines at once, thereby significantly reducing the scanning time. This approach, however, introduces a further pilot study on how to select the stellar line list for the withdrawal of information about the planetary signal. This study, in turn, reveals that using a line list that is similar to that of the solar spectrum reduces the RV scatter to a minimum. This finding provides a preliminary direction for the development of new line lists that are optimised for the detection of exoplanets. This is to be followed by a more in-depth analysis of the techniques that are being considered, including the application of neural networks to select the most informative lines to reduce the RV scatter. This paper presents a Wikipedia-based entity recommendation framework that utilizes an embedding approach, where the Wikipedia database is hierarchically divided into layered graphs to extract entity features and learn entity representations. By combining the extracted information with a lightweight ranking method, this framework effectively suggests related entities to users on Wikipedia. We evaluate our approach through both offline and real-world online tests, demonstrating that our embeddings and recommendations exhibit desirable quality and user engagement. Furthermore, this framework delivers entity recommendations in both English and non-English languages for the Yahoo! Knowledge Graph, where Wikipedia constitutes a fundamental subset. It is notable that this approach differs from existing recommendation methodologies by focusing on an open-domain scenario using Wikipedia, where entity descriptions may not always be descriptive. As a result, our approach relies on hierarchical graphs to extract entity relationships that underlie the Wikipedia structure. We divide the Wikipedia database into layered graphs based on category pages, where each graph represents a self-contained domain with interconnected entity pages. By extracting semantic signals from these graphs, we employ a multi-step embedding approach that results in entity representations reflecting their positions within the Wikipedia taxonomy. It is worth mentioning that Wikipedia's category-based structure poses both challenges and opportunities for entity recommendations. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. To address this issue, we introduce an enhanced version of the word2vec model, designed to separate the implicit distribution of co-occurring words from the explicit meanings of words. Our experiments demonstrate the advantages of this enhanced model in sentiment analysis and company name embedding, where the original word2vec model is found to be already quite effective, although it can be further improved with our new model. Our study provides a thorough mathematical examination of the word2vec model, highlighting its strengths and limitations, and lays out a blueprint for the design of future embedding methods. Initial findings from a measurement of the spin asymmetry of the top quark, 
relevant to the top quark's polarization, have been reported for events 
resulting from $t$-channel single top quark production. The data, derived from 
proton-proton collisions at 8 TeV and with a total luminosity of 19.7 fb^-1, 
included events characterized by an isolated muon. By comparing experimental 
data to theoretical models, the signal and background components were quantified, 
enabling a measurement of the differential cross-section of an angular observable 
correlated with the top quark's polarization, taking into account detection biases. 
The results revealed a spin asymmetry value of 0.26, with a 95% confidence interval, 
which does not differ significantly from the standard model's predicted value of 0.44. 
This value will be refined as the amount of data becomes greater. 
The present value corresponds to an upper limit to the real part of the top quark's 
electroweak matrix element at a 95% confidence interval of 0.19. 
This study employed a method that is applicable to other experiments.

We have conducted an in-depth examination of the correlated metallic state of LaNiO$_3$ using $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR within LaNiO$_3$/LaAlO$_3$ superlattices of varying bilayer thickness. Our spin-lattice relaxation studies in a 6.55 T magnetic field yielded distinct components, characterized by different temperature dependences in their recovery times, with one being temperature-linear and the other exhibiting more intricate temperature variation. These results demonstrate that the slow-recovering component is resistant to changes in LaNiO$_3$ layer thickness, while the fast-recovering component is significantly affected, displaying an opposing temperature dependence in thinner samples. This complex phenomenon is explored to identify its underlying cause. We propose that the slow-recovering component is associated with correlated metallic state shared by LaNiO$_3$ layers in different units of the superlattices, whereas the fast-recovering component originates from localized spin states within LaNiO$_3$ layers. Furthermore, we observe that the spin diffusion length in these superlattices exceeds 20 $\mu$m, underscoring the utility of $^8$Li $\beta$-detected NMR in investigating LaNiO$_3$-based materials. This knowledge is particularly valuable in understanding the physics of LaNiO$_3$ when it is part of heterostructures. Additionally, we have measured the temperature dependence of the $^8$Li NMR chemical shift in LaAlO$_3$, finding a linear relationship that serves as a reference point for future studies. For $f(R)$ gravity, MG-GLAM includes multiple variations that mimic distinct behaviors of these models and offers tailored algorithms to maintain speed and precision. The code excels at producing a broad spectrum of modified gravity simulations and offers significant computational benefits, outperforming existing N-body simulations by a factor of over a hundred while yielding accurate results for key cosmological metrics. MG-GLAM is suited for creating large sets of modified gravity simulations that can be utilized in mock galaxy catalogues and emulators for ongoing and future galaxy surveys. biology lab, WorkingWiki enables multiple users to work together on a range of
tasks by utilizing command-line tools to translate raw'source code' into desired outputs.

like R, Python, and C, and it boasts specialized tools for seamless LaTeX editing.

version control systems, and publishing platforms, WorkingWiki unlocks the
full potential of wiki-based collaboration, and its customizable'makefiles'
and modular architecture enable users to tailor and repurpose its functionality.

The unexplored nature of ultra-high energy photons and limitations of existing methods in identifying them prompt research on new approaches to simulation and observational strategies. One such approach, presented in this report, involves novel indicators to indirectly identify these photons by observing cosmic ray phenomena composed of spatially correlated air showers of multiple cosmic rays observed simultaneously. The proposed method relies on simulations of interactions between high-energy photons and the Sun's magnetic field, utilizing the PRESHOWER program with significant modifications. The expected outcome of these interactions includes the creation of cosmic ray ensembles consisting of extremely narrow and elongated cascades of secondary photons spanning the full cosmic ray energy spectrum. When entering the Earth's atmosphere, these cascades or their components might generate distinct walls of spatially correlated air showers, which could also occur even if the primary photons are not directed towards Earth. Furthermore, it is anticipated that the particle distributions within these multi-photon footprints will possess thicknesses of up to meters and extensions of up to hundreds of millions of kilometers, rendering them potentially observable with a collaborative global approach, incorporating re-evaluation of historical data and exceeding the capacity of even the largest cosmic ray observatories. Distributed storage systems rely on replication to enhance both performance and reliability, but ensuring low latency data access requires handling updates without prior coordination. Asynchronous updates inevitably lead to conflict resolution issues with concurrent changes. A specific technique addressing this challenge is the Conflict-free Replicated Data Type (CRDT). Despite existing CRDT designs' complexity and difficulty to adapt to other data types, there's a clear need for a design framework to facilitate creating new CRDTs with consistency. We propose the RWF, a Remove-Win design framework that utilizes a conflict-resolution approach to update conflicts, allowing its use across various data types. Through two practical applications using Redis, RWF showcases its effectiveness and performance in developing new CRDTs that can handle conflicts efficiently. By breaking down conflict resolution into three distinct categories and providing corresponding implementation strategies, RWF can handle update conflicts in replication systems. Furthermore, by standardizing conflict resolution strategies, RWF enables greater flexibility in system configuration, including the ability to switch between different conflict resolution strategies and even dynamic strategy changes that minimize latency. With Redis-4.0 as the testbed, RWF demonstrates that new data types built with its framework can achieve high performance levels, reducing latency and maximizing throughput. By designing a new data type for a distributed chat room system and thoroughly testing it with Emu, a large-scale distributed testbed, we validate that RWF-built data types can handle real-world applications with low latency and high throughput. With its clear and modular architecture, along with easily extensible features, the RWF framework serves as an ideal base for building other types of distributed data types. By providing a practical approach to resolving update conflicts, RWF enables the development of new replicable data types that can handle conflicts efficiently, thus making them suitable for any distributed system that requires real-time data accessibility. With its ease of extension and modification, the RWF framework is now available online at its official website. Additionally, we've open-sourced the Redis implementation of two new data types, such as set and counter, built using the RWF framework. By utilizing the PinYuan distributed storage framework and a suite of microbenchmarks, we validate that RWF can handle various scenarios, including quorum, single-type updates, and mixed-type updates. To further evaluate the performance of RWF under heavy loads and network latency, we've conducted a series of TPC-C-style benchmarks, with all results showing that RWF can handle updates with low latency and high throughput. We've developed a statistical approach to pinpoint relevant genomic elements, based on associations across the entire genome, by identifying patterns of influence in trait-associated SNPs. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. Moreover, to reconcile the total population of neutron star binaries with observed and radio pulsar populations within the Milky Way, researchers find that a significant majority of these binaries have recurrence times exceeding a century for outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope and most remain undiscovered. As a result, there is a large likelihood that all sources with outburst patterns similar to those exhibiting large amplitudes within the Milky Way actually contain neutron stars rather than black holes. Consequently, there is a relatively low chance of discovering a neutron star binary that exhibits bursting behavior and is located close to the Milky Way's center. This leads to an inference that any unreported outbursts from these sources within the region remain undetected, and as a result, the likelihood of finding an X-ray transient with a short recurrence time within the Milky Way's center is even lower, at less than 0.5%. Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, resulting from objects losing mass and experiencing extreme spin. This research was applied to model the development of sub-stellar objects. For the former, simulations showed distinct boundaries until about one-third of the mass was lost. For the latter, simulations demonstrated the star would eventually shed mass quickly, resulting in a smaller, rapidly spinning star. Deep neural network approaches have achieved great success in various AI tasks, particularly in image recognition tasks, yet some challenges remain unresolved. The issue of processing continuous visual data streams and dealing with unbalanced datasets in the learning process continues to persist. Past research has tackled these issues independently, despite their concurrent presence in real-world applications. In this work, we address the challenge of learning incrementally from datasets that are not only unbalanced but also grow over time. We examine algorithms that rely on fixed deep neural network architectures and employ bounded memory to retain examples from previously encountered classes throughout the learning process. Given the constraint of limited memory, older classes are learned from fewer examples compared to newer ones, further exacerbating the initial dataset imbalance. Consequently, a scoring bias emerges, favoring newer classes over older ones. We experiment with a comprehensive range of score calibration methods to counter this bias. The evaluation was conducted across three datasets, utilizing two scenarios representing varying degrees of dataset imbalance, and testing three distinct memory capacity constraints. The findings indicate that most calibration methods yield beneficial results, and their effectiveness is particularly pronounced when memory constraints are tighter – a scenario that holds practical relevance. Moreover, our research discovers that incorporating the usual distillation component into incremental learning algorithms is unnecessary. By removing it, a simplified fine-tuning approach emerges as a more robust foundation for tackling imbalanced incremental learning challenges. Reasoning about and sequencing unordered events is a crucial skill to understand real-world procedures, which often require grasping temporal common sense and incorporating various forms of information. Real-world procedures are commonly communicated through a combination of written text and visual aids. The ability to accomplish this task is essential for complex tasks like planning sequential tasks and summarizing instructional content from multiple sources. Although humans can easily understand and sequence unordered multimodal procedural instructions, the same cannot be said about current machine learning models. In our research, we assess the ability of machine learning models to understand and sequence unordered multimodal instructions by compiling datasets from widely-used instructional manuals and gathering extensive human feedback. Our findings show that these models not only perform much worse than humans but also struggle to efficiently use the information provided in both textual and visual forms. In an effort to enhance the performance of machines on this task, we introduce sequential-aware pretraining techniques that make use of the sequential connections present in both written text and visual aids, leading to significant improvements exceeding 5%. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that machine learning models require the ability to process temporal relationships and make use of the distinct characteristics of different modalities in order to accurately understand and sequence unordered multimodal procedural instructions. In addition to achieving better performance, our research introduces new challenges for the natural language processing community that revolve around the evaluation of sequential reasoning skills that rely on multiple sources of information and that are resistant to sequential aerosol attacks. We hope that our research will contribute to further exploring the possibilities of machine learning models that are capable of understanding the temporal aspects of unsorted events and that will one day be able to accomplish complex tasks like planning and task execution. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Moreover, our method displays robustness in the face of occlusions, which is further confirmed by a ablation study and in-depth analysis of our results. In particular, our method achieves superior metrics to state-of-the-art techniques like JigSaW and RFL on the Florence dataset, achieving a notable mean deviation of 5.03 mm, which indicates our method's effectiveness in addressing the face reconstruction problem. To further validate our model's capabilities, we generate code and models available at https://github.com/zhk2/SAfourier. However, recently we discovered an issue with the official code provided for the state-of-the-art method JigSaW, which led to us re-running and re-verifying our results against a revised code, and consequently our findings were impacted, and as such no longer reflect the best performance on the Florence dataset. Nonetheless, our method still demonstrates superior performance on the AFLW2000-3D dataset, and significantly, achieves results on par with the revised baseline on the Florence dataset, which is also indicative of face head poses greater than 60 degrees often resulting in models with significantly larger mean deviation. In such cases, even our method's best efforts at reconstruction often yield models with a mean deviation of over 7 mm. Nonetheless, our method's overall strength lies in its robust performance in the face of occlusions as well as head poses exceeding 60 degrees, which is also a significant shortcoming of current 3D face models, and consequently, we believe our method represents an important step towards addressing the long-standing issue of model variability, which is a critical requirement for any model of the head, and is expected to accelerate progress in the development of more versatile and robust 3D face models.

Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing its reliability. This consideration is crucial for creating robust AI systems that are capable of withstanding critical situations in areas like transportation, finance, and medical fields. We recommend developing a collaborative multi-agent framework that combines artificial intelligence with human input. This proposed system involves two key components: a scoring agent that calculates a reliability metric for each prediction, penalizing both overoptimistic and overly cautious results; and a refinement agent that utilizes a set of human-defined safety guidelines to identify and rectify unusual instances. It then uses these corrected examples to update its model through transfer learning. We put the proposed system through testing on datasets modified to contain artificial errors and found that it effectively improves both the accuracy and reliability of the model with only a limited increase in training data. Furthermore, the time taken for prediction remains comparable to that of a traditional model. Additionally, we explored the incorporation of diversity in data augmentation, which resulting in a reduction of the performance drop in scenarios with limited data. The code for this project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/gush18/rml. Therefore, we suggest establishing guidelines for what constitutes a reliable instance and using these to select the most trustworthy examples from the larger dataset. This is then used to further refine the model in an ongoing process. We refer to this combined approach as our semi-batch iterative strategy, which results in greater performance improvements than either traditional batch learning or simple augmentation. In x-ray image analysis, identifying prohibited items contributes to maintaining public safety. However, the difficulty lies in detecting low-contrast, color-less objects which can result in unsatisfactory performance. Until now, there have been limited studies in this field due to the absence of high-quality specialized datasets. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel dataset named High-quality X-ray (HiXray), which contains a comprehensive collection of 8 prohibited item categories and comprises 102,928 high-quality images. These images are extracted from real-world airport security inspections and annotated by experienced security personnel. Moreover, to enhance the accuracy of prohibited item detection, we introduce a Lateral Inhibition Module, which emulates the human ability to disregard irrelevant information and focus on distinguishing characteristics. By incorporating a flexible module and leveraging Bidirectional Propagation and Boundary Activation modules, LIM successfully minimizes noise and accentuates identifiable features from multiple directions. Experimental results on HiXray and OPIXray demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to existing detection approaches. Additionally, our research indicates that incorporating spatial and texture information can significantly improve the accuracy of prohibited item detection. LIM, a novel module introduced in this paper, has the potential for applications beyond prohibited item detection, such as in medical imaging. With the introduction of HiXray, the baseline code for LIM is open-sourced for the benefit of the research community. HiXray is a pioneering dataset that is publicly available, and we anticipate it will play a pivotal role in the development of advanced prohibited item detection algorithms. Furthermore, to ensure the reliable evaluation of prohibited item detection performance, we introduce a revised version of the dataset named HiXray-V2, along with the corresponding evaluation metrics and protocol. This revised version prioritizes the real-world scenario by incorporating video imaging, over-reliance on artificial enhancement, and varying inspection practices. HiXray-V2 is a more realistic representation of real-world x-ray images, and it has been used to assess the progression of prohibited item detection algorithms. Unfortunately, our investigation uncovered evidence of widespread overfitting among models trained on HiXray-V2, indicating that there is considerable headroom for further research in this field. A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established for links in a thickened torus. Dubbed $J_n^T$, this polynomial demonstrates numerous properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and notably displays volume conjecture behavior. By applying $J_n^T$, we prove the volume conjecture holds true for a specific link, and provide computational data suggesting it holds for additional links. Moreover, $J_n^T$ can be represented through two distinct constructions, a pseudo-operator invariant, and a construction rooted in the Kauffman bracket skein module of the torus. Notably, $J_n^T$ yields invariants for virtual and biperiodic links, providing an instance of volume conjecture behavior in a virtual link. Moreover, $J_n^T$ is connected to a series of polynomial invariants defined on the torus, and establishes a connection between the original colored Jones polynomial and the toroidal version. Additionally, $J_n^T$ can be defined using a nested construction, resulting in a sequence of polynomials that demonstrate behavior consistent with the volume conjecture. This work also introduces the notion of a link being $J_n^T$ invariant, and proves that the figure-eight link becomes $J_n^T$ invariant when its component is divided by a specific torus-based link, referred to as the white snake link. The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to combine structured knowledge for enhanced performance.  Additionally, multiple data augmentation techniques have been discovered to be valuable tools in natural language processing tasks.  Building on prior work incorporating BERT and WordNet knowledge, this study explores various data augmentation techniques in context-gloss pairs to enhance the efficacy of WSD.  Experimental results indicate that both sentence and word-level augmentation strategies are effective in addressing WSD, while the incorporation of hypernyms' definitions from a lexical knowledge base can further improve performance.  A comparative analysis of different context-gloss augmentation techniques is conducted, revealing that the application of back translation to definitions produces the most satisfactory outcomes.  Moreover, this research introduces two novel methods, named definition-to-sentence and definition-to-word, which yield superior WSD performance compared to baseline models and existing approaches incorporating structured knowledge.  The models' code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/zwang83/ContextGlossAug.  Experimental evaluations are performed on three diverse datasets, encompassing 24 different synsets, and indicate that several state-of-the-art models experience a decline in performance, while others including BERT-based models encounter difficulties in scaling to larger-scale datasets and diverse synsets.  Ultimately, this study demonstrates that the incorporation of context-gloss augmentation, particularly definition-to-sentence and definition-to-word methods, yields superior WSD performance and holds significant potential for applying augmented definitions in other NLP tasks.  Additionally, the research highlights the necessity for further exploration into why certain models underperform and why they struggle with a wider range of synsets.  It is concluded that the combination of BERT and context-gloss augmentation provides a compelling reason to revisit prior-solved NLP problems with diverse synsets and that the application of such models can facilitate better performance in other NLP areas.  Lastly, it is contemplated that the incorporation of augmented definitions combined with BERT may also be beneficial for other tasks dealing with meaning-based applications.  Furthermore, it is believed that the application of context-gloss augmentation, along with a lexical knowledge base such as WordNet, will become a standard practice in developing and evaluating NLP systems.  It is also thought that the study's findings will prompt researchers to examine the augmented definitions in relation to other knowledge
