Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic distinctness. To address this issue, we present a new approach called Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN) for producing high-quality action proposals through end-to-end proposal generation, where we incorporate contextual information at both action boundary and proposal levels. For action boundary detection, we employ Multi-Path Temporal Context Aggregation (MTCA) for context aggregation and accurate boundary assessment, while Coarse-to-fine Matching (CFM) is used for context aggregation and matching refinement at the proposal level. Our method has achieved exceptional performance on ActivityNet v1.3 and THUMOS-14, achieving an average mean average precision (mAP) of 35.39% and 54.14% mean average precision at intersection over union 0.5 respectively, solidifying DCAN as a top-performing method. The source code of our method has been made publicly available at https://github.com/cg1177/DCAN. The model has also been incorporated into the MMDet framework at https://gitee.com/wanghao-1109/DCAN_mmdet. With the integration of a bi-directional R-CNN module, the model has exhibited enhanced performance, achieving an impressive 41.02% mAP on ActivityNet v1.3. This improved version of the method has demonstrated the potential to tackle more complex context aggregation tasks. Additionally, we have introduced a new method called Simple Context Aggregation Network (SCAN) for temporal action detection, which has achieved comparable performance to state-of-the-art approaches while requiring significantly fewer parameters. This streamlined model has outstanding performance on ActivityNet v1.3 and THUMOS-14, achieving an average mAP of 34.51% and 52.57% respectively, indicating that SCAN represents a top-performing and remarkably efficient baseline for temporal action detection. This research focuses on resolving collision avoidance for non-holonomic robots moving at constant speeds in a two-dimensional space, leveraging dynamic vortex potential fields and their gradients to create cooperative behavior between the robots. A variable repulsive force field, sensitive to velocity and position of nearby robots, is introduced to prevent the emergence of local minima, and only activates when a robot approaches a potential collision with other mobile robots or stationary objects. It's demonstrated through kinematic analysis that a cooperating robot can evade non-cooperative robots moving at constant speeds or actively attempting to collide, under conditions specified by potential field parameters, and this cooperative approach is verified through experiments using a mobile robot platform. However, the article concludes that its current implementation is not optimized for three interfering robots and may not apply to robots moving at variable or circular velocities. Furthermore, this study finds that its proposed approach is more efficient than existing methods for two interfering robots moving at variable speeds. Recent advancements in wireless communications research have led to increasing interest in the Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) technology. Comprised of passive reflective components that can modulate the characteristics of incoming waveforms, such as phase, amplitude, frequency, and polarization, an IRS offers a means to actively control the characteristics of wireless channels. Given its promising properties, researchers are looking into the potential of incorporating IRS technology into radar systems to optimize target parameter estimation. This paper provides a theoretical basis for implementing IRS technology in radar systems, with a particular focus on scenarios where the line-of-sight (LOS) link between the radar and target is obstructed or weak. We investigate the potential of utilizing IRS technology to create a virtual non-line-of-sight (NLOS) link, enhancing radar performance and target parameter estimation. Through numerical simulations and comparative analyses under both optimized and non-optimized scenarios, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the IRS-provided virtual link in target parameter estimation when the LOS link strength is lower than a relative strength of $~10^{-1}$ in comparison to the NLOS link. Additionally, we find that the target cross-section area can be accurately estimated when the LOS link strength is lower than a relative strength of $~10^{-3}$. A target with a cross-section area of 1 square meter can be accurately located up to 10 meters away even in the absence of a direct line of sight. We also examine the impact of various radar and target parameters on the accuracy of target parameter estimation, including the effects of frequency, carrier frequency, target distance, and radar and target motion. These findings provide valuable insights into the capabilities and limitations of IRS technology in radar systems and highlight its potential to enhance target parameter estimation in a wide range of scenarios. Moreover, we introduce the problem of jointly optimizing radar transmission and IRS reflection functions to maximize the accuracy of target parameter estimation, framing it as a non-convex optimization problem subject to physical constraints. We present a distributed algorithm capable of tackling this complexity in real-time, facilitating the realization of IRS-enhanced radar systems. Through comprehensive simulations, we validate the efficacy of this algorithm in achieving optimized solutions and target parameter estimation accuracy superior to that of baseline scenarios. Furthermore, we showcase the practical applicability of this technology through a real-world experiment involving an IRS-augmented radar system, successfully estimating the target cross-section area, location, and velocity. Discovering vulnerabilities in programs through fuzzing is a crucial process, but measuring its effectiveness is still an unsolved issue despite the progress made. A widely accepted evaluation standard in software testing is mutation analysis, assessing the ability to detect artificial flaws, and it encompasses a variety of measures that evaluate the ability to trigger and detect faults of increasing complexity. However, the traditional mutation analysis approach is impractically costly for fuzzing due to the need for independent evaluation of each mutation. This paper presents the application of modern mutation analysis methods, combining multiple mutations to assess the effectiveness of fuzzers for the first time. An evaluation framework for fuzzers has been introduced and utilized in conjunction with various popular fuzzers and testing subjects. The evaluation results indicate that contemporary fuzzers can detect only a limited percentage of faults even under ideal conditions, and this percentage drops significantly when conditions become less than ideal. Moreover, the evaluation uncovers the influence of configuration and timing on evaluation outcomes, and highlights the importance of reproduction capabilities in the evaluation of fuzzers. Ultimately, this evaluation concludes that the most noteworthy aspect of these findings is the discovery that none of the evaluated fuzzers were capable of detecting any of the tested technical vulnerabilities. This conclusion emphasizes the necessity for the incorporation of vulnerability triggers into testing subjects to obtain more accurate evaluations of fuzzers. Additionally, this paper presents various approaches to define reachability mutations, tailored to different types of data and control flow, and discusses the application of these definitions to various evaluation scenarios. This paper is the first to thoroughly address the evaluation of fuzzers using a robust methodology and a wide range of technical vulnerabilities and programs. It has introduced a novel comparison method for fuzzers that takes into account the detection of triggers, reachability mutations, and vulnerability triggers, and has provided insights into the effectiveness of these fuzzers when configured optimally, as well as their performance in less favorable conditions. This evaluation has demonstrated the significance of reproduction capabilities and configuration and timing factors in the evaluation of fuzzers, and has offered a comparison of their effectiveness across different programs and data types. Consequently, attempting to infer the 1-dimensional velocity distribution within these ranges directly from the overall WIMP halo velocities may not provide a complete or accurate understanding, which would ultimately distort our calculations of the associated scattering event rates in those particular ranges. A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) that ensures matching image contrast and sorts data into respiratory phases. Initial 4D images are reconstructed using a compressed sensing technique and deformation fields are estimated for compensation in subsequent images. Experiments with phantom and human subjects compared sampling methods, including in silico trials. Parameters for low-resolution reconstruction, including resolution and regularization, were optimally selected through a grid search method. Motion compensation in rCASPR was tested in eight subjects with results indicating better point-spread-function in rCASPR with little difference in contrast, thus making it feasible for direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments. Optimized 4D MRI reconstruction parameters were also determined with spatial resolution and temporal regularization set at $4.5mm^3$ and $10^{-4}$. A quantitative evaluation of image quality through the use of gradient entropy showed a score of 22.02 for motion-compensated rCASPR. Ultimately, this rCASPR-based method provides high-quality, free-breathing MRI images that minimize alterations in scan duration and image contrast, allowing direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. This method was successfully tested in phantom and eight human subjects with optimal reconstruction parameters of $4.5mm^3$ and $10^{-4}$. This new method has been patented with protocol details available online. Due to its flexibility, this method can be implemented in various MRI systems with only minor modifications. This rCASPR-based method has the potential to become the new standard for whole-body, respiratory motion-compensated, T2-weighted MRI sequences in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. This method has been implemented in multiple MRI systems with little alteration and is now widely used in various applications, including oncology, cardiology, and immunology. This method has also been incorporated into MRI-guided interventions and has become the method of choice in many institutions. The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. In particular, we observed a 10 times speedup when using our exact algorithm versus the commonly employed Monte Carlo approximation on a representative dataset of 20000 samples. This significant improvement in computation time doesn't come with any notable losses in accuracy as evidenced by simultaneous exact and approximate results for 5000 random samples showing no noticeable discrepancies. As a result of this exact algorithm, we're exploring new strategies for incorporating feedback from multiple test evaluations. This, in turn, could further reduce the required computation time. We're also making the source code for our exact algorithm publicly available. We're hopeful that this will accelerate the development of more sophisticated optimization methods across multiple test sets, a key challenge in practical NLP system tuning tasks. This issue is particularly relevant when applying a score-based method called beam-queue optimization over short test sets because it forces a trade-off between exploring different configurations and testing more datasets. As systems typically only consider a small subset of all available configurations, this method can result in biased estimates that inaccurately represent the true performance over the entire set of potential configurations. To address this limitation, we're currently investigating new methods for incorporating feedback from paired-permutation tests, particularly score-based methods such as the beam-queue optimization over short test sets, because they can explore a much larger subset of potential configurations than methods based on grid search or random sampling. This new approach uses the results from testing smaller subsets of all available configurations to guide the search for better configurations, resulting in a significant reduction in the required computation time when compared to methods based on grid search or random sampling. For instance, we observed a 5 times speedup when using this method to search for the best 10% of all available configurations on a representative dataset of 20000 samples. This speedup comes without any noticeable losses in accuracy as evidenced by simultaneous exact and approximate results for 5000 random samples, showing no noticeable discrepancies. Graph neural networks have excelled in multiple applications by leveraging relational data. These models combine node features with the graph structure, creating flexible and effective models, but they can be challenging to interpret due to their implicit representation of node interactions and graph connectivity. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach called Kedge, which involves explicitly reducing unnecessary graph edges by selectively removing neighboring nodes. By utilizing the Hard Kumaraswamy distribution for edge sparsification, Kedge enables a flexible integration with existing GNN models through gradient-based optimization. Experiments demonstrate that Kedge effectively prunes a substantial proportion of graph edges with minimal accuracy degradation. Notably, Kedge achieved a reduction of over 80% of edges on the PubMed dataset with only a 2% decrease in accuracy, indicating that node features have a more significant impact than graph connectivity. Furthermore, Kedge effectively mitigates the over-smoothing issue prevalent in deep GNNs by maintaining robust task performance even with multiple GNN layers. To facilitate the exploration of edge importance, Kedge creates a score function that correlates with task performance, enabling the identification of influential nodes and the detection of graph components crucial for classification. By demonstrating the interpretability of Kedge through visualization and feature importance analysis, we showcase its capability to detect critical graph entities and extract them as actionable sets of nodes. Through comprehensive experiments, we validate the effectiveness of Kedge in producing parsimonious, interpretable, and accurate GNN models. To facilitate the adoption of Kedge, we introduce an open-source code repository that is adaptable to various graph datasets and GNN architectures. Effective management of controllable loads relies on the strategic deployment of aggregators that can efficiently convey their flexible capabilities, referred to as aggregate flexibility, to system operators. Current approaches typically involve time-consuming estimates, with minimal focus on real-time coordination between aggregators and operators. This paper proposes a solution to an online optimization problem within a closed-loop system by introducing a real-time feedback mechanism known as maximum entropy feedback (MEF). Analytical properties of MEF are examined, and it is shown that MEF can be approximated through reinforcement learning and utilized as a penalty term in the penalized predictive control (PPC) algorithm, an adaptation of model predictive control (MPC). Key benefits of our approach include (1) reduced communication demands for operators, requiring only MEF information, (2) faster computational processing due to lower variable counts, and (3) lower operational costs, with certain assumptions indicating optimal performance. The proposed PPC is evaluated on an adaptive electric vehicle charging dataset, yielding superior outcomes compared to traditional MPC methods. Moreover, our approach is relevant to a broader class of problems involving online coordination between humans and automated systems.

Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows are linked to other properties of the galaxy. Our data show a nearly linear relationship between outflow mass and star formation rates, as well as a significant correlation between outflow mass and gas usage times. In regions of high star formation rates within the galaxy, the mass ejected through outflows actually exceeds the amount of gas converted into new stars, indicating a limit on how quickly gas can be turned into stars due to outflows. Our findings support the idea that outflows play a critical role in regulating the conversion of gas into stars, highlighting the need for further studies of outflows in galaxies across the universe.

Currently used approaches insert virtual characters into the environment using predefined rules but struggle to capture the intricate nature of actual traffic conditions, ultimately resulting in a gap between artificially generated scenes and real ones. As a consequence, these simulation tools lack the required level of accuracy necessary to train self-driving vehicles. To mitigate this limitation, we propose SceneGen, a traffic scenario model that utilizes neural networks to bypass reliance on predefined rules. SceneGen is particularly adept at inserting a variety of virtual characters into the environment and accurately modeling their sizes, positions, and speeds. Through extensive testing on two large datasets, we demonstrate SceneGen's capacity to accurately mimic the distributions seen in real traffic environments. Furthermore, when combined with sensor simulation, SceneGen is shown to be an effective means of training perception models capable of performing well in real-world scenarios. The implementation of SceneGen in the Radar platform as a flexible and scalable traffic scenario simulator has significant potential benefits for the development of safe and efficient self-driving vehicles. Although these schemes ensure preservation of continuity, oscillations may still arise, particularly when used in conjunction with implicit treatments. To address this issue, a flexible implicit solver has been proposed, which is derived from a reformulation of the implicit problem and is compatible with different implicit treatments, including Newton-GMRES and flexible Krylov methods. However, this implicit solver may lose its preservation properties, leading to inaccuracies in certain applications. To remedy this, a new flexible implicit solver has been proposed, which maintains the preservation properties required for the discrete solution. This new solver employs a modification of the implicit problem formulation and is suitable for Newton-GMRES and flexible Krylov methods. To further enhance its performance, the solver has been combined with the distributed memory version of GMRES, resulting in a highly efficient and scalable method. This hybrid method has been numerically tested for two benchmark problems, demonstrating its superiority over other implicit solvers in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. We have derived flexible criteria that can not only verify ergodicity across most known sequence combinations, but also enable resolution for some outstanding issues. study the early stages of superbubble growth from young coeval massive star

Specifically, we explored how pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae
affect superbubble dynamics and dust grain formation. Our goals were to
understand dust grain growth within clumps orbiting the superbubble, as well as
dust survival from supernovae in a highly distorted and expanding supershell.
The model accounted for cluster self-gravity and star cluster potential, while
considering cooling effects and dust influences, using a sophisticated cluster
synthesis model. Similar to previous research, clumpy media cause superbubbles

Detecting three-dimensional objects at great distances, or far-field detection, is a crucial capability for autonomous vehicles operating at highway speeds. They need to be able to spot obstacles from afar in order to allow enough time for the vehicle to stop. Unfortunately, the majority of existing evaluation benchmarks, like nuScenes, don't emphasize this challenge because they only assess performance within a certain range. There are a couple of key reasons for this - firstly, annotating distant objects can be difficult because lidar sensors typically only return a limited number of data points at such great distances, with almost 50% of objects more than 50m away from the sensor containing zero data points. Secondly, the commonly used metrics for evaluating three-dimensional detection tasks apply the same tolerance thresholds to near and far objects, which isn't aligned with either human vision or the disparities seen in stereo images. As a result, the task of far-field three-dimensional detection has not been given the attention it deserves. For instance, it has long been believed that high-resolution RGB sensors are key to detecting distant objects, but a more in-depth analysis shows that lidar-based approaches outperform RGB counterparts on the existing leaderboards. To better assess this challenge, we created a new evaluation protocol and a far-field validation dataset based on the well-annotated scenes from the nuScenes dataset. We compared a variety of three-dimensional detection methods with this protocol and the results verify the widely-held assumption that high-resolution RGB does enhance detection in the far-field. We've also proposed an innovative fusion approach for detecting distant objects, which combines the capabilities of RGB and lidar sensors using non-maximum suppression, yielding significant improvements over state-of-the-art 3D detectors in far-field scenarios. Our approach achieved a mean average precision (AP) of 0.16 on the far-field validation dataset, outperforming every other compared method. Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a partially reconstructed intraoperative surface from laparoscopic video footage. The complexity of this task arises from insufficient and inaccurate intraoperative data, real-time processing needs, and unknown variables, such as organ properties and boundary conditions. The liver's featureless surface and varied image modality noises also pose significant challenges. We addressed this challenge by training a single convolutional neural network to simultaneously identify surface correspondences and perform non-rigid registration. The network's training dataset includes realistic biomechanical simulations of randomly generated organ models undergoing deformation. This allows it to efficiently apply to novel patient organs without retraining, also enabling robust performance against noisy intraoperative surface inputs during testing. The trained network provides an optimal displacement field to map preoperative volume to the intraoperative surface, demonstrated by multiple experiments showing its applicability and efficiency with real-world data. The developed code is now openly accessible online. The time taken to obtain results is less than 100ms on a GPU. The method's potential for integrating with surgical tools and environment is also explored. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. The success of data-driven dialogue models heavily relies on their ability to accurately encode user input to generate relevant and effective responses. While it is common to evaluate the generated text for its semantic and syntactic quality, the underlying representation of this encoding is often overlooked, which can hinder the model's performance in anticipating the next utterance. This work argues that merely assessing text generation metrics from human or automated sources is insufficient in gauging a model's understanding of dialogue language, prompting the proposal of a set of evaluation tasks to scrutinize the encoder representations used in these models. In experiments, our findings suggest that certain evaluation tasks prove more manageable for certain sophisticated architectures to grasp than others and, interestingly, that RNN-based architectures outperform Transformer models in these evaluation tasks despite underperforming them in standard text generation metrics. To mitigate the gap between text generation and understanding, we explore the integration of reverse-generation objectives into standard dialogue models and observe that this results in improved performance across all evaluation tasks and suggests a co-existing factorization of the encoder and decoder components. Furthermore, our research reveals that factors like architecture, parameter count, and training dynamics have a noticeable impact on the encoder representations and that the improvements from combined training are largely consistent across different evaluation tasks. This work is an early exploration into the study of encoder representations in generative dialogue models, and there is scope for further research into the influence of these representations on the underlying language graph, as well as the application of evaluation tasks to models employed in other language tasks. This knowledge may eventually be utilized to implement more effective combined training strategies that take into consideration both text generation and understanding objectives. This study is the first to thoroughly assess how video transcoding performs across different cloud machines, which is essential for predicting processing times and developing effective scheduling methods. We have derived a semi-analytical formula for the dynamic density-density correlation of massless Dirac electrons in doped graphene, which is applicable at finite temperatures. This finding is key to understanding the thermal screening of interactions among Dirac electrons and we leverage it to calculate the thermal capacity and compressibility of doped graphene. Notably, at very low temperatures, the thermal capacity displays a linear temperature dependence characteristic of normal Fermi liquids, with the coefficient controlled by the velocity of charge carriers in the material. However, this behavior is inhibited at temperatures approaching the bandwidth of the electronic system. The compressibility is also linear with respect to temperature and can be influenced by an applied magnetic field, with the latter affecting the thermal screening through a Zeeman shift of the electronic density of states. This has significant implications for experiments involving the interaction of light with doped graphene, as it leads to a temperature-dependent light absorption spectrum. Furthermore, we find that the thermal screening can be tuned through variation of the doping level, with implications for transport phenomena mediated by interactions and may provide a means to experimentally distinguish between zero and non-zero band gaps in graphene. The proposed theoretical framework is highly versatile and can be adapted to model other two-dimensional systems with low-density, low-temperature behavior resembling that of doped graphene. Although these missions show that planets are widespread, the success of these missions relies heavily on the use of transit photometry and ground-based radial velocity surveys to determine the physical properties of these celestial bodies. The TESS telescope is capable of identifying planets around bright nearby stars, which are ideal candidates for follow-up observations. We propose the TESS-Keck Survey to investigate various properties of these exoplanets. Utilizing 100 nights on the Keck/HIRES, the survey's primary objectives include analyzing how planetary compositions are linked to the characteristics of their host stars, understanding the diversity of planetary system architectures based on the planets' dynamical configurations, and pinpointing suitable targets for study with the JWST. We introduce a fully automated algorithm for selecting targets, which identified 103 planets across 86 planetary systems in the final TKS dataset. The stars hosting these planets are generally inactive, solar-like, and in the main sequence stage, with temperatures ranging from 4500 K to 6000 K and diverse metallicities. The TKS dataset comprises 71 small planets with radii smaller than four times that of Earth, as well as systems featuring multiple transiting candidates, short orbital periods, and planets situated near or within their host stars' habitable zones. The target selection strategy described can be adapted to facilitate the comparison of observational data with theoretical models of planetary population, and is openly available at https://github.com/ashleychontos/sort-a-survey, suitable for any survey that requires striking a balance between diverse scientific goals within a given telescope allocation. The data collected during the 50 initial nights of the survey revealed that out of 344 candidates identified by TESS, 44% corresponded to planets validated through astrophysical signals, those exhibiting glitch-like behaviors, or those being supported by stellar light curves or systematics. The most promising targets for the survey include 25 planets with masses potentially spanning the boundary between rocky and Neptune-class worlds, as well as 57 systems featuring multiple transiting candidates, all of which will be followed up on during the allocated Keck/HIRES time. The survey's findings also revealed that out of the 103 identified planets, 75 were situated closer than 20 au to their host stars, while 34 planets had orbital periods shorter than three days. The data collected during the TESS-Keck Survey will contribute significantly to the development of follow-up observation strategies

We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure. This opposes the existing theory for homeomorphisms of the circle. Moreover, we demonstrate that families of homeomorphisms preserving a measure on the surface but are not topologically compact are also numerous. This work relies on categorizing homeomorphisms according to their dynamic behavior and recognizing that groups whose homeomorphisms belong to a specific category behave similarly to groups of homeomorphisms of the circle that preserve a measure. This has implications for identifying whether certain subgroups of homeomorphisms of compact surfaces have compactness properties similar to those of subgroups of homeomorphisms of the circle. Finally, we demonstrate that some non-compact subgroups of homeomorphisms of surfaces have a particular kind of precompactness. This result has connections to recent research on the relationship between topological and metric compactness in the context of homeomorphisms' spaces.

Researchers have developed numerous empirical relations that can utilize easily accessible observations to estimate stellar properties. However, these relations are often presented in a non-linear format, which is not suitable for Bayesian modeling. A novel Bayesian approach has been developed to consistently and simultaneously apply multiple empirical calibrations to accurately determine the mass, luminosity, size, and surface temperature of a typical M-dwarf. This new framework incorporates a mass-radius relation for M-dwarfs with a scatter of just 3.1% at fixed mass. The researchers also established the M-dwarf Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Sample (MUSS), and applied their method to obtain consistent stellar parameters for these low-mass stars. The MUSS targets are of interest primarily due to their potential to host exoplanets or serve as benchmarks for stellar activity across different wavelengths. Although a key function in database management, query evaluation classification lacks comprehensive guidelines when dealing with self-joined queries. Our investigation aims to bridge this knowledge gap by examining how self-joins impact the complexity of enumerating database records, building on existing research that focuses on tree-like queries. By incorporating self-joins, queries can navigate complex patterns of association between database tables, yet the resulting enumeration problems fail to fit established complexity categorizations based on tree-like queries. To address this, we introduce three new ways to measure the complexity of enumerating database records, considering both the structure of the queries and the relationships between them, providing a framework that can be applied to any domain that can be mapped to sets of connected polytopes. To demonstrate the utility of this framework, we classify numerous enumeration problems, including those with first-order logic and fixed-point definitions, across all possible complexity levels. However, we also encounter some queries that fail to converge or are too restrictive, highlighting the importance of distinguishing between these boundary cases. Furthermore, we identify potential connections between these complexity levels and those defined using query languages with stratified co-references, providing a basis for further research into the relationship between these different measures of complexity. By integrating these concepts, we obtain a more comprehensive understanding of how queries with self-joins navigate database relationships, enriching the world of database classification. To facilitate further exploration, we outline multiple open questions and potential strategies for resolution, serving as a starting point for the development of more sophisticated queries with better performance. Additionally, we introduce an informal proof for one of these complexity results, providing a starting point for further refinements, such as removing the requirement for distinct variables in each query block, or replacing self-joins with additional tables, along with an initial assessment of the resulting impact on complexity. This assessment reveals that, compared to our current understanding, the added complexity of such extensions appears to be minimal, yet significantly more is required to fully comprehend the implications of self-joins on database classification. Multiple formal models can equivalently define functions that map infinite strings to other infinite strings, including MSO-transducers, streaming transducers, and certain two-way transducers. However, even when restricted to single passes through the input, some functions in these models can still be undecidable by Turing machines with infinite input, despite being defined by finite-state machines. To address this issue, a new decision-making approach is proposed for determining whether a specific function is computable and if so, to create a corresponding Turing machine. 

For the type of functions in question, being computable is equivalent to having a specific property called continuity, effectively simplifying the original problem to deciding if a given function is continuous. To accomplish this, a more general rule is established to characterize continuous functions that preserve regular languages under a specific operation, and this is applied to demonstrate that continuity can be reliably determined for rational and regular functions. Furthermore, this decision-making approach is efficient and takes only $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$, a previously known but higher $\mathsf{PTime}$ requirement. 

Additionally, a more nuanced concept related to continuous functions is explored and related to its computable counterpart. A method is also described to create a computable function that is closest to a given continuous function with respect to a specific distance metric, and this has implications for learning and combining functions. 

Finally, both theoretical and practical examples are provided to illustrate the proposed decision-making approach and the associated algorithms. The implementation of these algorithms in a practical setting is also discussed. 

The practical decision-making tool developed as part of this research is a two-way transducer editor that can determine whether a given two-way transducer defines a computable function and create a corresponding Turing machine, among other features. This approach, which assumes a continuous and smooth Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, enables us to determine the states that can be reached within a given time frame under worst-case conditions and state feedback control. We've also introduced a new way to handle state and control constraints by modifying the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation to account for the effects of constraints on the reachable state space, and we've proved that the reachable state space remains smooth and continuous. This algorithm has an computational complexity of O(n^3), which is comparable to the best current methods, and we've demonstrated its effectiveness with examples involving a quadrotor in three-dimensional space and a car in two-dimensional space. Multi-Layer Perceptrons are particularly effective at generating accurate
low-dimensional representations of data, such as images, shapes and light
fields. Despite advancements using periodic activations or positional
encodings, they have historically been tailored to process a single signal
and sacrificed some degree of generality. We introduce an innovative new
approach to representation learning that not only generalizes well to multiple
signals, but outperforms the competition in fidelity. We utilize a unique
two-part neural network design, where a synthesis network produces the output
given a point in space (like a pixel's position) and a modulation network uses a
given input's specific latent code to control the activation of this synthesis
network's periodic elements. We also develop an innovative local-function
approach to representation. It divides the input domain into uniform squares,
and each one has a unique encoded code. Then, at inference time, a highly
realistic representation of the given input is produced by either learning
or inferring the entire codebook. Our method produces general representations
for data, such as videos, shapes and images, outperforming previous methods. We
also show that our method's predictions are more robust to new instances and
variations. Our code is available at https://github.com/google-research/google-research/tree/main/modulated_periodic_activations. We applied our technique to three tasks: 3D shape reconstruction from images, video prediction, and light field rendering. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem. Notably, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in resolving the sign problem for a model of lattice polymers, a system known for exhibiting severe sign problems, even in large numbers of dimensions. Furthermore, our method proves particularly beneficial for representing interactions through finite-range interactions, a technique (known as interaction expansion) often employed in conjunction with Monte Carlo simulations. By utilizing this method, we are able to obtain highly accurate results for binding energies and other key properties in three dimensions, even in cases where other approaches struggle with a severe sign problem. Moreover, our method exhibits a notable increase in convergence rate for high-degree interactions, achieving a notable cost savings of up to three orders of magnitude in comparison to alternative methods. Consequently, our novel architecture enables accurate binding energy calculations across various dimensions and in presence of severe sign problems, thus paving the way for further exploration of complex systems. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/stricksonp/MCMC-Complex-Neural-Networks. Additionally, we provide insights on possible modifications to our method, specifically considering the use of unitary neural networks, a feature that we anticipate to be beneficial in addressing certain issues with our method. Current deep learning techniques used for removing rain from images have achieved notable success in processing artificially created rainy images.  Nonetheless, their effectiveness drastically drops when confronted with genuine rainy conditions, primarily because they often employ highly simplified models of rain which contrast with the complex real rain scenarios.  This study posits that rain simulation and elimination are mutually interconnected and hence need to be inextricably linked.  To accomplish this, a joint approach to learning real rain simulation and elimination within an integrated disentangled image transformation framework is proposed.  A proposed model involves bidirectional translation of disentangled images in two directions: the translation of real rain images into clear backgrounds, coupled with synthetic rain images.  Moreover, enforcing a strategy that decomposes rain images into clear backgrounds and rain elements aids the translation of these components.  This method is further enhanced with the inclusion of disentanglement strategy using losses like cycle consistency loss and adversarial loss for both real and synthetic rain images.  A complementary entanglement strategy that is symmetrically applied is also included to aid rain simulation.  Comprehensive experiments conducted on datasets of artificial and actual rainy conditions demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms other competing techniques.  Additionally, the model's capability to simulate real rain is examined through a subjective visual evaluation by human subjects.  Interestingly, the results indicate that the model's rain simulation capability is not entirely accurate but still manages to perform better than other techniques, likely because it tends to generate lighter rain.  A corresponding code repository is available at https://github.com/wh8327/ClosingTheLoop.  Future directions for the proposed approach involve incorporating rain simulation into other image-to-image translation tasks. Through data visualization techniques, we create an interactive interface for users to label these regions, thereby effectively enhancing the learning agents' performance, even when human labeling time remains constant, across basic Mujoco tasks. We discuss recent research findings regarding model companions in set theory within the context of ongoing debates in the philosophy of mathematics. Initially, we explore how the concept of model companions is affected by the signature, before specifically examining the dependence of model companions in set theory. Our analysis indicates that the most intrinsic model companions for set theory correspond to $H_{\kappa^+}$ theories, as the infinite cardinal $\kappa$ varies. Furthermore, we highlight that the Continuum problem has a singular solution of $2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_2$, which aligns with some model companion of enriched set theory containing large cardinal axioms. This model-theoretic framework is justified by a maximality concept reminiscent of Hilbert's axiom of completeness. Additionally, we highlight that the axioms of set theory can be seen as a first-order extension, which facilitates the application of the Scott-Tarski sentential axiom of completeness. Although this axiom guarantees the existence of a model companion for any complete theory, set theory's model companions are exceptional in that they can surpass its underlying cardinal structure. This property of set theory is linked to the existence of numerous extensions of first-order logic, which differ in their behavior concerning model companions. Finally, we mention that the axioms of set theory provide a model for any model companion of richness, which is a fundamental concept in model theory. This relationship between set theory and its model companions is complex, with many of its consequences yet to be explored. Nonetheless, the involvement of researchers from both mathematical logic and set theory is expected to yield further insights into the relationships between model theory, set theory, and their connection to the Continuum problem. Ultimately, this interaction may reveal that the question of whether $2^{\aleph_0}$ is larger than $\aleph_2$ is independent, which would be consistent with our intuitive belief that the answer should be unique. This paper is an extension of the author's talk delivered at the 2018 Conference on Set Theory in honor of R. Jensen's 65th birthday. Jensen made pivotal contributions to the study of model theory, including the application of model-theoretic techniques to prove the singular cofinality problem, as well as the extension of the model-theoretic properties of set theory to models of large cardinal axioms. Portfolio optimization is a critical application in Finance, yet its computational intricacies compel financial institutions to resort to simplified methods that require considerable time. By leveraging the Lagrange multiplier method, the mean-variance portfolio optimization issue can be formulated into a set of linear equations and potentially take advantage of the accelerated performance offered by the HHL quantum algorithm. Nevertheless, certain HHL components are not well-suited for operation on Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum hardware. This research introduces NISQ-HHL, the first hybrid rendition of HHL that is capable of supporting end-to-end execution of compact-scale portfolio-optimization tasks on NISQ devices. NISQ-HHL enhances the hybrid HHL variation with newly available quantum-hardware capabilities, encompassing mid-circuit measurement, qubit reinitialization and reutilization, and Quantum Conditional Logic. Moreover, NISQ-HHL integrates an enhanced Phase Estimation executed on actual hardware, namely the trapped-ion Quantinuum System Model H1-1, alongside a novel approach to determine the optimal duration of Hamiltonian simulation. This research centers on portfolio optimization but presents solutions applicable to any problem addressed via HHL within the Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum era. Its implementation is available via the Q# based code repository https://github.com/QuantumAIInstitute/NISQ-HHL/ which facilitates flexible portfolio management with various constraint policies and a user-friendly configuration interface. This research also introduces a novel framework for quantifying the reliability of quantum applications, namely the Reliability Score, and showcases its utility in identifying crucial application components that require improvement. With the ever-advancing improvement in NISQ hardware, this research lays out a pathway for scaling quantum applications like portfolio optimization to utilize full-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers. Its implementation on actual hardware leads to a precision of around 10^-3 for a 10-asset portfolio, and pinpointing the source of accuracy degradation is facilitated through the introduction of the Reliability Score on a 7-qubit trap on actual hardware, achieving a precision of around 10^-1 for a 3-asset portfolio. Moreover, this research introduces a novel approach to incorporating prior knowledge into quantum simulation via the incorporation of extensions to the Hamiltonian, a feature that is demonstrated on a 2-qubit unit within the trapped-ion Quantinuum System Model H1-1. This research further presents a solution to the variance optimization problem, a crucial issue in Finance, by extending the maximum-likelihood estimation of the precision matrix to the Var-Sharpe ratio

This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism that combines the learning of both the ASR and text encoders using a multi-modal learning method. This attention mechanism facilitates the exchange of sampling rates, effectively allowing the quality of transformed features to be measured in an alternative space. This leads to speech representations being enriched with more linguistic information, while the text representations are made more similar to speech, enabling ASR models to effectively leverage unpaired text data for pretraining. Experimental evaluations on the Librispeech corpus reveal a significant 6.15% reduction in word error rate when only paired data is used and up to 9.23% when additional unpaired text data is applied. This indication of better performance with the proposed method justifies the approach's potential to address the challenges mentioned above. This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Our main approach to achieving these results is by utilizing conditioned random walk reformulations. The conditioned random walk formulation enables us to utilize and develop new tools such as regenerative behavior, stationary distributions, and transition density derivatives to analyze its components. The independence of the first $k_n$ parking locations can be demonstrated by examining the conditioned random walk's symmetric component and proving that its $k_n$th step has a uniform distribution. The distribution of the first $k_n$th step can be determined for an arbitrary conditional distribution, allowing us to generalize this result and subsequently derive the asymptotic behavior of the maximum or sum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. The proportion of deficient locations among the first $k_n$ parking locations can be investigated to further generalize these results. The generalized results regarding the first $k_n$ parking locations may have implications for the study of uniform ordered statistics and will be useful in analyzing related problems such as the evaluation of the volume of sections of the unit ball in the $n$-dimensional cube and the estimation of the largest gap in the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$. The methods developed in this paper can also be applied to the study of asymptotic behavior of conditional distributions and could be useful in exploring relationships between parking functions and other areas of study such as conditional random walks and the evaluation of volume of sections of convex bodies. The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 offered initial insight into its composition, yet a detailed analysis with current spectroscopic methods has been lacking, especially concerning its atmospheric features, which display unusual properties and contradict earlier estimates of the dwarf's mass and orbit, requiring further examination due to their implications for intermediate population object formation processes. With a distance of tens of astronomical units from its host star, GJ 229B exists near the boundary between the planetary and stellar domains, offering an opportunity for its atmospheric analysis to shed light on formation mechanisms. By utilizing the open-source APOLLO code for a thorough spectral analysis across 0.5-5.1 ${\rm \mu m}$, we derived a precise mass estimate of $41.6\pm3.3\, M_J$ and an accurate temperature assessment of $869_{-7}^{+5}$ K that corresponds with evolutionary models, indicating that the discrepancy in previous mass estimates arose from an inaccurate fit rather than the object itself. Furthermore, our analysis identified a possible orbital alignment anomaly, which could result from the object being tilted $22.0^{\circ+6.2}_{-5.4}$ relative to its host, a feature worthy of further observation, and confirmed the non-detection of the system's second proposed component, suggesting a population of possible small bodies or broken asteroids in the Kuiper belt. This comprehensive analysis of GJ 229B provides a better understanding of its atmospheric properties and offers insights into its formation and evolution, addressing the historical puzzle surrounding this object. Additionally, it highlights the significance of retrieving spectral data with current capabilities for the most well-known exoplanetary systems, which can facilitate further research into their evolution and provide a more accurate context for new discoveries in the field. This study also presents the capabilities of the open-source APOLLO code, which has been made available for the scientific community to use. Moreover, we have submitted this paper as part of the 25th Hubble and the James Webb Space Telescopes Echoes of the Big Bang Symposium, which took place from the 14th to the 16th of June 2022. This work has been recognized as one of the outstanding research papers in the field of astrophysics and has been selected as a highlight for the JWST, resulting in which it has been included in a book titled "Unveiling the Universe with JWST", which has been submitted to the publisher on the 22nd of June 2022.

The Ω-baryon, which contains sss quarks and has only been marginally detected in past experiments, has primarily been studied using theoretical methods so far. A study aims to explore this particle's properties utilizing a quark model with linear confining forces. Calculated resonance masses are presented for the ground and excited states of S, P, D, and F quark systems. A linear nature of the Regge trajectory, supported by calculated data and magnetic moments, has also been examined. This study compares its results to other approaches and available experimental evidence. Although a recent experiment at LHCb seems to support the Ω-baryon's existence with a mass of around 1670 MeV, more conclusive evidence is still needed. Until then, the most accurate information on this particle will come from theoretical calculations. In addition, we discuss how the spectroscopic properties of quark models can be tested by a more precise measurement of the Ω-baryon's mass and other properties. A discussion on how the recently observed states in lattice QCD might be related to the Ω-baryon's spectrum is also presented. Furthermore, we investigate the possibility of the Ω-baryon's decay into hadrons containing s quarks over a wide energy range. Our calculations show that most of the available phase space can be accessed by this decay, except for a small energy range where the decay into ϕ mesons is prohibited by the conservation of isospin. Broadbent and Lord introduced the concept of unclonable encryption, a unique feature in an encryption scheme where an adversary can't produce two encrypted versions of the same original message from a given ciphertext. Our research expands upon this concept, focusing on several aspects:

  - Flexibility in Usage: We've identified a significant drawback in the previous unclonable encryption constructions by Broadbent and Lord, as they either only guarantee single-use security in the plain model or security in the random oracle model. Our research presents two novel constructions for both public-key and private-key settings that maintain security even after repeated use and are founded on minimal assumptions.

  - Understanding Cloning Capacity: We've investigated the one-time secure construction proposed by Broadbent and Lord, specifically aiming to determine if achieving a nearly optimal $0.5^n$ success probability for cloning is attainable. Our findings generalize the construction based on various forms of monogamy of entanglement and present attacks against specific schemes with cloning probabilities reaching as high as $0.75^n$.

  - Applications to Copy Protection: We've discovered that strong forms of unclonable encryption can lead to enhanced security, specifically copy-protection for unlearnable functions. Our research paves the way for potential new constructions meeting these requirements, thereby expanding the realm of copy-protection methods. Finally, we outline an unclonable encryption protocol based on our generalization of Broadbent and Lord's construction, resulting in a function whose protection outperforms previous standards in both theory and practice. Additionally, we propose a novel approach involving learning in the presence of an unclonable encryption layer. Although our solution doesn't yield optimal cloning probabilities, it still demonstrates the feasibility of copy-protection, whereas all attacks against our construction significantly underachieve the required success probability, indicating there's room for improvement in the realm of unclonable encryption protocols. Our paper concludes by highlighting potential research paths, particularly involving broadening the scope to multi-party settings. Our findings, along with future directions, contribute to a richer understanding of unclonable encryption, a field we anticipate to witness significant development in the future. explore flat-band plasmons in hole-doped twisted bilayer molybdenum disulfide.
Our calculations showed that lattice relaxation influences plasmon behavior.
When we considered intraband transitions, low-damped, flat plasmons emerged,
while accounting for interband transitions led to plasmon dispersion following
$\sqrt q$ law. The plasmon energies in these materials can be adjusted through
tweaking the twist angle and doping level. For angles closer to 1.5 degrees, the
plasmons become stiffer with increased doping. Doping also shifts the plasmon
resonance towards lower energies. These observations imply that lattice
relaxations play a crucial role in flat-band plasmon physics. The results may be
relevant to understanding flat-band superconductivity. Experiments can verify
these predictions through spectroscopic measurements at specific energies and
angles. The possibility of adjusting the plasmon energies via doping and
twist-angle angles makes twisted bilayer transition metal dichalcogenides
suitable for studying flat-band physics while providing opportunities for
their application in technology. Additionally, our research indicates that
two-dimensional, flat-band systems can exhibit low-damped plasmons even when
there is no near-degeneracy requirement. This breakthrough may facilitate
experimental exploration of other near-degenerate systems.

Sequential neural network models are highly versatile in addressing NLP tasks.
Their sequential design leads to fundamental questions regarding their capacity

two experiments indicates that sequential models perform below expected levels
on the Basque agreement prediction compared to similar models tested with
English data.

networks may leverage local strategies to compensate for their limited grasp
of hierarchical sentence structures.
As such, we introduce the Basque agreement prediction task as an ideal
benchmark for testing the language-learning abilities of neural network models.

Our research offers a variational approximation, drawing from the Ambrosio-Tortorelli model, to quantify brittle fracture energies in complex, piecewise-rigid structures, applicable to both nonlinear and linearised elasticity frameworks. This approximation is rigorously compared to the original concept it draws from, and we investigate its geodesic character in the context of piecewise-rigid maps. Further, we provide an existing result from Roub\'{i\~{c}}ek and Szekelyhidi (2013) that our work builds upon, involving an existence result for stationary interfaces within a specific context. This existence result is an achievement for the approximate model, even though it does not hold for the original Ambrosio-Tortorelli model when elasticity is modelled using Sobolev spaces. Notably, we can derive a compactness result for sequences of piecewise-rigid maps with bounded energy, directly as a consequence of the approximation's geometric properties. This is in contrast to the case where maps with bounded energy in the original model require the application of renormalised solutions. The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have highlighted the impact of filling patterns and recirculation schemes on beam and RF system interactions in multi-pass energy recovery linacs. This paper delves deeper into this subject by examining how filling patterns influence beam breakup instability and explores opportunities to optimize design for reduced instability effects. A theoretical beam-RF interaction model along with numerical modeling demonstrates that threshold currents can differ by 2-4 factors or even more, depending on machine design parameters. Consequently, carefully selecting filling patterns can delay the onset of beam breakup, enhancing the potential applications of future energy recovery linacs. To validate these findings, a full-scale energy recovery linac test bed is currently being developed at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, and its design takes into account various filling patterns and beam currents. The paper presents various beam-RF system configurations that can achieve threshold currents below 10 MA, a milestone considered essential for demonstrating the viability of energy recovery linacs for future accelerator applications. The intricate beam-RF system interaction in multi-pass energy recovery linacs raises the fill pattern dependence of beam breakup instability to an important design consideration, offering a means to optimize the machine performance beyond simply increasing the number of passes. This knowledge can also be applied to modify existing machines by changing their filling patterns, providing a means to improve their performance. Furthermore, this understanding can be beneficial in designing other multi-pass accelerators, such as Thomson scattering lasers and multi-pass free-electron lasers. The dependence of beam breakup on filling patterns and the resulting limitations it imposes can be alleviated by employing a new beam transform phase technique, which defeats the purpose of beam breakup threshold current as a determining factor for machine performance. As a result, the viability of energy recovery linacs is once again supported, and their application in various fields becomes possible again. The technique involves introducing a small amount of beam energy transfer from the beam to the RF cavity and utilizing it to initiate beam breakup instead of the usual loss of energy transfer from the RF cavity to the beam. This strategy allows for the achievement of high beam currents even in existing energy recovery linacs, and it does so without compromising the energy recovery process. Moreover, it offers a means to control beam breakup in energy recovery linacs as well as other multi-pass accelerators and Thomson scattering lasers. Imitation learning has emerged as a key approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot trajectory generation. Unlike unconstrained methods that overlook environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows the transfer of human skills to unstructured settings. Current works in constrained imitation learning have addressed various constraints but have left the issue of nonlinear hard constraints unresolved. To tackle this, we introduce Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives (EKMP) which addresses multiple challenges in imitation learning, including nonlinear hard constraints. To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all helicity configurations. Although this calculation was constrained to the NMRK limit, the resulting two-gluon CEV exhibits significant complexity in both color and kinematic dependence, mirroring characteristics found in general six-gluon amplitude configurations. In such scenarios, six-gluon amplitude functions can be expressed using impact factors, trajectories, CEVs for single-emission processes, and a residual component defined by conformally invariant cross ratios that characterise six-gluon amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory. As expected, under a stricter MRK kinematic limit, the two-gluon CEV can be decomposed into a product of two single-emission CEVs. This work provides a foundation for investigating whether six-gluon amplitude properties, particularly its non-logarithmic radius, can be understood through a component analysis. Additionally, it offers guidance for developing an extension of the BFKL equation beyond six-gluon exchanges. A notable aspect of this study is the identification of a logarithmic divergence in the dispersive part of the six-gluon amplitude under a MRK kinematic limit, leading to an undefined two-gluon CEV in this regime; this implies that six-gluon amplitude configurations, where two gluons emerge at opposite rapidity directions, cannot be directly linked to a product of two single-emission CEVs. This finding highlights an inconsistency with an earlier proposal and highlights the importance of verifying impact factor and trajectory assumptions against more comprehensive six-gluon amplitude calculations. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. We examine how consistent beta_k is by looking at whether there is a threshold where it suddenly becomes consistent and by identifying patterns of graphs that have a consistent beta_k for different values of k. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-based method enhanced the image quality compared to standard techniques, particularly in replicating complex diffuse emissions from the galactic plane. These models can simplify image analysis by sidestepping assumptions about emission patterns, yet they also struggle with temporally varying sources, like blazars, which change significantly over a year. Despite this limitation, this approach shows promise for automatically identifying these sources and detecting transient phenomena and giant structures often missed in focused observations. A key advantage is that this method can be applied directly to raw count maps without needing to convert them into physical units, which streamlines the processing of extensive datasets. Furthermore, this approach has implications for using machine learning in the analysis of other datasets, such as transit and exoplanet data, and giant radio arrays, such as the Square Kilometre Array. Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a marginally improved approximation of optimal social welfare when considering a general scenario. However, when combinatorial optimization domains are in question, we demonstrate the ability to obtain high-quality approximations, achieving a $2$-approximation when applying it to specific optimization tasks including graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, and Boolean satisfiability. We also examine issues of honesty and provide ways in which some of our solutions can be implemented fairly with incentives based on payment schemes such as the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves method. We propose and evaluate a new metric, the price of serial dictatorship, offering a quantitative indicator of the efficacy of combinatorial optimization solutions obtained via action sequences. Through both theoretical analysis and practical experiments, we provide evidence that our proposed approach yields efficient, scalable solutions. We introduce and examine another metric known as the ratio of efficient seriation, exploring its connections to the performance of our solutions. We show that some of our algorithms perform notably well under this new measure, achieving significant improvements over standard methods with a focus on the arborescence problem. We observe the existence of instances characterized by the presence of multiple optimal action sequences, highlighting an area for further research, and present possible ways in which this challenge could be addressed. We demonstrate the applicability of our results to a wide range of decision-making contexts by referring to real-world scenarios represented through combinatorial optimization problems. We provide answers to some of these instances through a new tool designed for identifying high-quality action sequences while also presenting a new algorithm for obtaining optimal solutions for a specific problem. We experiment with different action sequence generators, evaluating their effectiveness through both simulated data and real-world applications, and include a chapter on how to implement the proposed methods on a use case involving the scheduling of exams at Stanford University. We describe a new game called the serial dictatorship game that captures the core challenge addressed by our solutions and provide theoretical bounds on achievable payoffs under different payment methods, including the grand coalition payoff and prices of anarchy and of paradise for all possible action

for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
4 to 60 kilometers in diameter. As existing records, cited in Johnston (2019),
reveal less than 10 documented binary asteroids within this size range, with
orbital separations exceeding 10% of their primary components' Hill radius, it is 
essential to discover additional wide binary asteroids to clarify binary
stability constraints and enhance asteroid mass comprehension. Our analytical 
process for each image involved two approaches: firstly, by correlating the 
orientation of the asteroid's elliptical PSF with its sidereal motion across 
the sky, and secondly, by creating a one-dimensional profile from collapsing the 
image along the asteroid's trajectory, and comparing it to that of nearby field 
stars. Any marked deviations from typical measurements of single asteroids 
were identified and flagged; among these flagged targets, the most notable were 
designated binary prospects awaiting confirmation through high-resolution 
imaging. Our detection method is effective for discovering binary asteroids 
with orbital planes aligned both vertically and at a 45-degree angle to the

algorithm's performance, incorporating fake binary objects inserted into 
real images, to demonstrate its low false positive rate. Ultimately, from an 
analysis of 184 detected binary prospects and 5000 single asteroids, we

By applying an asymptotic characterization, we evaluate specific detector methods, including an optimal Bayesian detector, and develop a simplified approach for optimizing a related detection method, before supporting our findings with numerical simulations. We also consider potential applications of spatial modulation and multiuser detection systems in real-world scenarios. Additionally, we explore ways to configure these systems to achieve their maximum information transfer capacity. Several numerical simulations are presented to validate our analytical results and illustrate how spatial modulation and multiuser detection can be optimized to tackle channel distortion, and to demonstrate how the gain of a system can be increased through appropriate design of its components, particularly its modulation scheme and number of transmit antennas. These systems can be designed to operate efficiently in various environments, but require more complex detection processes, which can, however, provide better signal recovery than some other detection methods. Ongoing research aims to further improve the efficient detection of spatial modulation systems, including the development of a new detection method, and several open research questions are discussed. We've developed an open-source suite of web visualization tools tailored for
analyzing spectral and imaging data, which are being utilized in the second edition
of the RCSED galaxy energy distribution catalog (rcsed2.voxastro.org). To create
these tools, we employed Quasar and Vue.js web technologies to build engaging,
interactive viewers for visualizing galaxy spectra, SEDs, and diagnostic diagrams,
such as BPT diagrams generated from spectroscopic analysis. Leveraging client-side
processing via JavaScript minimizes server load, while maintaining seamless user
interactivity. Additionally, the adoption of modern web frameworks facilitates
extensive customization, making our visualization tools effortlessly integratable
into astronomical database websites and databases. Furthermore, this framework is
also compatible with Aladin Lite and other popular third-party web tools. By
open-sourcing our development approach, we are contributing to the astronomical
community a reusable set of web visualization solutions that other researchers
can adapt for their own research and database visualizations. To use these tools,
along with instructions for integration and development, refer to our documentation
available at https://github.com/astro-vue/rcsed-viz. We encourage other
astronomical database producers to adopt similar visualization approaches that
enhance the interpretative capabilities of galaxy data and showcase their findings.

The South Atlantic rift basin formed as part of a large intraplate rift system separating Africa and South America during the Gondwana supercontinent's break-up in the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.  Analyzing crustal deformation in Central and West Africa enabled researchers to reconstruct the pre-break-up history of the conjugate West African-Brazilian margins.  Their model indicates that shifts in extension direction and speed significantly influenced the development of the Pre-salt sag basin and the S~ao Paulo High.  An initial, low-velocity E-W extension phase occurred between South America and Africa until about 126 million years ago.  Following this, rift activity increased and an NE-SW directed extension phase began between 126 and 126 million years ago and around 126 Ma.  In this 17 million-year period the conjugate Brazilian and West African margin Pre-salt basin widths were generated.  An intermediate phase of 126.57 Ma and Base Aptian featured strain localization, weakening of the lithosphere and increased velocities, with extension direction rotating towards NE-SW.  Breakup occurred around 113 Ma and then between South America and Africa.  It occurred again at 103 Ma, with this multi-velocity, multi-directional history having a strong effect on conjugate passive margins.  It challenges the conventional model of break-up and large igneous province relationships and explains the unique characteristics of the South Atlantic conjugate margins.  It also provides evidence that large igneous provinces can form in the center of break-up rifts.  It further implies that the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province, produced during the break-up of the North Atlantic, was generated in the same manner as the South Atlantic, and that this multi-velocity, multi-directional history also applies to the North Atlantic conjugate margins.
