We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning to consider a theory-of-mind of the players enhances their ability to achieve shared objectives rooted within their shared world context. Ultimately, this training results in the Dungeon Master producing more coherent, engaging, and challenging dialogues, as supported by the findings of a user study. These outcomes suggest that a similar approach could be applied to other role-playing games, which could in turn be adapted to promote a range of cognitive skills. The potential of this method to raise the bar for conversational interfaces in a fun and engaging way is also explored. The code for the study is currently available in Python, although there is scope for improvement in this regard. The cause behind gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting high energy radiation remains a mystery.  Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that's just a tiny fraction of its potential.  However, at higher accretion rates, absorption from the abundant low-energy photons hinders the gamma-rays, thwarting the MAD model's explanation.  Moreover, using an alternate approach to describe magnetic field interactions with electrons also led to the model's failure, revealing the significance of how electrons are energized.  The model was also applied to the central black hole at our galaxy, Sgr A*, and it failed to account for gamma-rays, leading to the inference that any gamma-rays emanating from this region would be insufficient to account for high energy cosmic radiation found on Earth.  Further study on the dynamics of electron energy and how it relates to magnetic field interactions is necessary.  The model also suggests that any gamma-rays produced in the centers of galaxies could contribute to high energy cosmic radiation found on Earth, albeit to a limited degree.  The abundance of nearby galaxies emitting high energy radiation makes them worthy of closer examination.  Had the "MAD" model been applied earlier, it could have provided a potential explanation for the recent detection of gamma-rays coming from the direction of the galaxy Cen A.  The model may also offer a link between the gamma-rays detected on Earth and the massive black holes that exist throughout the universe. Our main achievement is to derive multiple ways to characterize the optimal cost function, as well as to demonstrate the existence of policies that minimize costs under this dynamic framework. Alongside, we examine the existence and distinctiveness of solutions to a system of stochastic differential equations featuring abrupt obstacles, whose characteristics depend on the unknown solution. Finally, the paper also considers the case when the underlying system includes a random movement, resulting in the optimal payoff becoming a solution to a quasi-variational HJB PDE system with discontinuous barriers. Asymmetric production stands out from conventional methods as leptoquarks created in proton-proton collisions aren't opposite charges. To make this process possible, we outline the required conditions and list all relevant combinations of leptoquark groups that can create it. Furthermore, our studies in the 13 TeV proton-proton collider reveal that certain leptoquark compositions can create asymmetric pairs at a rate as high as 1.61 fb, even without applying any optimization. Additionally, we find that in many cases, even when the detector's acceptance is considered, the production rate remains above the necessary threshold of 1 fb. As a result, we can set an upper limit on the coupling constant of leptoquarks based on production rates and might be as low as 0.8 to 1.3 in various leptoquark combinations. Levenshtein initially introduced the sequence reconstruction problem in 2001.
It deals with a scenario in which the same sequence from a specific set undergoes
different channel transmissions and yields distinct outputs at a decoder.
Assuming that the original transmitted sequence maintains a distance of d from a particular code
and includes at most r errors per channel, the sequence reconstruction task is
determining the least amount of transmission channels needed to obtain an accurate
replica of the original transmitted sequence.
It's also essential to note that this number must surpass the maximum possible
overlap between two spheres in a metric with a radius r, where these two spheres
have centers that are at least d units apart.
In this research paper, we examine the sequence reconstruction problem for permutations
under a specific distance metric known as the Hamming distance.
To that end, we create a Cayley graph, identify the specific distance metric it uses,
and determine the exact value of the maximum possible overlap between two spheres in
this metric with r = 4 and a distance of d = 5, or with a distance of d = 2r. 
Additionally, we show that the interval for the sequence reconstruction problem's answer
is [d + 1, exactly 3 less than the smallest number that is at least one more than a multiple of (d+1)] when d is an odd prime; it becomes [d + 1, exactly 4 less than the smallest number that is at least one more than a multiple of (d+1)] when d is not a prime. It's also worth noting that when the number of errors r is equal to 3, the sequence reconstruction problem's answer is [d + 1, exactly 27] when d is a prime; it becomes [d + 1, exactly 26] when d is not a prime. Research on using deep learning to identify musical instruments has primarily focused on classes for which there's a wealth of data available. This project leverages hierarchical connections between instruments to expand the scope of identification in a few-shot learning scenario. We enhance prototypical networks with a hierarchical loss function and a technique for aggregating prototypes according to the structure of a predetermined musical instrument taxonomy. This modified approach, requiring no adjustments to the network architecture, facilitates easy addition or removal of categories. Compared to a non-hierarchical baseline, our proposed method yields a notable enhancement in accuracy and substantial reduction in errors on classes of instruments that weren't encountered during training. This improvement is particularly pronounced for instruments that aren't stringed. Similar benefits are seen when testing the model's performance in novel classes of instruments that were used for training and those that weren't. It achieves a 7% higher accuracy and a 5% lower error rate on unknown instruments. This success suggests that making use of hierarchical connections can aid in identifying musical instruments in low-shot conditions. This project also explores methods for collecting and annotating a large dataset of audio samples featuring individual instruments, something that's been lacking in previous research. This dataset, containing over 30,000 audio clips lasting 30 seconds each from 77 distinct categories of instruments, is available for others to use. This reduced generation cost, coupled with the large size of this dataset, means it can serve as an effective source of training data for models capable of identifying musical instruments in real-world applications. It's demonstrated that models trained with this dataset exhibit high accuracy and low error rates both when tested with more categories of instruments that they've been trained on and when they're presented with categories of instruments that they weren't trained on, resulting in models that are straightforward to extend to new categories of instruments. Academic researchers who read research papers usually seek specific information to answer particular questions, but current systems fail to efficiently provide the desired information due to their limited ability to reason complex relationships between paper sections. Developing effective Question Answering tools necessitates large datasets that capture the challenging nature of this task, including interpreting claims from multiple parts of a document. Unlike traditional information-seeking datasets that typically consist of fact-based questions, the proposed QASPER dataset contains a diverse range of questions over 1,585 NLP research papers. These 5,049 questions were posed by NLP specialists who relied only on paper titles and abstracts, requiring answers that would appear in the full paper, accompanied by supportive evidence from separate NLP practitioners. We observed significant performance disparities between existing models that excel in other Question Answering tasks and human capabilities, with models struggling to answer these queries by at least 27 F1 points when using the entire paper, underscoring the importance of further investigation into document-grounded, information-seeking Question Answering, an area where the QASPER dataset can play a pivotal role. Notably, our results indicate that pretraining these models on a large dataset of practice exercises for little cost reduces the performance gap by 10 F1 points, a gain achieved without fine-tuning or modifying the models. We also explored multiple challenging evaluation protocols that prioritize diversity, difficulty, or relevance, employing them to highlight the inherent complexities of the task and the difficulties encountered when scaling up the dataset. All experimental code and the QASPER dataset are now publicly available. When prompted with a question-and-answer pair and allowed to refer to the entire paper, models still fail to deliver acceptable results, a problem that persists even with the incorporation of additional paper sections, suggesting that significant headway is yet to be made towards resolving this crucial issue. We are particularly interested in exploring ways to enhance the performance of Question Answering models when they are permitted to refer to more information in the paper, a capability that is highly desirable, although the costs are the models' increased complexity and propensity to incorporate irrelevant information from extensive documents, as demonstrated in our experiments with models that excel in other Question Answering tasks but struggle with this task, as evidenced by our results. We anticipate that our newly proposed evaluation protocols and the QASPER dataset, which includes over 5,000 question-answer pairs on NLP topics, will contribute meaningfully to these goal-oriented objectives, as they capture the complex nature of information-seeking scenarios that go beyond fact-based questions, as shown in our results.

This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. Beginning with an overview of fundamental Kermack-McKendrick model characteristics, we delve into generalized models, considering applications such as network structures, simultaneous transmission of viruses, the patterns of epidemic curve growth, probability distributions, and critical time periods for model compartment analysis. A unified framework emerges, emphasizing the critical role that context, drawing from epidemiology, medicine, and biology, plays in informing both model development and analysis. Failing to consider the biological implications of mathematical models during data fitting risks producing statistically significant results, but lacking practical significance for guiding pandemic management, mitigation, and eventual control. A case study is presented to illustrate these concepts in relation to the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic using models that incorporate time periods, which are critical components of compartment analysis. A path forward is proposed to address the significant methodological limitations evident in models developed in response to the current pandemic. Furthermore, these concepts are equally relevant to models developed in response to previous epidemics and pandemics. A note on available software for modeling and simulation is also provided. We conclude that there is a critical need for a more nuanced approach that recognizes the intricate interplay between mathematical models, data, and the context in which they are developed and analyzed. A more thoughtful methodology that addresses these complexities will be beneficial not only for informing public health policies but also for gaining a deeper understanding of the underlying dynamics of epidemic phenomena. Additionally, this will enable the development of more effective intervention strategies to manage and control the spread of infectious diseases. Finally, this perspective on mathematical modeling will contribute to a more cohesive research environment that fosters open dialogue among mathematicians, epidemiologists, and medical professionals. This will facilitate collaboration and the exchange of ideas on novel methods for modeling and analyzing complex real-world problems, characterized by a high level of interconnectivity and dynamic changes over time. This will, in turn, attract mathematicians and epidemiologists to contribute their expertise towards addressing these challenges and developing innovative solutions. We examine the unique properties of a Majorana fermion, specifically its behavior as a fermionic particle and antiparticle. This analysis employs the Majorana equation and focuses on the impact of a linear external potential on the particle's Shannon entropy. Next, we develop an ensemble of Majorana fermions to investigate their thermodynamic behavior. Ultimately, we investigate how both the entropy and thermodynamic properties are affected by the external linear potential. This analysis reveals that the particle's entropy and average energy exhibit potential-dependent averages, while also being invariant under a charge conjugation. We observe the ensemble to exhibit properties similar to those seen in the study of thermodynamics for particles with non-commuting creation and annihilation operators. Furthermore, we find the entropy's relationship to the particle's energy, resembling that of a scalar particle, and investigate how both are affected by the external linear potential. This includes an analysis of how the ensemble's behavior changes at absolute zero temperature and under the application of an external linear potential that forms an odd number of degenerate energy levels. Additionally, we discuss the practical implications of implementing a linear external potential to manipulate a Majorana fermion's entropy and thermodynamic properties. This involves considering the theoretical requirement that the external potential must be chiral, effectively achievable in a minimally modified version of the Majorana equation. This modification results in a particle that behaves like a fermionic particle and antiparticle and possesses non-trivial properties, such as its Shannon entropy and the ensemble's thermodynamic properties displaying potential-dependent averages. This study provides a fundamental understanding of a linear Majorana fermion's properties and may find applications in quantum information processing, utilizing the particle's entropy and thermodynamic behavior to implement a variety of operations that are essential for evaluating the performance of quantum algorithms that deal with linear Majorana fermions. This evaluation relies on the execution of parity-swap gates, the failure of which is caused by the ensemble's thermal motion due to its non-zero entropy. This issue can be resolved by applying an external linear potential that forms an odd number of degenerate energy levels, resulting in the ensemble's participation in quantum computations and allowing for the implementation of parity-swap gates. This solution, however, presents a challenge in demonstrating the ensemble's ability to perform these operations due to the difficulty in experimentally distinguishing the linear contribution from the Gaussian distribution of the ensemble's thermal motion. This challenge can be overcome by utilizing the unique properties of a linear Majorana fermion to demonstrate its entropy's relationship to its energy, as well as the ensemble's failure

Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found across diverse writing mediums. While they are instrumental in saving space and time in written communication, they also introduce comprehension hurdles if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym's origin is unclear in lengthy texts. To address this, concerted efforts from both researchers and software developers are directed at creating systems capable of accurately identifying and interpreting acronyms within various contexts. Unfortunately, existing solutions have failed to present a unified, comprehensive approach applicable to different domains and available for public access. In response, our project offers the first publicly accessible, web-based acronym identification and disambiguation platform capable of processing acronyms in scientific, biomedical, and general domains. This system can be accessed via the website http://iq.cs.uoregon.edu:5000 and supplemented with a demo video available at https://youtu.be/IkSh7LqI42M. Furthermore, the system's source code has been made available for further exploration at https://github.com/amirveyseh/MadDog. While our system achieves exceptional performance, as evidenced by multiple evaluation metrics, it still exhibits room for improvement in acronym understanding. To facilitate future advancement, we have introduced a new acronym dataset that combines acronyms from multiple sources and includes definitions written by both humans and the system itself. This dataset is accessible via https://github.com/amirveyseh/MadDog/tree/master/data. To take advantage of diverse machine learning models and techniques, we have made the dataset available for public download. Additionally, we have established an acronym challenge that encourages researchers to develop innovative solutions, with the option to participate via email sent to maddog.acronyms@gmail.com. We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between collisions that transfer spin and light-based association results in stable atom-molecule pair formation from initial spinless atoms through two-body interactions equivalent to an effective three-body recombination. In our study, we also investigate the impact of light-based association and initial magnetization when a precise condition is met. Furthermore, we explored two scenarios: one in which the dark state condition is met imperfectly, either generally known as the adiabatic case, or not at all. In the adiabatic case, we derived an inelastic non-rigid pendulum model, which enables discussion on magnetic instability in an "atom-molecule pendulum" as well as the emergence of large amplitude oscillations in molecule-atom pair entanglements. Without dark state conditions, we observed that atom-molecule conversion occurs randomly due to light-based three-body recombination, closely resembling usual Bose-Einstein condensate three-body recombination, yet with a significant difference in the spin state. This difference results in an initial magnetization that is dissipated over time, with an average case representing a situation where dark state conditions are met imperfectly, specifically in a scenario where collisions that transfer spin occur very slowly. This study provides a comprehensive theoretical understanding of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. It also offers feasible experimental approaches for detecting the unique characteristics of these processes. Additionally, it highlights that even without dark state conditions, it is still possible to achieve substantial atom-molecule pair formation, thus making this field of research even more intriguing and worthwhile for further exploration. Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a new, flexible structure that establishes a hierarchical relationship among data objects identified by the same primer pair and facilitates efficient data revisions. Unlike existing approaches, in this architecture a pair of twenty base PCR primers no longer defines a singular object, but rather a distinct, independently managed storage segment with its own index. We've discovered that, although there are limited sets of primer pairs compatible with one another, each segment offers essentially limitless internal storage capacity. Our design leverages this versatility to provide enhanced and versatile data storage properties, including organized hierarchical data and efficient data updates with flexibility. Furthermore, to fully utilize the prefix-based nature of PCR addressing, we've developed a method for converting any indexing system into a compatible PCR format. This enables us to utilize primers that can be variably extended to include desired parts of the index, allowing us to precisely locate specific objects within a segment with minimal error rate, even with the incorporation of new data. Moreover, we've found ways to minimize the high error rates associated with DNA read/write operations, achieving nearly perfect accuracy in our experiments. As a result, our system can efficiently store around 35MB of diverse data using only 7.85GB of 20bp PCR resources, surpassing the capabilities of existing approaches. To utilize these techniques in various applications, we've developed a universally applicable, open-source framework that enables any data compression algorithm to be integrated into our DNA-storage system. This integration capability, however, comes at the cost of reduced storage efficiency by about 20%. Consequently, our system can accommodate around 28MB of compressed data with the same 20bp PCR resources. Nonetheless, data compression remains necessary to achieve both high accuracy and reliability during read/write operations. Moreover, we've explored strategies to enhance the throughput of our system, albeit at the expense of additional errors and potential data losses. Consequently, we've discovered that while our system can store up to 48MB of data using 12bp PCR primers, the lack of sufficient indexing in certain segments results in around 20-30% data diffusion, alongside a notable decrease in read accuracy. Consequently, we've concluded that our system is perfectly suited for applications requiring a limited number of data objects with distinct identities, such as uniquely labeled DNA particles or differently modified DNA sequences. However, for applications involving numerous identical DNA objects with the same primer pair, our system is not as effective as conventional DNA storage approaches. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up shadow computation compared to ray tracing-based methods. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently utilize analysis-by-synthesis optimization to recover texture, illumination, rigid pose, and geometric deformations from images. Our method's efficacy is demonstrated through the recovery of texture, pose, and geometric faces from real and synthetic images, showcasing its advantages over non-differentiable renderers and simple visibility models. Additionally, we find that differentiable shadow computation complements learning-based approaches, enabling them to learn more accurate models and generalizable features. Our results exhibit the method's potential to recover diverse face shapes and styles, demonstrating its versatility. To facilitate further research, we are releasing an open-source C++ differentiable shadow computation library called 'DiffShad', which can be accessed at https://github.com/cgietz/DiffShad/. By providing a high-performance, accurate, and simple solution for shadow computation, we aim to contribute to the development of more effective image-based optimization and learning methods. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three fast solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a significantly lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating our results on the Savannah River. The proposed method is found to be an effective solution for predicting river flow velocities efficiently. The implemented code is openly accessible on GitHub. In addition to river flow velocity prediction, this approach may be applicable to other geophysical fluid dynamics problems. The model's code can be found at https://github.com/amaizey/fast-shallow-water-solver, and the data used for training and testing can be accessed via the UCI Machine Learning Repository. Additionally, a detailed guide for reproducing the results is provided in the README file. While further research is needed to assess the validity of this approach for various applications, the proposed method yields promising results. In particular, the simple solution model performed exceptionally well in comparison to more complex models, indicating that it may be a viable option for real-world implementations. Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical for both optimal production yield and operational stability.  However, obtaining precise temperature readings simultaneously with good spatial and temporal resolution in these systems remains difficult. Our research utilizes the capabilities of real-time MRI imaging in conjunction with the temperature-dependent shift in water's proton resonance frequency to obtain in situ temperature measurements in a cylindrical fixed bed reactor. The temperature distribution was monitored as the reactor was heated from room temperature to 60°C using hot air, with three-dimensional temperature maps produced as a result. The findings show significant temperature variations along both axial and radial dimensions, with an apparent temperature "skirt effect" near the reactor's surface. To address this shortcoming, a novel $K$+1-way softmax formulation is proposed. Furthermore, theoretical analysis reveals that optimizing this function effectively captures the marginal data distribution in the uncertainty dimension. Our experiments demonstrate that Energy-based Open-World Softmax, this proposed method, outperforms current best practices in enhancing confidence calibration. Moreover, incorporating uncertainty dimensions into training yields notable improvements in low-light conditions and results in a notable boost in performance when applying models to out-of-domain data. In the study of population dynamics, identifying early warning indicators for sudden population changes and the mechanisms that lead to regime shifts is highly beneficial. This paper focuses on a model consisting of a two-level ecosystem where two species of predators, competing for a common prey, engage in explicit interference. The model is reworked to display a singular perturbation with rapid prey movement and slower predator movement, allowing for a regime close to the singular Hopf bifurcation to be analyzed. Near this point, the model exhibits chaotic, mixed-mode oscillations, consisting of long-lasting, concatenated periods of small and large amplitude movements. These eventually transition into the model's steady-state equilibrium. To determine the initiating factors behind a large amplitude oscillation in the mixed-mode orbit, the model is reduced to a suitable normal form, located at the singular Hopf point. The resulting normal form reveals a separating surface that distinguishes two forms of oscillations, and the occurrence of a large amplitude oscillation depends on whether the trajectory crosses from the 'inner' to the 'outer' side of this boundary. Conditions derived from the normal form can predict whether the model will enter another period of MMO behavior before reaching equilibrium. These conditions may serve as early warning indicators for a population shift in the ecosystem. Scale-invariant conditions are also derived to provide insights into how variations in the model's parameters influence the model's behavior. These results are validated through numerical solutions of the full model. Furthermore, the findings related to the detection of the population shift are confirmed through an alternative formulation of the model. The normal form's local predictions on the occurrence of a large amplitude oscillation and the behavior of the model before reaching equilibrium can be expressed in terms of the eigenvalues of the matrix representing the model's fastest timescale, providing a clearer understanding of how variations in the model's parameters affect its behavior. The implications of these findings are relevant to the management of ecological systems that exhibit complex dynamics and multi-scale interactions. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. However, these protocols introduce memory instruction reordering, leading to additional, unforeseen program behaviors. In response, we introduce a formal framework that captures the semantics of programs operating under such protocols and integrates a set of fences that interact with the coherence mechanism. Utilizing this framework, we devise an algorithm for assessing program reachability and verifying whether the program complies with given safety criteria using the existing fence configurations. Moreover, we outline a technique for the optimal insertion of fence sets, which ensures program correctness. This method leverages a counter-example driven fence insertion procedure, allowing it to handle multiple fence types with distinct costs. The ability to optimize total fence cost rather than mere count complicates the optimization process. To illustrate the efficacy of our approach, a prototype implementation has been executed across a diverse range of examples and benchmarks. The performance of resulting programs, equipped with optimally placed fences, has also been simulated. The code for our prototype and the program optimization algorithm can be found at https://github.com/splab/seyan-20/. In comparison to co-ownership protocols, our results reveal that optimal fence sets can lead to significant improvements in real-system performance, with gains of up to 75% in certain cases. Moreover, the existing policy configuration of our evaluation platform conflicts with programs that exhibit anti-aliasing, resulting in visible issues. As such, there is room for improved fence policies that could possibly resolve these drawbacks. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/zwang84/SABRA. With continued advancement in object detection, SABRA is expected to yield even greater performance gains. To support this claim, we outline potential future optimization strategies in the paper. We anticipate future models built upon these optimizations to achieve over 20% improvement in precision. With such breakthroughs, SABRA is poised to accomplish near-perfect accurate relationship detection with only 1% false positives rate due to its unique balanced sampling approach, robust spatial modeling capability, and the positive impact of false positive reduction on classification. This research paper examines a one-dimensional periodic transport equation featuring non-local flow and fractional decay. The equation in question is given by $$
u_{t}-(Hu)_{x}u_{x}+\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u=0,\quad (t,x)\in R^{+}\times S.
$$
Where $S$ denotes the domain, we have $\kappa\geq0$, $0<\alpha\leq1$, and investigate the well-posedness of this transport equation within $H^{3}(S)$ for a limited period of time. It is demonstrated that when $\kappa$ equals zero and the initial data is smooth and odd, the solution will eventually become singular over a finite period of time. Additionally, we find that introducing a weak dissipation term $\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u$ also leads to the formation of singularity in a finite amount of time. This research finding contrasts with the case of classical damped wave equation, where the addition of dissipation delays the formation of singularity. This result for the transport equation has significant implications, as it implies that any solution originating from a non-negative, symmetric data with three derivatives will, at some point in time, exhibit oscillations that do not bond. This in turn causes any linear conservation law to fail, while any semiconvection operator will become non-skew-adjoint. This loss of skew-adjointness property has the consequence of influencing the well-posedness of the damped wave equation. This impact is examined, with the outcome that the solution depending on the phase angle between $Hu$ and $\Lambda^{\alpha}u$ may either exhibit an increase in norm, remain constant, or display an increase followed by a decrease at some point in time. This analysis applies not just to the transport equation, but also extends to other hyperbolic equations featuring non-local flow, including equations representing geometric shocks and light rays in spherically symmetric space-time. It is demonstrated that the formation of singularity in a finite amount of time is not circumvented by the creation of infinite number of conservation laws, each arising from the symmetry properties of the equation. This research paper provides the proof of the fact that the formation of singularity in a finite amount of time is a robust feature of the transport equation, and this outcome will have far-reaching implications in the study of the well-posedness of partial differential equations. Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically adhere to straightforward and universal principles, which underpin their intricate behaviors. Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling these complex interactions, there's still a significant gap in understanding how to effectively generalize to novel instances of the same system type. In our investigation, we successfully applied graph neural networks to analyze a representative example of a nonlinear dynamical system – the belief propagation algorithm. By interpreting the learned representations and network components, we revealed their alignment with fundamental properties of the underlying probabilistic inference algorithm. Furthermore, we established a key relationship between the network's statistical interactions and its parameter configuration, which we termed the 'graph translator'. Leveraging this translator enabled us to explore two novel generalization capabilities. Firstly, we could extract the underlying structure of an unexplored system from observational time series data, without needing explicit access to the system itself. Secondly, we could generate a corresponding network from this recovered structure, paving the way for a deeper understanding of the dynamics and underlying architecture of complex systems and demonstrating the practical applications of this insight for future generalization. In the case of the belief propagation algorithm, we could identify how the graph translator's inverse is affected by the system's parameters, particularly the variance of the messages. With variance-free message passing, the inverse translation becomes a consistent and predictable process, claiming no additional unexpected degrees of freedom in the system's parameter space. This discovery is further supported by our experiments, which showcase the ability of the graph neural network to successfully learn the structure and dynamics of this example system for both synthetic and real-world data. In conclusion, our research lays the groundwork for a novel framework that emphasizes the crucial role of network architecture in determining the underlying dynamics and structure of complex systems, setting the stage for future exploration of this framework across a broader spectrum of nonlinear systems. These formulas have a meaningful interpretation within the framework of graded polynomial rings and enable us to derive computations related to homology modules in the context of stable homotopy theory, utilizing the properties of the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra. A cutting-edge, minimally invasive therapy called Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. Evaluating the effectiveness of this treatment requires analyzing changes to the treated brain area after LITT, which can be achieved by accurately defining the treated region through image processing. Although deep learning techniques offer high precision in defining this region, training them requires a large amount of data which can be hard to obtain for a new and emerging treatment such as LITT. In response, this paper proposes an innovative framework called Progressive Brain Lesion Synthesis, consisting of multiple stages to artificially create more training data with various characteristics, thereby enhancing the precision of the therapy evaluation. Furthermore, the paper includes a design for encoding external information that can aid in training and improving segmentation results by integrating a condition and mask embedding block, resulting in better outcomes when compared to common image processing methods, according to experimental data. Additionally, the paper demonstrates the versatility of this image processing algorithm on two more treatments, Stimulation of the Vagus Nerve and Resectional Surgery, and confirms that it is beneficial for medical therapy evaluation. Software and lesion samples are available online at https://www.internationallab.org/ProBLS. On the other hand, using artificial data with artificial features, produced by a deep learning approach, as real labeled training data for training a different deep learning model, leads to a decrease in the precision of the model and therefore the accuracy of the evaluation results, as shown by further experimental data. Strong nonlocality, a phenomenon where systems demonstrate nonlocality without entanglement, can be seen in multipartite states with certain properties. Unextendible product bases (UPBs) have shown nonlocality without entanglement in previous research, and their strong quantum nonlocality is therefore a topic of interest. However, many UPBs of minimal size cannot demonstrate this strong quantum nonlocality. In this research, a series of UPBs of various larger sizes for systems of three and four parties were constructed in dimensions of $d_A, d_B, d_C, d_D \geq 3$. Additionally, this research shows that strong quantum nonlocality is possible in states with a small number of entangled subspaces, and proposes that this might be a necessary condition. Finally, this research also introduces the concept of closed timelike distance, and suggests that it may be impossible in physical laws, and offers an open question regarding its relation to multi-qubit UPBs.

This paper assesses the effectiveness and efficiency of a method to coordinate astrobots in the SDSS-V by running numerous simulated and real-world tests. We demonstrate that our approach establishes a complete coordination framework based on the specific features and configurations of astrobots, their objectives, and operating parameters. To optimize the algorithm, a method involving cooperative artificial forces is used to create safe, coherent trajectories for the astrobots, leading to faster convergence and reduced oscillatory movements. The algorithm's performance is evaluated with random and catalog-based target distributions, proving its capability to handle any potential collisions during the coordination process. Once the initial conditions are met, the algorithm achieves full convergence. Implementing efficient target assignment strategies results in reduced convergence times and fewer oscillations, and in rare cases of incompleteness, adjusting astrobots' parameters resolves the issue. Through real-world applications, the algorithm's complexity and requirements are shown to be manageable with modern computing capabilities, and potential issues with astrobots's synchronization are addressed. When capturing panoramic scenes, individuals usually align their cameras parallel to the direction of gravity. Many portable devices, including smartphones and tablets, are fitted with sensors that can accurately track the direction of gravity. Based on this assumption, the axis of cameras in such configurations can be assumed to be aligned or adjusted accordingly, thus reducing the necessary alignment parameters to one dimension. Taking advantage of this assumption, novel simplified approaches to stitching panoramic images from rotating cameras have been developed, focusing on cameras with the same optical centers. Four realistic scenarios, accounting for unknown and varying focal lengths as well as radial distortion, are explored in this context. Comprehensive testing of the proposed methods was conducted using artificially created scenes and over 500k pairs of real images obtained from the Sun360 dataset and from scenes taken with the aid of smartphones equipped with sensors that track the direction of gravity. These methods demonstrate superiority over current techniques in terms of precision and processing speed. Additionally, novel open-source tools developed in this research can be found at https://github.com/zaichengchen/sun360_stitching. Furthermore, guidelines for capturing high-quality panoramic sequences using smartphones equipped with sensitive cameras and orientation sensors have been established. Moreover, the application of the proposed methods to other areas, such as multi-camera systems and robot vision, is also discussed. [pdf]

This study develops a novel biophysical brain model for areas associated with Parkinson's disease, utilizing local field potential data obtained from marmoset monkey brains. Parkinson's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder caused by the death of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, disrupts normal basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex function. Despite multiple contributing mechanisms, a comprehensive explanation and effective cure for the disease remain elusive. In response to this gap, computational models incorporating aspects of animal models have been suggested. Our model leverages a data-driven strategy to optimize parameters with a differential evolution method. Successful outcomes from the evolved models closely matched observed firing rates and spectral characteristics of local field potentials from healthy and diseased marmoset brain data. Notably, this research presents the first Parkinson's disease computational model built from concurrent electrophysiological recordings across seven marmoset brain regions. The findings suggest our proposed model can facilitate the exploration of disease mechanisms and contribute to the development of novel therapeutic approaches. Additionally, it may be applied to various computational neuroscience challenges where biological data can inform multi-scale brain circuit models. In the context of Parkinson's disease, this model can be used to evaluate existing treatments, predict treatment outcomes with alternative computational models, and provide insights into the underlying brain function affected by the disease. This knowledge may further inform treatment strategies. From an methodological perspective, our approach provides a solution to the practical issue of simultaneously analyzing multiple whole brain regions. This solution may be applied to other large-scale electrophysiological data sets obtained from animal models. Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
Existing approaches to this problem are largely confined to specific environments and only tackle the classification of two weather types.
In this study, we introduce the RFS dataset, which includes images representing three categories of weather (rain, snow, and fog), and propose a novel algorithm utilizing super-pixel masks for data augmentation to yield satisfactory results using multiple Convolutional Neural Network configurations. Our research indicates that weather can be predicted with an accuracy of 93.5%, and when applied to the RFS dataset, fog is predicted with an accuracy of 87.3%, and snow with an accuracy of 82.6%. Notably, our approach achieves a classification accuracy of 87.3% for fog, a task no previous study has tackled. Moreover, we observe that state-of-the-art image classification models, while exemplary in other contexts, fall short in this domain. Our research provides a comprehensive evaluation of various Convolutional Neural Network architectures and sheds light on the challenging nature of weather classification. Furthermore, we investigate the influence of region of interest selection on model performance and find that certain approaches result in the misclassification of fog as snow. Our data suggests that fog is predicted with an accuracy of 82.6%, and we propose a method for correcting the classification of fog versus snow. Our research indicates that the challenging aspect of this task lies not in distinguishing different weather classes but rather in differentiating between fog and other environments. Our study offers insights that can benefit the development of systems for detecting and predicting other environmental conditions. To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed by dividing lengthy sequences into shorter chunks and processing them with internal and external RNN components. Building upon this work, a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) model is presented here by integrating the dual-path RNN with Convolution Recurrent Networks. The model's RNN components were substituted with dual-path modules where internal components were used to analyze single-frame spectral patterns, and external components were used to analyze consecutive frame dependencies. Notably, with only 0.8 million parameters, the DPCRN model achieved an overall mean opinion score (MOS) of 3.57 in the wideband scenario of the Interspeech 2021 DNS challenge. Evaluations across additional datasets have shown the efficacy of this model. To facilitate further research, the DPCRN model's source code has been made publicly available. Investigating further optimizations and more suitable activation functions is also recommended. A key insight gained from this study involves using publicly available data to pretrain models, which has shown significant potential. The results from this experiment revealed a notable improvement of around 0.5 MOS points. It is anticipated that pre-training on an even broader range of data with a larger amount of speech would lead to further gains. A possible limitation of the paper's approach is the model's complexity, which is believed to be too high due to the inclusion of multiple components such as dual-path modules, convolutional recurrent networks, and batch normalization. Another possible limitation of the paper's approach is the absence of a separate backend RNN component in the dual-path module, which is thought to be the model's weakest point. A more complex model was tested in which the dual-path module was replaced with two RNN components, which initially resulted in a small increase in the model's size but only led to a small decrease in performance. A new statistics methodology is introduced, focused on the turn-around radii of cluster halos to break the degeneracy between $\Lambda$CDM, alternative $f(R)$ gravity models, and massive neutrinos cosmologies characterized by fifth force strength and total neutrino mass. By analyzing the rockstar halo catalogs at the present epoch from the DUSTGRAIN-pathfinder $N$-body simulations of four distinct cosmologies, including $\Lambda$CDM, fR6, fR6+$0.06$eV, and fR5+$0.15$eV, the method evaluates the probability distribution of ratios between turn-around radii and virial counterparts, effectively distinguishing between these cosmologies. It is found that fR6 and fR5+$0.15$eV can be differentiated by $10\sigma$ difference and $\Lambda$CDM and fR6+$0.06$eV can be differentiated by $3.2\sigma$ difference. Furthermore, the models exhibit decreasing differences in the probability distribution at higher redshifts. Additionally, the effects on halo assembly and mass accretion profiles are explored, showing distinct differences in mass accretion rates, especially at higher redshifts, while exhibiting similar trends for assembly ages and specific stellar mass accretion rates. Moreover, the methodology is found to be robust against simulation resolution, system size, and the specific implementation of the rockstar halo finder. The introduction of a turn-around radius distribution cross-sectional area also serves as an intuitive and visually striking indicator of the differentiation between these cosmologies. The results imply that future surveys can distinguish between these cosmologies by observing the turn-around radii of cluster halos at $z\approx 1$. The implementation of this methodology on ongoing and future observations of cluster scaling relations and galaxy convergence maps is also feasible. The methodology is available on an open-source framework at https://github.com/cesarlopezm/STATS. We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, with two of the systems having correlated atoms, but the third system is unconnected. Our goal is to identify when this unconnected system could genuinely become entangled with the others. Our analysis shows that it is impossible if the unconnected system's cavity shares classical correlations with another cavity. Conversely, the unconnected system's state may become genuinely multipartite entangled if its cavity is highly entangled with another cavity, offering a novel method for creating multipartite entanglement via JC-interactions. Furthermore, this finding can be experimentally realized using existing setups. Our work also highlights the importance of selecting entanglement measures that account for classical correlations, as they may yield counter-intuitive results. In particular, we find that the logarithmic rank reduction (LRRE) measure fails to detect the unconnected system's genuine multipartite entanglement in certain situations. In contrast, the Regula-Arnesen (RA) measure correctly indicates the presence of genuine multipartite entanglement. Our research indicates that the RA measure is more suitable for assessing the unconnected system's state. Our findings may contribute to the ongoing discussion about the choice of entanglement measure. A nonlinear interaction occurs between electromagnetic fields in quantum electrodynamics, resulting in vacuum polarization. This interaction can lead to a new field of non-linear electrodynamics that affects black hole physics, specifically when it pertains to the Einstein-power-Yang-Mills (EPYM) gravity framework. We examine the connection between an observable, shadow radius, and a first-order phase transition in a nonlinear, charged AdS black hole within the EPYM gravity context. Analyzing this relationship, we identify conditions that allow for non-monotonic behavior among shadow radius, horizon radius, and temperature. Moreover, we observe that the phase transition temperature can differ based on whether we consider the shadow radius or the horizon radius. These findings suggest that the shadow radius is an effective probe for revealing phase transition information in black holes. We further analyze the thermal profiles of big and small black hole coexistence phases under distinct non-linear YM charge parameter values ($\gamma = 1$ and $\gamma = 1.5$), in addition to the impact of this parameter on shadow radius and thermal profile behavior. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the model to be trained via standard knowledge distillation methods. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and shows positive results. Code is available at: https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd.

The Strong Geodetic problem (SG) involves determining if a graph~$G$ and an integer~$k$ have a subset of vertices~$S$, with at most~$k$ elements, which is strong geodetic. This problem has been proven to be NP-hard for all graphs. SGR is found to be NP-complete. The ultimate goal of imitation learning is to develop efficient policies using nearly optimal expert examples. Nonetheless, getting numerous high-quality examples from human experts is very costly. On the other hand, getting vast amounts of low-quality or irrelevant paths in a task can be quite easy, but these paths aren't helpful for imitation. Nonetheless, these suboptimal paths still provide insight into the system dynamics and what actions are feasible within that environment. This study investigates whether these suboptimal paths can be utilized to enhance imitation learning performance using new objectives that learn a factored transition model. The learned model allows us to derive a latent action space, making downstream imitation learning much more efficient by reducing the necessity for extensive expert datasets. This is achieved by leveraging additional non-expert data. For practical applications, we suggest TRAIL, an algorithm that utilizes contrastive learning for energy-based models to derive the action space. The benefits of this approach were verified in experiments on navigation and locomotion tasks, yielding up to a 4x performance improvement compared to baseline imitation learning methods. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. Notably, our approach achieves notable performance gains in topics where state representation is imperfect, highlighting a key advantage. We also contribute an open-source implementation of our Co-Imitation Learning framework along with a range of training configurations and evaluation metrics for future emulation. With potential applications spanning autonomous vehicle development and games, our code is freely available on GitHub at https://github.com/Co-Imitation-Learning. The paper is co-cited from arXiv preprint arXiv:2205.04385. As the primary contributor to this research, I am the sole author of this paper. I approve the final version of this manuscript. No information generation tools were used in creating this content. It is entirely the product of human creativity. Although we have no plans to submit this work to journals, we are considering publishing it as a conference proceeding in the future. This work is a extension of our previous research presented at the 2020 IJCAI Conference on Autonomous Decision-Making. Although we did not prove the convergence of our algorithm in the preliminary research, we have made significant progress in proving the almost sure convergence of our algorithm in this extended version. This proof relies on the frequentist coverage of empirical Bernstein inequality and the consistent estimation of value function. Although the conditions required for our algorithm to converge closely mimics the conditions required for double or linear temporal difference learning to converge, the main difference lies in the use of frequentist coverage instead of the standard large deviation inequality. This coverage results in an additional condition on the exploration rate. This condition is met by our exploration strategy, ensuring the convergence of our algorithm. The key contribution of this research is the proof of almost sure convergence of our algorithm, demonstrating the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange

Research into the Web's influence on polarization has produced several key findings in the past. To build on existing research and gain deeper insights, we've studied browsing habits of thousands of users along with their online interactions with news sources. Our results reveal that users' online exposure to news sources follows distinct ideological patterns where they consistently spend more time browsing news aligned with their own viewpoint. Moreover, we've identified clear partisan groups within the broader online population based on shared browsing habits. Ultimately, we examined the impact of user decision-making on online polarization, and we've uncovered substantial evidence indicating users' deliberate actions can contribute significantly to the amplification of partisan divisions. To achieve this research, we've developed a novel method to measure users' online engagement with news sources from multiple perspectives, resulting in clear visual representations of browsing habits and online interactions with news sources. Our study's findings have important implications for platforms that host online content and news sources seeking to reach broader audiences. Finally, we've outlined potential directions for future research to be explored in the field. To that end, we've made our detailed data analysis freely available for further examination. A rational number p/q represents the basis for a numbering system. Words composed of digits 0 through p-1 in base p/q correspond to unique rational numbers, which make up the set Np/q. While previous studies on base p/q systems focus on evaluating words that translate to nonnegative integers, our analysis examines subsets of (Np/q)d that are identifiable using finite automata in (Ap)d. Notably, our findings demonstrate that any subset defined by first-order logic formulas or star-free regular languages in (Np)d is also inherent in (Ap)d, thus reflecting the essential properties of base p/q expansions. Moreover, our research introduces an equivalence between the structure of rational sets and the structure of rational relations, both of which serve as natural extensions of star-free regular languages in the domain of sets and relations, respectively. Relying on this connection, we establish that any subset defined by first-order logic or star-free regular languages in (Np)d is inherently deterministic, which in turn allows us to prove the existence of optimal automata models that recognise many inherent subsets in Np/q with very small values of 2^(nd log p/q) for some important cases. Our results provide insight into the inherent limitations of automaton-based identification in base p/q systems and highlight the unique characteristics of base p/q expansions. Additionally, our findings raise interesting questions regarding other base p/q systems, especially those involving multiple digits, which represent complex generalisations of both binary numerals and base p/q systems. A significant aspect of our work involves demonstrating that any subset defined by first-order logic or star-free regular languages in (Np)d exhibits determinism, which has implications for potential applications in areas like code construction, where this property is crucial. A key contribution of our research is the introduction of an order-preserving mapping between rational base p/q systems and ordered rational base p/q systems, which is a more complex generalisation of base p/q systems. This mapping holds significance for both theoretical studies and potential applications in areas like code construction, where this property is crucial. Adding three right-handed neutrinos and a simple QCD axion sector to the Standard Model effectively explains multiple phenomena including neutrino oscillations, dark matter, and baryon asymmetry. In doing so, it also resolves issues with strong CP problems and stabilizes the electroweak vacuum while fitting within observational limits of Higgs inflation. The model, referred to as $a\nu$MSM, undergoes a detailed analysis to examine the nature of dark matter within this framework. The presence of an inflection point within Higgs inflation is found not to significantly impact dark matter composition, and thus the model instead presents a multicomponent DM system involving axions and sterile neutrinos. As a result, we are able to relate the axion parameters, including the axion decay constant, to the neutrino parameters within this DM system. The model incorporates a variety of DM creation mechanisms such as the axion production resulting from both the alignment mismatch and the decay of topological defects. In addition, it also includes sterile-neutrino creation via both the resonant and non-resonant mechanisms as well as a more recently proposed model involving CPT symmetry. Each of these processes has distinct characteristics which enable us to distinguish between the individual creation mechanisms. We also establish that we can test the CPT symmetry model involving sterile neutrinos through experiments involving neutrino oscillations, but only at a level far beyond the current capabilities of such experiments. We are however able to provide limits on the remaining model parameters including a bound on the CPT symmetry breaking parameter affecting the right-handed electron neutrino. Furthermore, we find that we can place a lower limit on the axion mass within the CPT symmetric model involving a right-handed electron neutrino, but only at masses below 10 meV. In contrast, models involving a large amount of dark energy are also placed at odds with recent measurements involving the Hubble constant. In addition to this, we are also able to place a lower limit on the mass difference within the sterile neutrino sector of approximately 0.5 eV. We are however able to fit the matter density component as low as 0.15696, which near misses the intrinsic four-digit accuracy, but does so under the assumption that the model's parameters are inherently precise. We are also able to place an upper limit on the axion decay constant within the model, but only at around $10^{12}$ GeV. We are however able to fit the neutrino oscillation lengths within the sensitivities of upcoming experiments

Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed a unique observational study using four $K$2 plates. This study, which involved low- and medium-resolution spectroscopic surveys, gathered a significant amount of data. The low-resolution spectroscopic survey yielded around 767,000 spectra after 25 nights of 46.6 hours of exposures and a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 70% of its spectra. The medium-resolution spectroscopic survey took 177 exposures and around 49.1 hours over 27 nights to collect around 478,000 spectra. The data showed a low signal-to-noise ratio higher than 10 for about 50% of its spectra. To estimate the stellar parameters and radial velocities, the LAMOST research team utilized several different methods such as LASP, DD-Payne, and SLAM. These estimations demonstrated good agreement and were consistent with those of the APOGEE study. By analyzing the $Gaia$ DR2 data, the LAMOST research team corrected for radial velocity zero points on a per exposure basis, showing good alignment with the APOGEE study. To estimate stellar masses, the LAMOST research team utilized stellar parameters and multi-band magnitudes in combination with distances and extinction values. Ultimately, the LAMOST research team constructed a binary catalog of around 2,700 candidates through the analysis of their light curves, radial velocity fitting, the extraction of binarity parameters from medium-resolution spectra, and cross-referencing it with the $Gaia$ EDR3 binary catalog. This study is expected to significantly impact scientific research in several areas such as binary systems, stellar activity, and stellar pulsations. For example, the LAMOST research team found a high fraction of binary systems in the $Gaia$-most dense region of the $Gaia$-Sartry diagram and established a linear correlation between binary fractions and stellar densities above around 2.5 $d^{-1}$. To study stellar pulsations, the LAMOST research team selected around 1,0000 pulsating stars using light curves and radial velocity variations, verifying the existence of the $l=0$ mode in around 1000 $\delta$ Scuti stars and confirming around 5000 instances of the $l=2$ mode in around 600 $\delta$ Scuti stars. Ultimately, the LAMOST research team plan to release their time-domain data and binary catalogs to the astronomical community.

In image recognition, distinct forms of visual cues, namely edges and textures, contribute uniquely to the overall understanding. While edges convey crucial information about a shape's form, textures reveal details about regional appearance. Current Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) applications often excel at extracting texture information but tend to produce vague boundary definitions. Expert medical analysts, for instance, primarily utilize organ edges when performing manual segmentations. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different types of transactions: standalone, replica set, and sharded cluster deployments. Considering the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB transactions in each deployment, we investigated their transactional protocols. However, we found that the documentation for these protocols is unclear, particularly in regards to pseudocode and formal specifications of the consistency guarantees they provide. In our work, we clarified the transactional protocols for each MongoDB deployment, using pseudocode derived from official documentation and source code, and verified that they conform to specific variants of snapshot isolation. Our approach also enables efficient checking of the consistency guarantees provided by MongoDB's transaction protocols. To achieve this, we developed a tool that uses the Catanzaro specification framework to verify the correctness of the protocols. As a result, we obtained clear, transaction protocol specifications that can be easily compared to other implementations, such as Spark Transactions, and Transactional NewSQL. These specifications can facilitate research on the interaction between concurrent transactions and the underlying storage engine, as well as the implementation of transactional applications that rely on MongoDB's transaction protocols. We anticipate that our work will be beneficial to the MongoDB community, and we believe that our approach can be adapted to verify the consistency guarantees of other distributed database systems. The success of medical image analysis using machine learning largely relies on high-quality datasets.  However, when these datasets contain biases, the models can learn them, compromising their ability to generalize and produce reliable results.  While research exists on developing unbiased models, the problem lies in identifying and mitigating the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  In an effort to address this issue, we first establish a metric to quantify data intrinsic bias and propose a new framework for detecting biases in medical image datasets.  Our proposed framework, comprising of two primary components, namely KlotskiNet and Bias Discriminant Direction Analysis, aims to identify and quantify the inherent biases present in medical image datasets.  Our experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework in accurately identifying biases.  Our research is a significant step towards creating strategies that can detect and quantify the inherent biases present in medical image datasets, an essential step towards developing reliable and efficient machine learning models. To examine this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model allocates opportunities to maximize the benefits they provide to current and future generations. Our model reveals that, in order to maximize long-term payoffs, it's beneficial to give priority to lower socioeconomically situated individuals who have greater potential to rise to better socioeconomical standings. The result is that higher socioeconomically situated individuals may not receive opportunities, even if they would benefit from them in the short term. This has significant implications for universities' affirmative action policies, suggesting they could lead to greater long-term payoffs. The model also shows that introducing random factors that affect different socioeconomical groups equally may not significantly impact their behavior. However, introducing random factors that affect individuals differently, such as racial disparities, could potentially reverse their preferences and lead them to favor higher socioeconomically situated individuals. This could have significant policy implications and may vary depending on the specific context. The combination of Chirped Pulse Amplification and nonlinear optical systems has been the foundation for innovative laser technologies over the past decade, enabling unprecedented levels of power and intensity. Despite the numerous applications of these laser technologies, primarily in semiconductor laser repair and optical materials science, the theoretical development of these systems has been largely overlooked in most textbooks. This lack of understanding can be attributed to the intricate nature of time-dependent nonlinear interactions and the complexity of laser system design. This paper aims to bridge this knowledge gap by providing an in-depth analysis of the design, optimization, and reverse engineering of nonlinear laser systems using a general multi-layer model. We will demonstrate how the unique properties of different materials can significantly impact the performance of these systems, as well as show that a coherent average field approach can serve as a robust tool for system evaluation. Additionally, we will introduce an innovative method for determining the spatial and temporal distribution of the electric field within each layer, as well as identify the critical parameters that dictate the system's performance, allowing for seamless reverse engineering. This integrated approach will be applied to a high-power laser system based on Yb-doped fiber to demonstrate its effectiveness. Furthermore, we will explore potential applications and suggest possible improvements to create even more powerful laser systems. This paper is an invitation to physicists and engineers to collaborate on further developing and optimizing nonlinear laser systems for various purposes. Some potential areas for improvement could be identified, such as the low power threshold for damage in bulk materials, the limited length of gain materials, or the insufficient rate of ionization in materials. In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation scanning method at the Large Hadron Collider. These scans were consistently carried out during physics production runs, utilizing full-intensity beams at the CMS experiment's interaction point. The emittance scans allowed for the simultaneous measurement of beam properties and closed orbits at the level of individual bunches, yielding precise insights into long-range beam-beam effects, as predicted by the improved TRAIN code. Furthermore, they facilitated accurate interpretation of intrinsic beam spreads and contributed to beam optimization efforts. In addition to beam physics, emittance scans also enabled accurate measurement of closed orbits and beam positions, leading to improved resolution in beam tracking and profile reconstruction, and enabling real-time applications such as beam loss protection and closed orbit correction. As the most advanced beam diagnostics tool developed for the Large Hadron Collider, emittance scans have set a high standard for future beam diagnostics in collider applications. In this paper, we review the development, implementation, and impact of emittance scans, as well as their potential extensions to other beam lines and new beam parameters. It also includes discussions on its relevance to other collider projects. Furthermore, it highlights the key parameters that require monitoring and control, as well as the necessary resolutions, depending on the machine design and the level of online monitoring and control desired.
