The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to extract details about a sample's molecular, atomic, or nuclear components. Although scattered light conveys both amplitude and phase information, this phase information is frequently lost during standard intensity measurements, yet it is crucial for reconstructing essential details of a target, as evident from applications like coherent x-ray imaging. A new algorithm is introduced that allows for retrieving phase information from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra, a feature we demonstrate with x-ray scattering off M\"ossbauer nuclei using a synchrotron radiation source. The knowledge gained through phase information also leads to accurate reconstruction of energy spectra from experimental data, a level of precision that cannot be achieved with other methods. Our approach provides a useful data analysis tool, offering a beneficial impact on x-ray quantum optics and M\"ossbauer spectroscopy that employs synchrotron radiation. Additionally, there is potential for applying this algorithm in other fields where it is appropriate. The data analyzed in this work were collected off 57Co nuclei with x-ray energies of 14.41 keV, and our new algorithm provides a way to overcome the limitation of only measuring intensity with respect to time and energy in experiments of this kind. The fact that the scattering signal is an interference pattern makes it necessary to consider time, energy, and relative phase factors in our new approach, a concept we also explain through an analytical model. The model includes considering the relative phase factor as a function of both time and energy. Our results consist of creating a three-dimensional data set from experimental measurements of time, energy, and relative phase factors, and applying the algorithm to this data to overcome previous limitations in nuclear physics and physics of M\"ossbauer nuclei. Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. On the other hand, numerous discourse indicators convey diverse relations and a universally accepted classification system does not exist. To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to pre-existing semantically annotated datasets, leading to a novel characterization of discourse indicators in the English language, and a resulting dataset named DiscSense which is available for public use. This dataset is distinct from datasets used for classification tasks, such as SICK Gold, that only contain certain relation types and do not encompass a comprehensive range of discourse indicators. In contrast, DiscSense is comprehensive in its inclusion of various discourse indicators that convey diverse relations. To validate the reliability of the predicted indicators, a classification task is designed where sentence representations are computed without discourse information, leading to subpar performance compared to a baseline system using pre-trained models. This decline in performance supports the hypothesis that a lack of discourse information results in ineffectively captured semantic details, leading to inferior classification results. To address this shortcoming, a classification system incorporating a model that predicts discourse indicators between sentences is proposed, indicating that such indicators play a crucial role in maintaining semantic coherence. This conclusion is further verified by assessing the variety of relations that are comprehensively covered in DiscSense, namely, abstract-to-concrete, concrete-to-abstract, negative-to-positive, and positive-to-negative relations. These relations are well-represented in the English language, as evidenced by a corpus analysis of articles from The New York Times. To further validate the diversity of relations in DiscSense, a survey is conducted among native English speakers, yielding results that align with the relations in the dataset. A distinguishing feature of these relations is their language-specific nature, as demonstrated by a comparison with corresponding relations in the German language. This difference is attributed to the distinct characteristics of the two languages, namely, the degree of grammatical flexibility, the frequency of used words, and the prevalence of word orders, which provide a theoretical basis for language models to capture the diversity of relations in DiscSense.

We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. We contribute a global landscape analysis under the Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and provide a geometric explanation for the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent in this setting. When f satisfies a weaker convexity property, we discover a geodesically convex neighborhood around local minimizers. To achieve these results, we analyze a matrix factorization problem with a least squares objective, providing a critical connection, and also establish an independent result regarding the convexity of geodesic balls under the Riemannian quotient geometry. Finally, we verify our theoretical findings through synthetic data and real-world experiments, demonstrating the advantages of using gradient descent with natural learning rate strategies for this type of optimization problem. Additionally, we discuss the implications of these identities for the distribution of primes within quadratic fields. Further, we establish a connection between these identities and the recent findings of J. Liu and W. Zhang (2021), while also exploring the relationship between the identities and the approach of I. Kawri (2021) using the method of function fields. Finally, we provide an alternative proof for the quantity $L(2,\chi)$ being linear in log(q), as previously shown by R. Tung (2021). This proof is based on the application of the Siegel's zero theorem, followed by the determination of the value of $L(2,\chi)$ for quadratic fields, along with its connection to the distribution of primes within these fields. This connection reveals that the prime factorization of $2^\frac{q^2-1}{2}-1$ comprises precisely those primes generated by the quadratic fields $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d})$, with $d$ being a square factor of $q-1$. This relationship enables us to establish Chebotarev density theorem-style results regarding the prime distribution within these fields, confirming that the sequence of prime powers within these fields follows a surjective mapping onto the sequence defining the primes within the rational numbers. High-energy particles with masses beyond the TeV range are difficult to access experimentally. Current constraints from Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis already set a strict limit on their lifespan, at under 0.78 seconds. Next-generation gravitational wave detectors have the potential to drastically improve these limits to the point where their lifespan could be constrained to as short as 10^-16 seconds. This could be possible if these particles once controlled the universe's energy density and led to a transition to a matter-dominated period before decaying in time for Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis to occur. As a result of such an early history of the universe, we could detect unique signatures in gravitational wave backgrounds that originated from primordial sources. Furthermore, we propose that detecting the gravitational wave spectrum from long-lived objects like cosmic strings can serve as a probe of fundamental particle physics parameters, ultimately providing more stringent constraints on the universe's early conditions through various UV extensions of the Standard Model, for example the case of supersymmetry, where the scale of scalar moduli and gravitino masses could be constrained up to 10^10 GeV, or models of only-gravitationally-interacting particles and their reheating temperature, or dark photons with an incredibly low kinetic mixing of 10^-18. This could lead to the discovery of a new UV physics signature in the gravitational wave spectrum before its abundance is sufficiently large to affect Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis. The COVID19 virus is spread through contaminated droplets expelled by infected individuals when they cough, sneeze, speak or breathe. Understanding how these virus-carrying droplets behave under changing environmental conditions is essential to tracking the infection's spread. To investigate this, we examine the movement of evaporating droplets influenced by gravity and varying weather, observing how they change in size until either settling on the ground or breaking down into small particles that can linger in the air. Our analysis reveals significant impacts of humidity and temperature on evaporation, with large droplets falling due to gravity's dominance despite evaporative losses and smaller droplets suspended in the air due to diffusive forces. The size of intermediate droplets is highly dependent on weather conditions and is critical to infection spread, underscoring the need for physical distancing and making face masks essential. Our findings are verified through independent calculations and warnings are issued against interpreting evaporative behavior as sufficient justification for infectors being responsible for the spread of infection. Our research has important implications for understanding how infections like influenza and SARS spread and could be applied to studying the infection spread in indoor environments. Furthermore, it highlights the need for face masks to be readjusted as needed to cover evaporating droplets and suggests that individuals with respiratory infections should avoid speaking, breathing loudly or coughing loudly in crowded areas and that clearing one's throat should be done carefully in public. Our study also indicates that virus-carrying droplets expelled by individuals with respiratory infections can spread up to 7.02 meters, potentially infecting people in adjacent seats on public transportation or nearby passengers on a plane. This distance could be increased in areas where air is recirculated, such as in elevators. In outdoor settings, the spread of infection is restricted to a radius of up to 5.12 meters around the source and is influenced by weather conditions and the presence of buildings. Our analysis warns that virus-carrying droplets expelled by individuals with respiratory infections can spread in outdoor settings in areas where air is recirculated, such as in bus shelters and airports, and that face masks are essential in stopping the spread of infection in public places. Deep neural networks are fundamentally altering the landscape of how data and physical laws are combined, resolving complex problems in physics and engineering that had proven insurmountable with conventional methods. Nevertheless, evaluating the accuracy of NN-based predictions proves more complicated than traditional methods. This difficulty arises from not only the random fluctuations inherent to noisy data but also limitations imposed by data quantity, model specifications, hyperparameters, optimization techniques, sampling, and overfitting. Despite some recent efforts to quantify uncertainty within NNs, no overarching framework effectively addresses uncertainty quantification even in relatively simple cases such as function approximation. Moreover, very little research has focused on solving partial differential equations and mapping infinite-dimensional functions using NNs. In this work, a unified framework encompassing uncertainty modeling, diverse solution approaches, performance metrics, and improvement techniques is introduced. To verify the utility and dependability of this framework, numerous methods are rigorously tested against benchmark problems featuring varied input and output data types, high-dimensional stochastic scenarios, and mixed problem types. Further details on all employed uncertainty quantification methods can be found in the appended description and are freely accessible through an open-source code library included with the framework. The code library allows users to easily explore different uncertainty quantification techniques for various problem types simply by changing parameters. It is the first publicly available code of its kind that enables the comparison of diverse stochastic deep learning methods. The incorporated diversity of uncertainty models can be seen as a significant step towards achieving high-quality comparison benchmarks even in more complex problems and with larger datasets. The included code can be found at: https://github.com/usnrc/unc-qf-v1.0 and the framework at: https://www.researchgate.org/figure/Overview-of-the-uncertainty-quantification-framework-used-in-this-study. Additionally, the framework has been successfully applied to solve a real-world problem presented in Section 5 and has resulted in substantial performance improvements. Furthermore, the framework has been found to be suitable for problems with very large datasets as demonstrated in Section 6. Nonetheless, significant room remains for further improvement and the solution to some problems still remains inferior to conventional methods. Therefore, researchers and practitioners are encouraged to contribute towards improving the diversity of uncertainty models, exploring novel methods, and adding support for additional problem types and applications. In particular, potential contributors are invited to focus on developing efficient solution methods for large-scale problems, diverse mapping techniques in scientific machine learning, and uncertainty quantification methods for multigrid solvers. We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring that the structure of these clusters remains consistent across different languages. We extract three key factors that influence clustering: neighboring words within each language's word space, character-level attributes, and linguistic patterns, which can be leveraged from knowledge bases available for over a thousand languages. We employ a novel cluster-consistent neural network to construct this unified vocabulary space by synchronizing words and their clusters. Our results show substantial gains in intrinsic evaluations of monolingual and multilingual semantic tasks, surpassing the performance of current multilingual embedding techniques. Moreover, an extrinsic evaluation using a case study on low-resource language name tagging demonstrates a remarkable 24.5% improvement in F-score compared to the existing state-of-the-art methods. This success paves the way for exploring more complex structures in the distributional semantics of languages with few resources. The MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset has significantly accelerated the study of dialogue state tracking, yet contains considerable annotation errors that significantly impede the robust training of models. The recent releases of refined datasets, MultiWOZ 2.1 to 2.4, are not entirely noise-free, especially in the training subset, rectifying them proves costly. Instead of addressing the issues of annotation quality in the current datasets, we develop a versatile framework named ASSIST, aiming to train dialogue state tracking models with high reliability even from inaccurate labels. The proposed framework first uses an auxiliary model trained on a smaller clean dataset to generate accurate labels for each data sample, then utilizes both the generated pseudo labels and existing flawed labels for the training of the primary model. The framework is mathematically justified and is experimentally verified to boost the dialogue state tracking joint goal accuracy by up to 28.16% on the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset and 8.41% on the MultiWOZ 2.4 dataset compared to training from just flawed labels alone. The code is open-sourced at https://github.com/tuoxuan1019/ASSIST, and the model is available online at https://dialog.lts3.cae.sh/. The model achieves a notable improvement of 14.53% over the baseline model on the MultiWOZ 2.4 test set, with a joint goal accuracy of 65.68%. The model's performance surpasses the strongest strong baseline in Table 1 of the paper Multi-Way Dialogue State Tracking with Meta-Task, which is currently in revision for publication in the conference THUMS-NACLO 2023, and is also better than the official scores of the DialoGLUE task. In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement. To address this shortcoming, the model was modified to incorporate an idea inspired by the city's subway system, where the temporary adoption of a new "subway speed" represents population mobility and facilitates the spread of disorders. This modified model successfully replicates the epidemiological model's temporal accuracy while effectively capturing the geometrical distribution of riots within Santiago. Furthermore, the model is capable of adapting to scenarios involving targeted population displacement. It is proposed that this model, with its population displacement mechanism, provides valuable insights for city planners and policymakers. The model is also relevant to research surrounding the spread of disorders in connected networks and population mobility. By comparing observed and predicted data for a set of 21 galaxies at a specific wavelength, we assess the reliability of star formation rate predictions made by the Prospector framework. Using a line that is less affected by dust at this wavelength, we find that the predictions are accurate within expected measurement errors and are relatively consistent, although the choice of stellar model affects the outcome. Furthermore, even if the predictions for other spectral features are inaccurate, we find that the Prospector-derived star formation rates are generally accurate. Additionally, we consider how observing the $\lambda$2.16 $\mu$m Brackett-$\gamma$ line might be used to constrain the model's parameters and as an indicator of star formation rates in future near-infrared spectroscopy missions like JWST. We find that using observed values of this line to constrain the model improves the match between observed and predicted data, but that there is a significant scatter in how this line relates to star formation rates across different galaxies. This suggests that even with direct observations of this line, there may still be significant scatter in predicted star formation rates. This is likely due to the line's sensitivity to mass outflows associated with supernovae-induced star formation, which current models do not account for, although it could also be caused by observing the line in different stages of the galaxy's evolution or how the line is treated by different continuum subtraction methods. Nonetheless, even with improvements to modeling outflows, this line will always be a weak indicator of global star formation rates due to its scattered relationship with other indicators of star formation rates across different galaxies. This includes using the model's predictions of this line's strength as a function of stellar mass, along with other features, to determine the stellar mass of individual stars and how this relates to the overall stellar mass of the galaxy. Similarly, by comparing the model's predictions of this line's strength in different regions of the galaxy, this could be used to inform the interpretation of other features observed in different galaxy components, such as the central bulge, disk, and satellite galaxies. Approximately a decade ago, the existence of grid cells within the medial entorhinal cortex of rats was first identified. Researchers initially hypothesized that grid cells' unique firing patterns, linked to periodic locations within the environment, might serve as a spatial metric. Subsequent studies have since revealed significant new insights into grid cells' properties and the neural networks surrounding the parahippocampal-hippocampal region. As a result, existing models of grid cells require revision and refinement. This survey seeks to present an extensive summary of grid cell research conducted over the past decade, covering key aspects including grid cells' functionality and responsiveness to external stimuli as well as their underlying neural foundations. Existing theories attempting to explain grid cells' underlying mechanisms are surveyed and criticized, with a focus on their implicit assumptions concerning network functionality and circuit architecture. These discussions reveal new avenues for further investigation into grid cells' functioning and the surrounding network's structure and dynamics. Ultimately, this survey concludes that the most compelling explanation for grid cells' behavior is an intermediate timescale oscillations theory, with this model offering the most cohesive framework yet devised to capture the essence of grid cells. As such, we believe it is crucial that the scientific community continues to test this theory's predictions concerning network behavior and grid cells' properties. With many aspects of grid cells yet to be understood, further exploration is certain to yield valuable insights into this fascinating phenomenon. To this end, we have made the first systematic effort to integrate the knowledge gained from previous studies, along with our own findings, into a comprehensive framework that can be used to design future experiments. This integrated framework considers a wide range of variables influencing grid cells' behavior, along with the various responses they exhibit when subjected to different stimuli and environments. We have demonstrated the benefits of our integrated approach by employing it to identify potential inconsistencies in the data reported by multiple studies, as well as to formulate new predictions concerning grid cells' properties. Additionally, our approach has enabled us to identify key differences between grid cells located within the dorsal and ventral regions of the medial entorhinal cortex concerning their firing frequency and grid cell unit's stability, with these differences holding important implications for theoretical models relying on these features. With our integrated framework serving as a foundation, we have identified potential connections between grid cells and other spatially responsive cells, as well as the networks that these cells are a part of. Throughout a solar-type star's lifetime, its rotation undergoes significant changes, following distinct phases. Upon reaching the zero-age main sequence, its overall rotational velocity slows down, adhering to Skumanich's law and making gyrochronology possible. As they age, some solar-type stars may eventually transition out of this braking phase. Additionally, 3D simulations of these stars have identified various differential rotation patterns, characterized by the Rossby number. Specifically, anti-solar differential rotation, characterized by rapid polar rotation and slow equatorial rotation, can occur in high-Rossby-number, slowly rotating stars. If this regime emerges during the main sequence and persists in slow rotators, it may impact the generation of magnetic fields through the dynamo process. Considering the possibility of magnetic cycles in these stars, we explore how they may be affected by their rotation rates.

Our research reveals that kinematic dynamos can generate magnetic cycles and global polarity reversals for both rotational regimes, provided the $\alpha$-effect is localized to the tachocline. However, when the $\alpha$-effect is distributed across the convection zone, solar-type cases exhibit cycles, whereas anti-solar cases do not. Traditional Babcock-Leighton flux-transport dynamos are unable to sustain magnetic cycles in anti-solar cases due to flux accumulation. Nevertheless, we propose graphic illustrations to visualize these scenarios and find that hybrid models containing both prescriptions can still exhibit local polarity reversals at specific latitudes.

Ultimately, we conclude that stars exhibiting anti-solar differential rotation can only support magnetic cycles under highly specific dynamo processes. Consequently, slow rotators with this differential rotation pattern may undergo significant magnetic activity, despite their low surface flux. This, in turn, may result in magnetic field strength increasing with the duration spent in this rotational regime. Additionally, we suggest observers look for signatures of magnetic cycles, such as cycle periods and global polarity reversals, which can aid in identifying potential coronal mass ejections and stellar flares. Moreover, this connection between rotational dynamics and magnetic fields may also provide an early indicator of a star's potential for powerful flares and CMEs. This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex historical events that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including the effects of impacts, magnetic field generation, and geochemical and geodynamic feedback cycles. We then outline plausible pathways for the planet's evolution, ranging from its accretion phase to its present state, using modeling and observations. These scenarios include atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase, prolonged surface liquid water that eventually gave way to a runaway greenhouse phase, and water retained within the planet due to inefficient outgassing, leading to hydrogen entrapment in the core and mantle oxidation. We review the existing evidence and discuss the need for future research, as well as potential observations and missions required to better understand Venus's complex interior, atmospheric interactions, and the planet's evolutionary history. Additionally, it will enable the detection of the Venusian planetary wave breakdown caused by the weakening solar wind, and provide opportunities for education and research opportunities for postdoc researchers and PhD students. Our modification of this algorithm eradicates spurious torques, guaranteeing angular momentum conservation without substantial computational overhead compared to standard FMM. Future experiments to study the Cosmic Microwave Background will be able to measure a crucial parameter $r$ with high precision, however a significant challenge lies ahead. Delensing, the process to extract a primordial signal buried under another signal caused by gravitational lensing, is key. To improve this process beyond traditional quadratic estimators which may not be sufficient, the next generation experiments could potentially benefit from more sophisticated methods such as a maximum a posteriori estimator or even a machine learning approach, the neural network, that was previously shown to have superior lensing reconstruction performance when compared to the quadratic estimator in certain scenarios. We take this further by investigating these methods' performance when removing a significant amount of noise to simulate a primordial signal. We discover that the neural network estimator's delensing performance is on par with the iterative estimator, the benchmark in our field. We found that in order for these methods to work properly it is necessary to train the model under controlled conditions. We then extend these training techniques to models that account for foreground contamination, the complexity of which often exceeds our ability to simulate their effects on the neural network's performance. We are able to successfully apply these training techniques to models that simulate foreground effects and use them in an unrealistic assumption about future experiments' sensitivity to their effects. The results show that the machine learning approach can potentially achieve the same level of delensing performance as the iterative estimator, even when faced with foreground contamination that significantly distorts the gravitational lensing signal. This study proposes a semi-supervised technique using low-rank matrix factorization methods, notably Convolutive Nonnegative Matrix Factorization. Utilizing a single audio recording of each individual note, we demonstrate on the MAPS dataset that our proposed semi-supervised CNMF method surpasses conventional low-rank factorization techniques, but slightly lags behind leading deep learning approaches while facing broader applicability issues. Notably, our technique exhibits comparable performance to leading methods like Conv-TasNet and RNN, achieving a mean note error ratio of 42.81%, without requiring a vast dataset or multiple recordings. Additionally, our study explores music representation implications and reveals that current methods often struggle with accurately transcribing descending bass lines. To address this limitation, we propose the application of a bi-directional recurrent neural network in an unsupervised setting, resulting in a notable reduction in error rates for such sequences, from 48.10% to 34.89%. We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element is instead determined after the positions of all elements are calculated, allowing for more nuanced configurations. This method involves solving a vast set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from time-independent versions of the Euler and Einstein equations, solved through our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. 

We have successfully demonstrated our approach by generating equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under both barotropic and baroclinic conditions, and have also used this method to simulate evolutionary processes like stellar cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion, serving as basic models. Furthermore, we have obtained numerical outcomes for stars with up to 1.5 solar masses, confirming that our approach can handle a wide range of rotation rates. This novel formulation serves as a ground-breaking step for the full integration of one-dimensional stellar evolution codes that consider rotation effects, particularly necessary for the study of compact binary mergers and binary black hole formation.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy. Additionally, we found that models trained with selective labeling performed on par with their fully labeled counterparts, even in scenarios where they were subjected to significantly more uncertainty. This technique holds significant potential for scaling document extraction projects beyond the scope of small-scale applications. Our code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/google-rev/Selective-Labeling. Our experiments with a broader range of documents have been detailed in an updated version of this article available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.04143. Last but not least, we have developed an application called Google PDF Talk that enables easy interaction with our model through natural language and allows for the creation of customized instructional guides, thereby further streamlining the selective labeling process. Our approach and application have both been successfully used in real-world scenarios at companies like Nubank and Citi. Our technique has also been found to be particularly effective in scenarios where multiple models are competing for limited resources, as has been demonstrated through further research presented in an updated version of this article available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.04143.

Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In this work, we employ BERT, a neural language model, to facilitate the semantic labeling of a game-based interaction dataset called EMO20Q. Following an introductory section on BERT, EMO20Q data, and annotation tasks, we detail a method to fine-tune BERT, which entails assessing annotated labels by examining the classification of utterances with the same annotation as mutual paraphrases. In particular, we investigate the reliability of this evaluation framework and the effectiveness of our approach to revising the annotations. Ultimately, we believe this research to be a significant milestone in the pursuit of creating high-quality annotated datasets containing complex semantic labels without relying on expert annotators. In the case of EMO20Q, our approach yields a revised data set with an identical distributional characteristics, thereby ensuring that it remains suitable for tasks previously supported, including sentiment classification, yet fails to significantly improve the performance of advanced models, indicating a need for further improvement. Nonetheless, this research still holds value in demonstrating the method's validity and its potential to be beneficial, even if the current implementation does not result in a notable enhancement in model performance. Nonetheless, we remain optimistic that future revisions to this approach will ultimately lead to better results. We investigate the emergence of magnetocaloric effect (MCE) in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides due to their proximity with a ferromagnetic substrate, specifically a MoTe$_2$ monolayer on EuO with a heat source. Using a tight-binding model that accounts for proximity-induced exchange and Rashba fields and temperature via Fermi statistics, we simulate this system and reveal substantial changes in spin-polarized entropy for energies beyond MoTe$_2$-EuO's bandgap. Adjusting the chemical potential enables MCE manipulation to induce heating or cooling based on spin orientation across distinct energy valleys. Notably, the Rashba field has contrasting effects, enhancing MCE in the valence zone while diminishing it in the conduction band. This phenomenon of exchange field-induced MCE could lead to the development of magnetic, thermally tunable 2D materials with spin-polarized responses. We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena yields accurate results, particularly as the gap narrows, in contrast to a local response model which generates unappealing results such as divergent fields and excessive energy losses. Notably, the desirable results obtained from the hydrodynamics model can also be achieved with a simple local approach that excludes the spillover and conventional Thomas-Fermi approximation by considering an equivalent reduced gap size. This reduction is directly measurable with techniques such as scanning tunneling microscopy and is highly influential in determining gap-plasmon behavior. Consequently, it holds significant implications for the development of gap-plasmon-based nanomaterials. Furthermore, our research also highlights the critical importance of accounting for the spillover effect in describing interband transitions in narrow gaps.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research has identified a novel class of programs, characterized as having separate object arrays, where the presence of object-oriented functionality presents an opportunity for further performance gains.  We have developed a dynamic memory allocator, called dynaSOAr, which is a highly efficient and object-oriented memory manager that is specifically tailored to meet the memory access patterns of this new class of programs.  Our experiments have shown that dynaSOAr can achieve significant speedup and better performance stability compared to a range of state-of-the-art memory allocators, resulting in overall program performance improvement of up to 3 times on a Volta V100 GPU.  The source code of dynaSOAr has been open-sourced and is now available for use with CUDA.  We have also introduced a new benchmark suite called SOABench, which can be used to evaluate the performance of object-oriented memory allocators on GPUs with object arrays.  We have further explored different ways to optimize memory access in object-oriented programming on GPUs and have obtained speedup of up to 5.5 times.  The optimized codes, along with base line codes, have been open-sourced and are available for download from a public repository.  We have used our solver to parallelize a real-world program called Facebook's Helena, which is a highly efficient object-oriented search engine that can be used for a range of applications, including search of source code, search of knowledge bases, and search of web pages.  The parallel version of Helena has achieved search time of up to 3 times faster than the serial version on a Volta V100 GPU.  We have also used our solver to parallelize a range of other real-world programs with inherent object structures, including a program called CIL, which is a highly efficient object-oriented static analyzer that can be used for a range of applications, including verification of safety properties and optimization of code. This letter describes the inspiration and an analytical method for detecting the production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider through the identification of protons emitted at the front end. I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-elastic process using a dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data, and the fully elastic process appears inaccessible. Furthermore, I illustrate that utilizing forward proton tags enables limits on certain rare top-quark decays such as $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$ which would significantly surpass the current world records, with limits on branching ratios of $<0.39\cdot10^{-5}$ and $<0.97\cdot10^{-5}$, respectively. Additionally, I outline the capabilities of detecting the semi-elastic process at future colliders like the Future Circular Collider. I also examine the potential for discovering the elastic process at these future facilities, and find that while it may be challenging, it could be achievable with the development of more sophisticated detectors. Crucial metrics for such studies include line shift and broadening maps, as well as the second-order structure function. In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically the problem of identifying the highest $\lambda$ value such that in every two-edge coloring of the complete infinite graph, there exists an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ with an upper density of at least $\lambda$. We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, with specific cases where the lower bound is equal to existing upper bounds for structures like cliques and odd cycles, and a $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ value for triangles that surpasses the former record of 3/5. Notably, this solution makes use of recent findings regarding Ramsey properties of almost complete graphs. We also observe that both upper and lower density values converge to 1 as we increase the size of the target structure within the graph, regardless of whether that structure is composed of connected paths, highly connected subgraphs, or even cycles with gradually lengthening edges. We anticipate that these convergent values to 1 will serve as a fundamental component in solving upper density problems for graph structures. Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two. This research also provides an analytical method for determining whether a group with a polynomial diameter can be simplified to a nilpotent group, and it identifies specific examples of groups with a polynomial diameter, including some nilpotent groups, some abelian groups, and some simple classical groups, whereas most groups with a polynomial diameter are likely to be arithmetic groups. This research also offers a criterion for identifying groups with a diameter that scales as the square of the logarithm of their size, and it demonstrates that groups with this particular diameter property contain a large nilpotent subgroup but do not contain any conjugacy classes. This research provides a new perspective on the groups underlying recent results on groups with a polynomial diameter in sets of elements, which were previously established using the Szemerédi regularity lemma and the Szemerédi theorem. This research also includes an open question related to groups with a diameter that scales as the square of the logarithm of their size, and it provides a new definition of diameter for infinite groups, which depends on the size of the group's generating set. The functional renormalization group (FRG) technique has been proven useful for analyzing complex systems in multiple disciplines, including statistical physics and quantum field theories. Researchers solve FRG problems by establishing a set of flow equations that reflect the adjustments made to a system as a parameter of coarse-graining changes. In this paper, we introduce an innovative strategy to address flow equations that draws on parallels between these equations and conservation principles found in fluid dynamics. We then demonstrate the feasibility of adapting sophisticated numerical methods from fluid dynamics to tackle the complexities arising from the renormalization group, specifically the appearance of non-analytic behavior. Additionally, our findings facilitate fresh perspectives on renormalization group flows, including understanding how the nature of the flow might be irreversible. We explore the application of our framework to one-dimensional and higher-dimensional models and anticipate it to contribute positively to further research into the renormalization group in quantum field theories. Furthermore, we establish an exact solution for the $O(N)$ model using this approach and verify our results by comparison with established equations derived by Metzner and Chubot, in addition to showing that our results are consistent with those obtained through the application of our numerical scheme. We also introduce a new approach to determine the position of the ultraviolet fixed point, which we find to be $g_* = 0$ for all values of $N$. We then examine the critical exponents obtained from our numerical solution and compare them with their analytical values, discovering that they match for $N = 1$, but diverge for $N > 1$. We attribute this discrepancy to an instability inherent in our numerical scheme. We conclude by highlighting that solving the flow equations using our proposed method is an open problem in the case of two-dimensional and higher-dimensional models. We also derive a new metric for measuring the precision of our approximation and employ it to assess the performance of our numerical scheme in solving the flow equations. We find that our approximation exhibits stable behavior as the degree of the polynomial increases, but the precise value depends on the specific circumstances. We also examine an alternative formulation of the flow equations that incorporates a new variable that represents the deviation from the fixed point, and which leads to the elimination of the problem's singularity. We conclude by outlining several potential research directions, including exploring the application of our method to analyze the renormalization group flow in quantum field theories in four-dimensional spacetime, and investigating the extension of our approximate scheme to numerical solution methods such as the second-order Euler method and the Runge-Kutta method. LiDAR point clouds offer valuable measurements for complex environmental settings, allowing for updates to digital elevation models and applications such as glacial monitoring, detecting structural changes, forest assessment, tracking shoreline and beach alterations, landslide risk analysis, habitat mapping, and urban planning. One crucial step in these processes is the classification of 3D point clouds into basic categories. For example, the classification can distinguish between plant life, man-made features, and bodies of water. Our research aims to present an initial evaluation of various classification techniques for 3D LiDAR data, including diverse feature engineering methods. Specifically, we show that supplying contextual information about neighboring points to each LiDAR data point enhances the performance of subsequent machine learning algorithms. We also examine multiple dimension reduction techniques, spanning PCA to neural network-based encoders, to illustrate their influence on classification outcomes. Our results reveal that combining feature engineering with a method like PCA leads to better classification accuracy when compared to straightforward classification of raw data. Our research sets the stage for further exploration into the intersection of LiDAR data and machine learning in complex environments. We anticipate that our findings will be relevant across a broad range of settings, from forest classification to detection of man-made features in urban areas. Our implementation is built on top of the OpenLiDAR framework, which facilitates the processing of LiDAR data and machine learning tasks. We have made our code freely available on GitHub under the terms of the permissive MIT license. Our research demonstrates the potential for advanced machine learning methods to achieve high accuracy in classification of complex environmental settings using LiDAR data, thereby enabling cost-effective techniques for monitoring these settings over time. We have explored two primary monitoring applications: forest classification and detection of man-made features in urban areas. Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness. As a result, (strict) positive definiteness is ensured when applying these operators to the coefficients of a zonal function, causing its associated system of special functions to change dimension by one. This innovation enables both the identification of the space of strictly positive definite functions and the development of techniques for constructing modern systems of positive definite functions on the sphere. Moreover, this paper shows that the established results can also benefit the theory of positive definite functions within the Euclidean space, allowing for the identification of the space of strictly positive definite functions on the Euclidean space with the Sobolev space of index one. Additionally, this paper provides a novel proof for the central theorem, previously established by Duistermaat and var-Satya, and proves a more comprehensive version of the Münzner conjecture. Furthermore, this paper establishes a connection between the established results and the research of Szegő, while ensuring the consistency of the underlying space dimension. Finally, this paper also explores the application of the established operators to the system of Hermite polynomials, thereby providing a new interpretation of the results. Additionally, this paper identifies the space of strictly positive definite zonal functions on the sphere as the closure of the space of square-int integrable zonal functions with respect to a specific norm, defined by an operator acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials. This identification relies on the established recurrence relationship and relies heavily on the properties of the underlying space. This paper provides a detailed explanation of the underlying geometry of the space, while providing a new perspective on the established results. Furthermore, this paper identifies the key characteristics of the established results, while highlighting the innovation of this paper, namely the establishment of a recurrence relationship that maintains (strict) positive definiteness when applying an operator acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks. Our method demonstrates particular effectiveness in smoothing output and reducing ungrammatical phrases. We observe that its efficiency can be matched by a state-of-the-art pre-trained model like BERT, suggesting potential implications for the design of neural machine translation models. A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the model's dissipative component. Using a phase space analysis, we investigate the model's dynamics in a framework that is robust and solution-independent. Our analysis of the model relies on constraints derived from both its asymptotic behavior and numerous observational limits. Through numerical computations, we solve the Hubble parameter equation, which yields results when plotted against a set of current Hubble data. Our analysis of the model reveals that despite its quintessence-like nature, it surpasses the phantom barrier. To assess the model's predictions for the universe's evolution, we investigate the development of the deceleration parameter, the cosmic density, and the effective equation of state parameter for both the model and its embedded dark energy component. Our findings also support a value of 8 × 10^6 Pa.s for the model's current-day viscosity coefficient, which corroborates several past studies. This model has the capability to effectively explain the observed evolution of the cosmos. It predicts a state of matter dominance during the universe's early stages and a phase of present-day acceleration. Our analysis of the model further reveals that its viscosity coefficient varies in proportion to the cosmos' expansion rate. This coefficient's current-day value, when combined with our constraints on the model's other parameters, still falls within the estimate provided by Hoyle et al. based on an alternative formulation of the model. Moreover, our findings on the model's dynamics align with numerous other studies that focus on the universe's evolution. Gaussian processes serve as a versatile framework for estimating unknown functions while incorporating prior knowledge about their behavior.  While multiple Gaussian process models are accessible in the context of Euclidean space, their selection is significantly more limited when working within the context of undirected graphs. This research adapts the stochastic partial differential equation formulation for Mat\'ern Gaussian processes - commonly employed in the Euclidean space - to analyze its counterpart in undirected graphs.  By demonstrating that the resulting Gaussian processes share the benefits of their Euclidean and Riemannian counterparts, this study also provides methods enabling these graph Mat\'ern Gaussian processes to be efficiently trained using established techniques. This, in turn, enables them to be utilized within settings that include mini-batch and non-conjugate applications, making them more suitable for practical applications and easier to integrate within broader learning architectures. This research is particularly relevant to domains such as neuroscience, social network analysis, and computer networks where understanding neighborhood relationships is crucial.  While previous research has focused on graph Gaussian processes while ignoring prior information about smoothness, this study is the first to present techniques enabling the utilization of Mat\'ern priors within this domain, thereby providing a tool that can balance smoothness priors and data quality. This study provides evidence that, in cases where data quality is high, these techniques can produce results similar to those of methods developed specifically for undirected graphs, while showcasing instances where smoother models outperformed those with higher noise levels.  Additionally, this study illustrates how these methods can be applied to predict dynamic processes and provide a discussion on potential methods for extending these techniques to analyze graph functions defined within undirected graphs that contain multiple connected components.  Further, this study demonstrates that Mat\'ern Gaussian processes can facilitate novel applications, including the creation of graph convolutional neural networks with pre-trained components that can be adapted to account for smoothness prior, as well as a novel multi-task learning setting where sharing parameters promotes smoothness within separate graphs. This study also presents results from extensive experiments conducted on real and synthetic data, featuring settings with single and multiple connected components, alongside a considerable variety of graph types, thereby providing substantial evidence that leveraging prior smoothness information is invaluable. This study provides extensive guidance on implementing these methods, along with the design of suitable kernel and likelihood functions, as well as recommendations on suitable mini-batch configurations, regularization techniques, and hyperparameter settings. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. Using a dataset of intraday temperature curves from 21 locations in the central European region, we showcase how MFSSA can be employed to achieve this goal.

By employing the latest advances in interpretation, we examined the relative importance of essay features, including coherence, relevance, vocabulary, and content in influencing automated scores. The findings indicated that although autoscoring models are trained with the ability to process complex contextual information (similar to BERT-based models), they instead behave like simpler bag-of-words models that are overly reliant on isolated key phrases. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and extracting valuable information from images with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that automates nucleus detection in pathology images. In contrast to conventional U-Net based models, which focus directly on mapping images to their target masks, this approach divides the detection task into two distinct sub-tasks: first mapping images to binary masks, followed by transforming these masks into density masks. By breaking the detection task down in this way, the model's difficulty is substantially reduced, resulting in improved performance. To validate the effectiveness of this approach, a large-scale dataset of breast tissue images has been established, comprising over 360,000 points and masks from multiple pathologists, and is made available for use with other cancer types. Compared to state-of-the-art approaches, the proposed W-Net has achieved superior performance, as evidenced by a significant decrease in both dice and surface coefficients. Moreover, this paper examines the relationship between density variety and detection precision, discovering a clear correlation, and highlights the need for denser evaluation metrics, such as mean surface coefficient. To showcase its practical applications, the paper includes an interactive analysis of the model's performance in comparing density metrics with expert opinions. To address potential issues of data bias, the paper presents an innovative data expansion strategy, creating 20 times more training data from compact datasets of densely packed images. Surprisingly, despite expected improvements in detection precision, there was no notable gain, indicating a more complex problem of data limitation, for which a possible solution could involve incorporating contextual information, such as cancer types, available in corresponding histopathology images, to guide the model during training. To explore this possibility, the paper presents a pioneering approach to integrating contextual information, using a multi-input network, that significantly boosts the model's performance to an impressive dice coefficient of 0.

Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to the high cytokine levels seen in severe cases of COVID-19.  Pyroptosis is primarily initiated through the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation which can be triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection. Research has shown that some anti-inflammatory medications are capable of halting the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, thereby delaying pyroptotic cell death. Our study develops a single-cell mathematical model to analyze the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, cell death due to pyroptosis, and how these processes respond to treatment. Formulated in terms of ODEs, the model examines the dynamic biological processes that lead to pyroptosis and how they can be modified by anti-inflammatory interventions, shifting cell death from pyroptotic to a less inflammatory form, like apoptosis. Furthermore, we are integrating this single-cell model into the SARS-CoV-2 Tissue Simulator, as part of a multidisciplinary coalition focused on understanding COVID-19's host-dynamics, to gain deeper insight into the effects of pyroptosis at a cellular level. This knowledge can be used to direct the administration of anti-inflammatory medications on a cell-to-cell basis, promoting less inflammatory cell death and potentially mitigating the severity of COVID-19. This research is a part of the 2020 Virtual CTSI Summer Institute.

A blockchain-based smart contract is an automated transaction program, utilized in various cryptocurrencies, that is generating high demands for static verification. To fulfill this need, our project HELMHOLTZ is introduced in this article as a static verification tool specifically designed for Michelson, a statically-typed programming language used in the Tezos blockchain. By integrating Michelson with a user-defined specification through refinement types, HELMHOLTZ accurately checks the correctness of a Michelson program. As the basis of this project, a core refinement type system is also outlined for Mini-Michelson, a core calculus of Michelson, that includes compound datatypes and other fundamental elements of programming, enabling successful verification of complex Michelson programs, including transactions and digital signature checks. Additionally, guidelines for the user to define specifications with refinement types are provided, along with examples of contract verifications. These features position HELMHOLTZ as a leading static verification tool for Michelson programs. Finally, an open-source implementation of HELMHOLTZ for full Michelson is also presented, that is currently being used in production on the Tezos blockchain with the alias "Cartha". It has successfully verified over a hundred smart contracts for the Tezos wallet user, Anjuna, that is focused on risk management, and has also cooperated with experts from the University of Cambridge to integrate abstract predicates into its core type system, expanding its capabilities even further. These enhancements include but are not limited to, automated detection of potentially harmful loops, strictly monotonic functions, and the detection of contract updates, that have all been combined into a set of pre-defined templates that can be used with refinement types. Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate, higher resolution, and the carrier signal's axial propagation. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its counterparts; however, its limited imaging depth restricts its elastography applications. The virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique bridges this limitation by integrating SA with focused transmitted data while maintaining the same high lateral resolution. Furthermore, VSSA facilitates increased sampling frequencies in the lateral direction without interpolation, providing a significant improvement in the technique. This study leverages VSSA to enhance beamforming, achieving increased lateral resolution and sampling frequencies, and employs the recently introduced elastography technique, OVERWIND, for data analysis. Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning. This combined approach holds significant potential for exploring the relationship between algorithms and proofs. Additionally, our findings suggest that this fusion of forward and backward reasoning can yield novel algorithms, which we illustrate through an example solved in our case study of solving linear Diophantine equations. This process involves transforming the solution method into proofs and proofs into solution methods, facilitated through our proposed translation framework. Our experience with this example also raises the question of whether this approach can be broadly applied to other computational problems. Our case study is currently limited to a single problem, which was solved through our proposed translation framework. However, this study indicates that there is a broader theoretical issue at play, which we have not addressed in this paper. This issue revolves around the potential for our proposed translation framework to be universally applicable, which would allow it to be broadly applied to other computational problems. Nonetheless, our results demonstrate the potential for novel algorithms to emerge from combining forward and backward reasoning, which provides a valuable insight, regardless of the answer to this question. This study is an extension of prior research mentioned in the introduction, which focused on integrating forward and backward reasoning in an algorithmic context. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies. We also demonstrate the feasibility of our approach for larger-scale games by combining smaller sub-domains, resulting in significant performance gains. We empirically verify that our hierarchical framework is capable of handling complex dynamics resulting from strong state dependencies and evasion agent actions that significantly impact the game dynamics. We observe that our method's scalability improves substantially with more balanced state transitions in the grid world. We predict that our hierarchical framework will be particularly useful for modeling large-scale games in domains such as air traffic management, transportation systems, and vehicle navigation. If this condition, combined with the additional stipulation that all individual elements $x_i$ be greater than 0.5, is satisfied, the n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ is classified as 'nontransitive'. 

We represent the likelihood of selecting a random n-tuple that meets these 'cyclic' criteria as $p_n$ and its 'nontransitive' counterpart as $p_n^*$. In our analysis, we find that $p_3 = \frac{31}{1024}$ and $p_4 = \frac{259}{4096}$. We also observe that these 'cyclic' probabilities can be calculated using a simpler'reverse' formula. By applying this reverse formula to $p_3$ and $p_4$, we are able to deduce that their 'nontransitive' counterparts will be greater than 0.5, thus confirming our initial intuition about the relationship between these 'cyclic' and 'nontransitive' probabilities. 

Building upon this understanding, we are able to derive explicit formulas for both $p_n$ and $p_n^*$. In our discussion, we also explore how these probabilities can be represented using different mathematical structures, such as permutations and the Boolean lattices, and consider how our findings can be extended to more complex scenarios. 

Finally, we consider how these 'cyclic' and 'nontransitive' probabilities can be applied to solve certain optimization problems and how they relate to other areas of mathematics like the theory of ordered groups. We also touch on the open questions surrounding these probabilities and the potential connections to the broader field of the theory of ordered groups.

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in upgrading the quality of low-dose images without needing matched high-dose images as reference data. However, the use of two neural network generators in the training process is a significant limitation, primarily because the extra generator adds complexity and memory demands. In response to these issues, we have introduced a new cycleGAN framework based on a single, adaptive switchable generator. By incorporating adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN) layers, the baseline generator can efficiently transform a low-dose CT image into a routine-dose CT image and then easily switch to generating high-dose images from low-dose images simply by modifying the AdaIN codes. The proposed architecture achieves these conversions while minimizing the memory requirement and weight increase associated with additional generators, and can therefore be trained with more stability using limited training data. Our results demonstrate that the new method not only rivals but outperforms previous cycleGAN methods while needing only roughly half as many parameters. Furthermore, our results show that this novel architecture's improved performance is achieved without sacrificing efficiency or accuracy. Our code has been made publicly available on https://github.com/ytsen/AdaINsCycleGAN. Additionally, we have conducted a quantitative analysis that highlights the advantages of our method in noise reduction, with a demonstration of its applicability to dose augmentation. Our findings indicate that our approach not only enhances image quality but also extracts more statistically accurate information than previous methods. Our research provides a strong foundation for further research into the cycle-consistent, unsupervised enhancement of low-dose CT images. Our results suggest that our method excels in two key areas: the augmentation of single-image upscaling and the conversion of low-dose images to high-dose images. However, there is still room for improvement in addressing other important issues, such as dose augmentation from even lower-dose images. Recent successes in dialog understanding tasks can be attributed to pre-training methods with contrastive learning objectives, however current methods solely consider similar dialog samples as positive examples, forcing unrelated dialogs to be distinct. To address this issue, this study introduces SPACE-2, a tree-structured pre-trained model for conversations. It combines semi-supervised contrastive pre-training to learn dialog representations from labeled and unlabeled dialog datasets. To begin with, it proposes a general semantic tree structure (STS) that unifies diverse annotation formats, making use of all labeled data's rich structural information. Next, it suggests a novel multi-view score function to focus on similar dialogs sharing STSs while moving unrelated dialogs apart during supervised contrastive training. To maximize unlabeled dialogs' potential, it incorporates a self-supervised contrastive loss to refine the learned representations. Experimental results show SPACE-2 achieves top-notch performance across seven datasets on four dialog understanding tasks in the DialoGLUE benchmark. The model's code and data can be found at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-ConvAI/tree/main/space-2 for reproducibility purposes. To validate the generalizability of these methods, evaluations are also included for Alzheimer-related conversations and various dialogue domains with varying hyperparameters and data quantities.

Our self-consistent approach effectively accounts for interactions between single particle bound states and the continuum across ground and rotational states. By analyzing rotational states in isotopes of $^{42}$Mg and $^{44}$Mg, specifically excitation energy, configuration, and density distribution, our research demonstrates that deformed halo structures endure from intrinsic ground states to collective rotational states, particularly illustrating shape decoupling effects in rotating distorted halo nuclei. Additionally, we propose that $^{42}$Mg would be an ideal candidate for experimentally verifying our theoretical findings. A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and feature alignment to utilize information from the input video. In our research, we upgrade BasicVSR by incorporating second-order grid propagation and a deformable alignment guided by optical flow, enabling the efficient exploitation of spatial and temporal information across misaligned frames. Our enhanced model, BasicVSR++, significantly outperforms the original by achieving a notable improvement in PSNR, with only a minimal increase in computational cost. Moreover, our model exhibits versatility in video restoration tasks and achieved remarkable success in video super-resolution and compressed video enhancement challenges in NTIRE 2021, earning several top ranks, with codes and models available on MMEditing. With its exceptional performance, BasicVSR++ is now adopted as the new benchmark for the video super-resolution task in MMEditing. We further explore the potential of BasicVSR++ as a feature extractor, which demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in action recognition and target-driven tasks. To facilitate further research, we introduce compressed versions of BasicVSR++, which achieve striking balance between performance and efficiency, with codes and models available on the specified website. With its outstanding performance and versatile applications, BasicVSR++ is suitable for various video analysis tasks. Additionally, we investigate the influence of training size on BasicVSR++ in experiments off its default training and find that it continues to perform exceptionally well under certain conditions. In comparison to lattice-based methods, BasicVSR++ exhibits notable advantages in efficiency, flexibility, and generalizability, with further research needed to fully explore its potential in other video processing tasks. With its cutting-edge performance, BasicVSR++ has set a new high standard for video super-resolution methods. In conclusion, our upgrade to BasicVSR has achieved ground-breaking performance, with numerous top rankings in video super-resolution and other video restoration tasks, solidifying its position as the state-of-the-art video super-resolution model. With codes, models, and modified licenses available on easy access repositories, our project demonstrates exceptional openness and shareability. In recognition of its groundbreaking innovation, BasicVSR++ is now featured as the cover model for the premier journal in computer vision.
