In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Our results consistently demonstrate the advantages of task-specific
learning in our model-based multi-task reinforcement learning framework. We also
show that this catastrophe, which we term "catastrophic interference" through
shared dynamics, is exacerbated when the same actions are used for every task.
Finally, we highlight that our approach can be seen as a form of dynamic
abstraction, where each task has its own distinct underlying representation. We
conclude by exploring potential connections to topics such as the local universality
hypothesis and low-dimensional task representations. Our code is available at https://github.com/vayda/model-based-multi-task. We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques. A combination of these results is achieved through the application of the Diagonal Lemma to the saturation property of a consistent theory, resulting in a sentence that is not only undecidable but also incompatible with certain closed normal formulas. Notably, this undecidable property holds for any formal system capable of arithmetic, and we demonstrate that the inherent property of such systems - expressibility - is essentially equivalent to the capacity for implementing the Diagonal Lemma. Consequently, this union of the above mentioned theorems and the extension of Godel's first incompleteness theorem by Rosser is seen as a cornerstone of the philosophy of mathematical logic known as the Godel-Carnap theorem. Finally, we explore how this combination of the above mentioned theorems may be applied to provide undecidable sentences in a way that is independent of the model, and we show that this is a fundamental limitation on any system of definition within such systems. Additionally, we discuss the extension of these results to systems of higher order and the potential applications to the problem of the existence of models. Finally, we provide an informal discussion of the history behind the development of these theorems, and we speculate on the potential extensions of these results to other areas of mathematics. We also provide a more detailed discussion on the application of the Diagonal Lemma to the saturation property of a consistent theory, and we show that this combination of the above mentioned theorems and the extension of Godel's first incompleteness theorem by Rosser is a fundamental consequence of the existence of the function that maps the theorems of a system to their corresponding undecidable counterparts. Furthermore, we show that this function is inherently linked to the capacity for the expression of the property of saturation, and that this property is the underlying basis for the implementation of the Diagonal Lemma. This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space. Furthermore, our investigation expands to consider the Laplace operator in R^n+1, enabling us to draw connections to well-known results, including the original three balls theorem. Our approach builds upon the use of special series and orthogonal projection operators, which facilitate treatment of functions u through the application of Fourier analysis. Our main contribution is the derivation of a quantity bound, expressed in terms of the sum of the lengths of several circular arcs, which provides a measure of the geometric properties of u's zeros. This geometric interpretation holds significant value in potential theory, particularly for harmonic functions and monogenic functions. Our results also establish connections to the maximum principles and the representation of functions u via integral transforms. In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using image information is an essential task that has been extensively researched. We investigated using artificial intelligence-based methods for this purpose by leveraging only a single color image, utilizing exclusively simulated data to train the models. Our experiments involved comparing three approaches: one method predicting the camera's positioning directly from the image, another using 2D keypoints and subsequent PnP calculations, and a third method using estimated depth and segmentation maps to calculate the camera's position through iterative closest point alignment. When evaluating the methods against each other and established traditional approaches, we found an unexpected result in which direct prediction outperformed other strategies. Further analysis into these findings involved assessing the methods' performance under various noise levels. We found that artificial intelligence-based methods for eye-in-hand camera calibration using a single image demonstrate robustness in the face of increasing noise, with direct prediction exhibiting a notable increase in accuracy. These findings have significant implications for the use of artificial intelligence in robotics, suggesting that simple, direct approaches may often outperform more complex, hybrid strategies. Additionally, they highlight the need for rigorous testing and validation when evaluating the performance of novel algorithms against established benchmarks. In the context of eye-in-hand camera calibration, direct prediction methods outperform other strategies, with potential applications including the integration of computer vision and machine learning for robotics demos and the importance of considering the source of data used for benchmarking. Furthermore, artificial intelligence-based methods for this problem have significant potential for improvement, with potential solutions involving the exploration of self-supervised pretraining and the development of custom benchmark suites.

The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. This particular screen is also contributing to irregular scintillation patterns observed during certain Earth-pulsar-sun alignment conditions, known as "Earth effect". This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate. Conventional two-stage approaches using speech recognition and machine translation have inherent flaws, including the amplification of inaccuracies. By contrast, single-system approaches reduce errors but are complicated to deploy due to limited data availability. We delve into zero-shot translation, which allows for language pairs that weren't encountered during training, thereby circumventing the need for speech-to-text data. While proven for multilingual translation, zero-shot translation's feasibility for speech-to-text remains unexplored. We aim to build zero-shot speech-to-text models that learn speech recognition and machine translation but can execute the speech-to-text task. However, speech and text representations significantly differ, complicating the learning of these two tasks simultaneously. Our models tend to produce incorrect outputs during zero-shot speech-to-text tasks. We mitigate this issue by introducing supplementary data and a novel loss function, which minimizes text-audio disparities. Our results indicate that these approaches hold promise for zero-shot speech-to-text. Notably, they prove particularly useful in low-data settings, achieving improvements of up to +11.8 BLEU points over direct speech-to-text models and +3.9 BLEU points over models fine-tuned from pre-trained speech recognition models. These gains extend to additional language pairs with only speech-to-text data. Our models also excel in bilingual settings, achieving scores comparable to those obtained with models trained on vast audio datasets. The resulting parameters are expressed in terms of interaction strength, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting within relevant 4d and 5d transition metal oxide ranges. Through various limits, our perturbative and numerical results converge, highlighting that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, with up to 20% orbital occupation outside nominal ranges. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada. Additionally, our team created an interactive web application based on our disease-aware image editing model, which is available at www.cxedit.org. Leveraging this approach, we discovered various unexpected situations that could impact the performance of GAN-based medical applications. Furthermore, our results highlight the complexity of replicating subtle abnormalities and lung density using style-based generative models. In the case of cardiac enlargement, our findings showed that transferring this condition from one X-ray to another is highly dependent on the orientation of the heart in the image plane. Our work lays the groundwork for further exploration of GAN-based techniques in medicine, and our code is available for public access on the GitHub platform. Nonetheless, numerous issues with data quality remain unresolved, which were outlined by our research team. Additionally, our results were evaluated through a comprehensive set of experiments, which included both automatic evaluations and subjective assessments from multiple medical specialists, including radiologists. advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies. The application is designed to be
user-friendly and simple applications can be accomplished with minimal
configuration, while more intricate projects require little to no DaVis
knowledge. ViDaExpert is comprised of script-based algorithms that are freely
available on the DaVis website, permitting users to explore the application
functions via its built-in help feature and online documentation. Moreover,
ViDaExpert is built on top of DaVis, allowing it to utilize DaVis's 3D engine,
thereby providing a more comprehensive data analysis framework. ViDaExpert is
intended for users operating in fields like flow cytometry, where there is a
need for both in-depth data analysis and high-quality visualization, along with
text-based result documentation. ViDaExpert is best suited for users of

capable of handling up to 100,000 object features, whereas regular DaVis is

Evaluating Newtonian potentials over complex two-dimensional regions efficiently is crucial for solving Poisson's equation and volume integral equations numerically. For domains with irregular boundaries, using a grid without a set pattern to calculate the potential by splitting it into small areas becomes impractical due to high computational costs. In this paper, we propose an efficient and straightforward high-order method for calculating Newtonian potentials based on Green's identity, which simplifies the complex volume integration into boundary integrals. These boundary integrals can then be computed quickly using the Helsing-Ojala method. Our new method makes expensive computations of near field interactions on an unstructured grid comparable to the time it takes for far field interactions. An essential component of our method involves using a high-order approximation to represent a function over a grid cell, which traditionally poses an ill-conditioned problem due to solving a system of equations involving Vandermonde matrices. Notably, smooth functions and a backward-stable solver for linear systems allow this approximation to be accurate over a grid cell when done correctly. In this paper, we provide a precise proof of this concept. We demonstrate our algorithm's effectiveness through several numerical experiments. In one scenario, we use it to solve an exterior problem for a volume integral equation that arises from the method of fundamental solutions. The results show our algorithm can handle a large number of grid cells and accurately computes the solution with a high degree of precision. Furthermore, we find that using a smaller number of higher-order grid cells yields a more efficient result, which we confirm can be achieved with our method. In addition to its potential as a standalone method, we believe our research could also lead to an optimization of more recent algorithms that use grid cell approximations. In particular, we recently developed an optimized version of an algorithm from Natarajan (Numerische Mathematik, 2020), and we present the results of that optimization here. In some cases, with our method, we were able to achieve an order of magnitude improvement in computational time. In our experiments, we used double precision arithmetic with a tolerance of $10^{-12}$ to solve equations that were well-conditioned at that precision. We hope this optimized version could lead to further exploration of high-order methods for the near field in planar domains.
